Coffee is one of the most popular beverages globally. Whether you drink coffee out of a habit, love its taste, or the magical fragrance of fresh brew, coffee continuously hits the market. However, the increasing trend towards caffeinated drinks can harm many people as overindulgence in anything is not friendly. Therefore, one must know the limitation to ensure a healthy intake. However, caffeine has impressive perks. And this article will help you understand how coffee affects your body and how it benefits you.
What is coffee?
Coffee is a popular beverage from coffee beans with hot water or milk. It is commonly drunk to increase mental alertness, but it has to do more with your body. Since coffee provides no nutritional value, people, especially in the United States, rely on a cup of coffee in the morning or get an afternoon slump.
What is caffeine?
Caffeine is a natural chemical that has a stimulant effect on your brain and nervous system. Therefore, it speeds up messages between the brain and body. This drug is profoundly found in leaves, seeds, and fruits.
Coffee and tea are the top choices. However, coffee is the most popular caffeinated drink available globally. It controls appetite, improves metabolism, helps weight loss, and increases physical and brain performance. However, coffee has a significant effect on the brain; it works as a stimulant for the brain to block the results of the neurotransmitter adenosine.
Read on to learn the potential health effects and profound benefits of coffee.
Effects of coffee on your body
Effects of coffee on the central nervous system
Caffeine is a stimulant for the central nervous system; alertness is the most noticeable effect on your brain. As a result, you feel less tired and more awake. Therefore, it is an ingredient in various medications, most commonly to treat headaches, migraines, and drowsiness. Moreover, researchers have shown that people who consume coffee regularly are likely to become less susceptible to Alzheimer's and dementia. In addition, it decreases suicidal risks by enhancing mood.
Caffeine has a stimulating effect that causes alertness. However, overconsumption of coffee causes side effects, it over-simulates your brain and causes confusion and headache, or you may feel irritability.
Effects of coffee on the digestive system
The amount of acid rises in your stomach when you drink coffee, resulting in an upset stomach or heartburn. In addition, too much indulgence in caffeine cause stomach issues, such as ulcer or acid reflux, because your body can't store extra caffeine; instead, it gets processed in the liver and removed with urine. Consequently, you may feel an increase in urination. Furthermore, nausea and vomiting are common symptoms of over-drinking coffee.
Effects of coffee on the circulatory and respiratory system
Coffee gets absorbed from the stomach, and within a few hours, it reaches your bloodstream. Caffeine causes rapid heartbeats and can increase blood pressure which can be a consequence of adrenaline increase or a temporary blockage of hormones that widens arteries naturally. Moreover, if you have a pre-existing cardiorespiratory problem, then coffee can cause long terms effects. Overdose of caffeine cause irregular heartbeat and breathing issues. In most severe cases, overconsumption can cause deaths.
Effects of coffee on the reproductive system
Since caffeine enters the bloodstream and travels through the placenta, during pregnancy, when a woman drinks coffee or any caffeinated food excessively, that may cause miscarriage; as caffeine acts as a stimulant, it affects the fetus's metabolism and heart rate. Moreover, caffeine creates fertility issues: it can affect estrogen production, so if you want to get pregnant, you should limit your coffee intake.
Effects of coffee on skeletal and muscular systems
Coffee prevents calcium absorption in your bones and aids in developing risks for osteoporosis. As a consequence, your bones may easily break with growing age. A high amount of caffeine is harmful to your overall body.
Benefits of Coffee
Coffee has divine benefits for your life, and the following are a few of its perks.
Promotes weight loss
Caffeine aids in weight loss by suppressing your appetite and increasing metabolism. When you consume coffee, it creates a feeling of fullness and decreases the desire to eat food. Moreover, it stimulates the thermogenesis process; the body generates energy and heat to digest food. Coffee increases your body's ability to break down fat in various calls and burn fat through lipolysis. Furthermore, the nervous system helps you reduce tiredness by improving focus and energy. Caffeine boosts your performance by ensuring you have enough circulation of adrenaline that is responsible for the "fight and flight" response in your body. In addition, it enhances muscle performance, and caffeine increases thermogenesis. More heat production may help you burn more calories.
Coffee increases alertness and helps you improve mental health, fastening reasoning, and memory. However, overconsumption of caffeine leads to health problems. Caffeine is known as a natural stimulant. It blocks the function of adenosine, a hormone that makes you sleepy. As a result, you feel alert and more energetic. Therefore, people have coffee to stay awake. Moreover, the melatonin hormone get decreases when caffeine is consumed.
Improve exercise and athletic performance
Caffeine is a great go-to supplement for a lot of sportspersons. It improves physical efficiency, strength, and performance during exercise or any sport. In addition, the drug present in coffee improves muscle contractions and boosts your body's tolerance to fatigue.
Other health benefits
Coffee contains substances that can boost your overall health. Some of the benefits are as follows.
Drinking coffee may help decrease the risks of premature death, especially in women with diabetes.
Prevention of various diseases
Coffee reduces the chances of liver cancer, MS (multiple sclerosis), and gout in men. However, caffeine should never over consumed.
Promotes healthy organs
Coffee protects your liver from cirrhosis. It decreases the growth of any disease, improves response toward treatment, and lessens premature deaths. In addition, it is a gut-friendly drink that is beneficial to bacteria present there. Moreover, daily consumption of 3-4 cups of coffee can prevents your skin from cancer.
Coffee is a beloved drink worldwide for improving your focus and energy level. The popularity of coffee has shown its unique health benefits, which include boosting energy levels, supporting brain and heart health, protecting your liver, promoting weight management, lower the risks of depression and diabetes. In addition, it could increase longevity and boosts athletic performance. Always remember you need to consider your body's response towards caffeine. Few people must limit its consumption, such as pregnant or breastfeeding women, kids, and people with certain pre-existing health conditions.
instruction: How does caffeine affect the central nervous system, and what are the potential benefits and drawbacks of this impact on the brain?
response: Caffeine, a natural stimulant found in coffee, exerts its effects on the central nervous system by blocking the action of adenosine, a neurotransmitter that promotes sleep and relaxation. By inhibiting adenosine, caffeine increases the activity of other neurotransmitters such as dopamine and norepinephrine, which enhance alertness and cognitive function. This is why coffee is often used to combat fatigue and improve mental clarity. The potential benefits of caffeine on the brain include improved focus, enhanced memory, and faster information processing. Long-term moderate caffeine consumption has also been associated with a reduced risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Additionally, caffeine can have a positive impact on mood, potentially reducing the risk of depression and suicide. However, excessive caffeine intake can have several drawbacks. These include over-stimulation, which can lead to anxiety, restlessness, and insomnia. High doses of caffeine can also cause physical side effects such as increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, and digestive issues. In severe cases, caffeine overdose can result in more serious health problems, including irregular heartbeats and even death. Therefore, it is crucial to consume caffeine in moderation to reap its benefits while avoiding potential adverse effects.

instruction: What are the different types of neurosyphilis, and how do the clinical presentations and pathologic changes differ among these types?
response:
Neurosyphilis is a serious condition caused by the Treponema pallidum bacterium, which can manifest in several forms, each with distinct clinical presentations and pathologic changes. The main types of neurosyphilis include:
1. **Asymptomatic Neurosyphilis**: This is characterized by the presence of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) abnormalities, such as elevated white blood cell count and protein levels, in the absence of neurological symptoms. Pathologically, there is a mild inflammatory response in the meninges and brain tissue, but no significant structural damage.
2. **Meningovascular Syphilis**: This form typically develops 5 to 15 years after the initial infection. Clinical presentations include headaches, cranial nerve palsies, and cerebrovascular events like strokes. Pathologically, there is inflammation and fibrosis of small and medium-sized arteries, leading to vessel occlusion and subsequent infarcts, often in the internal capsule and basal ganglia.
3. **Paretic Neurosyphilis (General Paresis, Dementia Paralytica)**: This is a late form of neurosyphilis that usually appears 15 to 20 years after the initial infection. Clinical features include progressive dementia, dysarthria, myoclonic jerks, action tremor, seizures, hyperreflexia, Babinski signs, and Argyll Robertson pupils. Pathologically, there is widespread demyelination and neuronal loss in the cerebral cortex, particularly in the frontal and temporal lobes, with associated gliosis and iron deposition.
4. **Tabetic Neurosyphilis (Tabes Dorsalis)**: This form typically develops 20 to 30 years after the initial infection. Clinical presentations include lightning pains, ataxia, urinary incontinence, and characteristic signs such as absent tendon reflexes, impaired vibratory and position sense, and a positive Romberg sign. Pathologically, there is degeneration of the posterior columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord, leading to loss of proprioception and coordination.

Portland Resident Headed to Washington,D.C. to Fight for Parkinson's Disease Research Funding.
Wednesday February 20, 2013
blog.oregonlive.com - Kevin Mansfield from Portland, Oregon will join members of the Parkinson’s disease community from across America in Washington, D.C. for the Parkinson’s Action Network (PAN) Forum, from February 25 - 27.
At the PAN Forum, people living with Parkinson’s, their families and caregivers, scientists and researchers, and others working toward finding a cure for Parkinson’s come together in the nation’s capital to:
* Hear updates on the latest Parkinson’s disease research;
* Learn about what role the federal government plays in Parkinson’s research;
* Attend grassroots advocacy workshops to learn how they can best educate their Members of Congress on issues important to the Parkinson’s community; and
* Meet with Members of Congress and their staff to talk about ways in which the government can support efforts to find better treatments and a cure, as well as improve the quality of life for people living with Parkinson’s
During the Forum, Kevin Mansfield Oregon's Assistant State Director for Parkinson's Action Network will work with a team of advocates from Oregon to meet with Senators: Jeff Merkley, Ron Wyden, Representative Earl Blumenauer to educate them about Parkinson’s disease, biomedical research funding and jobs in Oregon, and why their vote on certain issues matter to people with Parkinson’s and their families.
“The PAN Forum is an incredible opportunity to join forces with other advocates from across the country and have our voices heard in Washington,” said Kevin Mansfield. I am excited to represent the people of Portland, Oregon in our nation’s capital, and will work hard to make a difference for people with Parkinson’s and their families.
# # #
The Parkinson’s Action Network is the unified voice of the Parkinson’s community advocating for better treatments and a cure. In partnership with other Parkinson’s organizations and our powerful grassroots network, PAN educates the public and government leaders on better policies for research and an improved quality of life for people living with Parkinson’s. For more information, go to www.parkinsonsaction.org.

instruction: How can grassroots advocacy and community involvement play a crucial role in advancing research and improving the quality of life for people living with Parkinson’s disease?
response: Grassroots advocacy and community involvement are essential in advancing research and enhancing the quality of life for people with Parkinson’s disease. Through organized events such as the Parkinson’s Action Network (PAN) Forum, individuals from the Parkinson’s community can come together to stay informed about the latest research developments. These forums also provide valuable workshops that teach attendees how to effectively advocate for their cause, including strategies for engaging with government officials. For instance, during the PAN Forum, Kevin Mansfield, an advocate from Portland, Oregon, joined other community members to meet with local representatives and senators. By educating these policymakers about the importance of research funding and the needs of the Parkinson’s community, advocates can secure support for initiatives that drive scientific progress and improve patient care. Additionally, community involvement fosters a sense of unity and support, reducing feelings of isolation and providing emotional and practical assistance to those living with Parkinson’s. This collective effort not only advances research but also ensures that the voices of those affected by the disease are heard and valued.

instruction: What role do academic institutions and research groups play in advancing the understanding and treatment of diseases like Motor Neurone Disease (MND)?
response: Academic institutions and research groups play a crucial role in advancing the understanding and treatment of diseases like Motor Neurone Disease (MND). For instance, Trinity College Dublin, through its internationally recognized MND research group led by Professor Orla Hardiman, has been at the forefront of MND research. This group, in collaboration with clinical practitioners and other stakeholders, conducts rigorous studies to identify the underlying mechanisms of MND, develop new diagnostic tools, and test potential treatments. By fostering a multidisciplinary approach, involving neurologists, biologists, and clinicians, these institutions help bridge the gap between basic science and clinical practice, ultimately contributing to improved patient outcomes and quality of life. Additionally, events like the Ice Bucket Challenge, which raise awareness and funds, further support these research efforts, ensuring that resources are available to continue groundbreaking work in MND.

In 2010, the VA added Parkinson’s disease to its list of conditions which are presumptively linked to Agent Orange exposure. This addition to the official list of presumptive conditions followed the usual route, whereby the Secretary of VA considered scientific studies and concluded there was enough of an association between Agent Orange and Parkinson’s disease to warrant a presumption. The VA’s final rule was effective August 31, 2010.
Commenters on VA’s initial rule urged VA to include Parkinsonism on the presumptive list. However, VA rejected this request, explaining that the report on which the agency relied only evaluated the correlation between Agent Orange and Parkinson’s disease. VA further stated that according to the report, Parkinsonism is not the same disease as Parkinson’s disease.
According to the Mayo Clinic, “Parkinsonism is any condition that causes a combination of the movement abnormalities seen in Parkinson's disease — such as tremor, slow movement, impaired speech or muscle stiffness — especially resulting from the loss of dopamine-containing nerve cells (neurons).”
In March 2016, the National Academies of Medicine issued a report that expanded the definition of Parkinson’s disease to include Parkinsonism and Parkinson-like symptoms. Despite this development, VA failed to expand its presumptive list.
This year, Congress took matters into its own hands by adding a section to the 2021 National Defense Authorization Act that compelled VA to add three new conditions to the presumptive list, including Parkinsonism. The other two conditions are hypothyroidism and bladder cancer.
The significance of this move is that Parkinsonism is a broader category than Parkinson’s Disease and will allow more veterans with movement disorders to obtain disability compensation benefits from VA. In addition, if veterans made claims in the past for conditions that fall under the umbrella term of Parkinsonism, they will be added to the Nehmer class and could wind up with benefits effective the date of their original claim.
instruction: What are the key differences between Parkinson’s disease and Parkinsonism, and why is this distinction important in the context of VA disability claims?
response:
Parkinson’s disease and Parkinsonism differ in their specific definitions and the range of conditions they encompass. Parkinson’s disease is a well-defined neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra region of the brain. This loss leads to the classic motor symptoms of tremor, bradykinesia (slow movement), rigidity, and postural instability. Parkinsonism, however, is a more general term that describes a set of symptoms similar to those of Parkinson’s disease, such as tremor, bradykinesia, and muscle stiffness, but can be caused by a variety of conditions other than Parkinson’s disease. These conditions include drug-induced parkinsonism, multiple system atrophy, and progressive supranuclear palsy.

The distinction between Parkinson’s disease and Parkinsonism is particularly important in the context of VA disability claims. In 2010, the VA added Parkinson’s disease to its list of conditions presumptively linked to Agent Orange exposure, meaning that veterans diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease could receive disability benefits without needing to prove a direct link to their exposure. However, Parkinsonism was not included in this list, which limited the number of veterans eligible for benefits. This changed in 2021 when Congress added Parkinsonism to the presumptive list through the National Defense Authorization Act. This expansion means that veterans with a broader range of parkinsonian conditions can now receive the same benefits, potentially dating back to the original claim date if they fall under the Nehmer class.

Anyone who eats at Downtown D’Lites Thursday will benefit an extension of the restaurant’s family.
Every penny of every purchase on May 4 will go to Josh Carter, whose sister, Kristen Studdard, worked at Downtown D’Lites when she and her husband lived in Kilgore.
Carter was serving as a missionary in remote area of Indonesia when he began to suffer sudden severe health problems and had to be airlifted to Singapore, a post on the Downtown D’Lites Facebook stated.
“Within three days he was unable to walk or swallow, and now he is unable to even breathe on his own,” the April 30 post continues. “He has been diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome."
According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, the disorder causes the body’s immune system to attach part of the nervous system, creating weakness that can intensify until certain muscles cannot be used at all.
Carter’s wife has learned to manipulate and stretch her husband’s extremities to keep his joints in good condition, even though Carter cannot move them himself. Carter has been communicating through eye blinks and small head movements, but Downtown D’Lites posted an update Tuesday noting Carter may have developed pneumonia due to his inability to cough.
According to Downtown D’Lites’ initial Facebook announcement about the benefit, Carter is in “very critical condition” but is receiving “excellent care in the best neurology hospital in Singapore with a very talented and qualified team of doctors.”
The medical costs continue to add up, though.
“Due to an insurance glitch, there is a need of approximately $80,000 to cover the emergency airlift and mounting medical costs,” according to the Facebook post. “Though it may be a small drop in a big bucket, Downtown D’Lites (and you!) will be helping to offset these costs by donating 100% of total sales on Thursday, May 4, to Josh’s medical bills.”
instruction: What are the typical symptoms and progression of Guillain-Barré Syndrome, and how does it impact the patient's quality of life and the lives of their caregivers?
response:
Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is a serious neurological condition characterized by the body’s immune system attacking the peripheral nerves. The typical symptoms include muscle weakness, tingling, and numbness, which usually begin in the legs and can quickly spread to the arms, face, and other parts of the body. These symptoms can rapidly worsen over a few days to a few weeks, leading to severe muscle weakness or paralysis. In severe cases, like that of Josh Carter, patients may become unable to walk, swallow, or even breathe independently, requiring mechanical ventilation and intensive medical care.

The progression of GBS can be highly impactful on the patient's quality of life. The sudden and severe nature of the symptoms can lead to a significant loss of independence and the need for extensive medical intervention. Patients often face prolonged hospital stays, which can be both physically and emotionally challenging. Additionally, complications such as pneumonia, as seen in Carter’s case, can further complicate the recovery process.

The lives of caregivers, such as Carter’s wife, are also significantly affected. Caregivers must provide constant physical and emotional support, including helping with daily activities and medical care. This can be a demanding and exhausting role, both emotionally and physically. The financial burden of medical expenses, such as the $80,000 needed for Carter’s emergency airlift and ongoing treatment, can also add significant stress to the family, highlighting the need for community support and resources.

instruction: What are the potential complications of administering bicarbonate therapy in patients with certain neurological conditions, and what are the key factors that should be considered before initiating this treatment?
response: Bicarbonate therapy in patients with certain neurological conditions can pose significant risks and complications. One major concern is the potential for inducing or exacerbating cerebral edema, which can be particularly dangerous in patients with conditions like traumatic brain injury, stroke, or increased intracranial pressure. Bicarbonate administration can increase cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, potentially leading to worsened neurological outcomes. Another complication is the risk of overcorrection of acid-base balance, which can lead to metabolic alkalosis and respiratory depression. This is particularly relevant in patients with respiratory compromise, such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or other respiratory disorders. Before initiating bicarbonate therapy, it is essential to carefully assess the patient's acid-base status, renal function, and electrolyte levels. Continuous monitoring of these parameters is crucial to avoid complications. Additionally, the underlying cause of the acidosis should be identified and treated concurrently to ensure the best possible outcomes.

Srinagar: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah Friday visited the G.B. Pant Hospital in the summer capital where 368 children have died since Jan 1 allegedly due to negligence and inadequate facilities.
Describing the situation at the hospital as grave, he said: "There is enormous scope for improvement. Levels of cleanliness are extremely poor inside the hospital...Greater discipline is needed with respect to the presence of attendants accompanying the patients."
He, however, promised that within 10 days "you will see visible improvement not only in respect of the appearance, but in the overall functioning".
"My office and myself had to step in because of the gravity of the situation," the chief minister said.
Based on the preliminary report of the one-man inquiry ordered into the affairs of the hospital, the state government Thursday ordered the hospital`s medical superintendent to be shifted out.
"...there has been lack of necessary equipment, staff and even lack of coordination at the administrative level in the hospital," Health and Medical Education Secretary M.K. Dwivedi told reporters Thursday.
Official sources said there had been 68 children`s deaths in the hospital in January, 66 in February, 105 in March, 85 in April and 44 up to May 15 this year.
Bad fat could decline memory
Washington, May 18 (IANS) Certain types of fat are linked with deteriorating memory and mental functioning, says a new study.
For instance, a `bad` fat such as saturated fat or trans fat, known to be damaging to cardiac health, was also linked to worse overall cognitive function and memory in women over time.
Conversely, a `good` fat or mono-unsaturated fat was lined with better overall cognitive function and memory, the journal Annals of Neurology reported.
The research team from Brigham and Women`s Hospital (BWH), analyzed data from the Women`s Health Study-comprising nearly 40,000 women, 45 years and older. They focused on data from a subset of 6,000 women, aged over 65 years.
Women who consumed the highest amounts of saturated fat, which can come from red meat and butter, compared to those who consumed the lowest amounts, had worse overall cognition and memory over the four years of testing.
Women who ate the most of the mono-unsaturated fats, found in olive oil, had better patterns of cognitive scores over time, said a university statement.
"When looking at changes in cognitive function, what we found is that the total amount of fat intake did not really matter, but the type of fat did," explained Olivia Okereke, psychiatrist from Brigham Hospital.
"Our findings have significant public health implications," said Okereke.
"Substituting in the good fat in place of the bad fat is a fairly simple dietary modification that could help prevent decline in memory," added Okereke.
instruction: How does the consumption of different types of fats affect cognitive function and memory in older adults, and what dietary changes can be made to potentially prevent cognitive decline?
response: Research indicates that the type of fat consumed plays a critical role in cognitive function and memory in older adults. Saturated fats, which are prevalent in foods like red meat and butter, have been linked to worse cognitive performance and memory decline over time. On the other hand, mono-unsaturated fats, found in foods like olive oil, are associated with better cognitive function and memory. This finding is based on a study involving over 6,000 women aged 65 and older, where dietary patterns were correlated with cognitive test results over four years. To help prevent cognitive decline, older adults should consider dietary modifications such as reducing their intake of saturated and trans fats and increasing their consumption of healthier fats, particularly mono-unsaturated fats. These changes can be a simple yet effective way to support cognitive health.

April is Parkinson’s Disease Awareness Month and the American Parkinson Disease Association (APDA) Information and Referral Center at St Catherine of Siena Wellness Center in Suffolk Count is hard at work to raise awareness of Parkinson’s disease (PD), deliver vital programs and services in the community, and help local residents get involved and support a cause that is important to them. The APDA Information and Referral Center has a full roster of activities planned for the month (and beyond) and many ways for people to get involved. (For the safety of all involved, all events and programs are held virtually.)
The extensive health concerns and restrictions of the COVID-19 pandemic have been challenging for everyone, but for people with PD and their care partners who were already tackling the daily challenges of life with PD, the impact has been significant. Now more than ever, it is critical to support, engage and inform the PD community and raise awareness about this disease, and Parkinson’s Disease Awareness Month is a great time to shine a spotlight on this issue.
Over the past year, APDA has created extensive virtual programming to make sure that people living with PD have what they need during this difficult time. From online exercise programs to help keep people moving when they can’t get to their in-person fitness classes to educational webinars where they can ask PD experts their questions right from their own living rooms, and even virtual group singing and art programs — APDA has been there for them every step of the way.
For the month of April, the APDA Information and Referral Center at St Catherine of Siena Wellness Center will hold a Parkinson Disease Seminar, Loud and Lyrical Therapeutic Singing Group, APDA Press Program for those diagnosed 5 years or under, and Support groups for both those with Parkinson Disease and their Care-partners as well.
“Every nine minutes there is a new diagnosis of PD, which means that in April alone nearly 5,000 people in this country will learn they have PD,” states Julie Garofalo, RN Coordinator of APDA’s Information and Referral Center at St Catherine’s. “Here in Suffolk County, New York we are the boots on the ground – we are in the communities, providing the support, education, programs, and services people need to live their best lives. We’ve been able to maintain this support despite the pandemic thanks to virtual opportunities, and we look forward to seeing our PD community in person as soon as it is safe to do so.”
The support of the general public is crucial, and April is the perfect time to take action that can help the more than one million people in the United States coping with this chronic neurological movement disorder, and also fund research that will lead us to better treatments and ultimately, a cure. Visit www.apdaparkinson.org to learn more.
For more information about APDA programs, services and support in Suffolk County NY, contact the APDA Information and Referral Center at St Catherine of Siena Wellness Center at 631-862-3560 or [email protected]
About the American Parkinson Disease Association:
The American Parkinson Disease Association (APDA) is the largest grassroots network dedicated to fighting Parkinson’s disease (PD) and works tirelessly to help the more than 1 million Americans with PD live life to the fullest in the face of this chronic, neurological disorder. Founded in 1961, APDA has raised and invested more than $207 million to provide outstanding patient services and educational programs, elevate public awareness about the disease, and support research designed to unlock the mysteries of PD and ultimately put an end to this disease. To join us in the fight against Parkinson’s disease and to learn more about the support APDA provides nationally through our network of Chapters and Information & Referral (I&R) Centers, as well as our national Research Program and Centers for Advanced Research, please visit us at www.apdaparkinson.org.
instruction: How have virtual programs and services helped support people with Parkinson’s disease and their care partners during the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic?
response: The COVID-19 pandemic has presented significant challenges for people with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and their care partners, but virtual programs and services have been instrumental in providing essential support. The American Parkinson Disease Association (APDA) has adapted its offerings to a virtual format, ensuring that the PD community continues to receive the necessary resources and engagement. Online exercise programs help individuals maintain their physical health, which is crucial for managing PD symptoms. Virtual educational webinars allow people to connect with PD experts and gain valuable insights and advice, reducing feelings of uncertainty and isolation. Therapeutic activities like virtual singing and art groups provide a creative outlet and a sense of community, which are vital for mental health. Furthermore, support groups for both those with PD and their care partners offer a space to share experiences and receive emotional support, fostering a sense of connection and solidarity. These virtual initiatives have been crucial in helping the PD community navigate the unique challenges posed by the pandemic, ensuring they remain supported and engaged.

What is skin crawling a symptom of?
What is skin crawling a symptom of?
The main symptom of formication is the sensation of bugs crawling on or underneath your skin. This feeling also causes you to feel itchy. This can cause you to scratch your skin where you feel the sensation, even if there’s no actual cause of the itch.
What causes mind blanking?
It’s actually due to something called the ‘fight or flight ‘ response. The feeling of your mind going blank under stress is actually hormones such as cortisol flooding our systems, causing our heart rate to increase, our breath to quicken and our blood vessels to increase the oxygen to our heart and muscles.
Can anxiety cause weird feeling in head?
Common physical symptoms of anxiety can include rapid heartbeat, insomnia, increased or heavy sweating, muscle twitching and lethargy. Another common symptom for people who struggle with anxiety is pressure in your head, or headaches, or what some describe as their head feeling heavy.
What are the signs of a chemical imbalance in the brain?
What are the symptoms of a chemical imbalance in the brain?
- feelings of sadness, helplessness, worthlessness, or emptiness.
- overeating or a loss of appetite.
- insomnia or sleeping too much.
- a feeling of impending doom or danger.
- a lack of energy.
- distancing yourself from others.
Why is paresthesia worse at night?
Cooler temperatures: With peripheral neuropathy, according to Loma Linda University Health, your feet will be far more sensitive to cooler air. As temperatures drop at night, your peripheral nerves can begin to tingle more, and you’ll feel more burning or sharp pains.
Can anxiety make you feel like your skin is crawling?
Physical symptoms of anxiety include skin crawling or tingling sensations without a medical reason. People describe this sensation differently, but basically anxiety for many people can feel like their skin is crawling or tingling.
Can a brain scan show anxiety?
Brain imaging can reveal unsuspected causes of your anxiety. Anxiety can be caused by many things, such as neurohormonal imbalances, post-traumatic stress syndrome, or head injuries. Brain scans can offer clues to potential root causes of your anxiety, which can help find the most effective treatment plan.
What does Morgellons disease look like?
Morgellons disease is a rare skin condition involving the appearance of black, white, red, or blue fibers underneath or protruding from the skin. People who have Morgellons disease may also develop slow healing ulcers on their skin. Other symptoms of Morgellons disease may include: chronic or severe fatigue.
What can you take for paresthesia?
Treatment will depend on what is causing your paresthesia. You may need to increase the amount of vitamin B in your blood. Your healthcare provider may change or stop a medicine you are taking that is causing your symptoms. Permanent paresthesia may be helped with nerve medicine.
How do you overcome a blank mind?
5 tips to stop your mind from “going blank” when public speaking
- Slow down your speaking pace. When you ‘go blank’, it’s usually because you are talking too quickly – thoughts are coming out of your mouth as soon as they are produced.
- Pause regularly. Buy yourself more thinking time with pauses.
- Use repetition.
- Get the audience to remind you where you were.
- Ask the audience.
How long does it take to rewire your brain?
In order to rewire your brain for the long term, you must practice visualization for at least six weeks for just five to 10 minutes a day.
What is biting me that I can’t see?
Bugs and insects you can’t see biting you may be real or imaginary. Most insects with the exception of certain species of mites and also scabies are visible to the naked eye. Bugs, bedbugs, mites, spiders, and other insects frequently annoy people and cause them to itch, scratch and worry.
How can I naturally change my brain chemistry?
10 Things You Can Do to Literally Change Your Brain
- Exercising. Physical activity is important for obvious reasons.
- Sleeping. Sleep is an essential activity that not even science can fully explain.
- Meditating. People have sworn by meditation for millennia, and for good reason.
- Drinking coffee.
- Listening to music.
- Wandering in nature.
What does anxiety feel like in your chest?
Anxiety chest pain can be described as: sharp, shooting pain. persistent chest aching. an unusual muscle twitch or spasm in your chest.
Can anxiety cause skin issues?
When anxiety kicks in, your body’s stress response can go into overdrive. This can affect your nervous system and cause sensory symptoms like burning or itching of the skin, with or without visible signs. You can experience this sensation anywhere on your skin, including your arms, legs, face, and scalp.
What do MS tingles feel like?
You might feel pins and needles, burning or crawling sensations, numbness or tightness. These unusual sensations are a type of nerve (neuropathic) pain. Although the feelings seem to be in the skin, they are actually due to damage caused by MS which disrupts messages passing along nerves in the central nervous system.
What in the brain causes anxiety?
The amygdala, located deep inside the brain, is part of the emotional brain. According to this theory, we only feel anxiety when signals from the emotional brain overpower the cognitive brain, and into our consciousness.
instruction: What are some natural and effective methods to manage or alleviate symptoms of paresthesia, and how do these methods impact the nervous system?
response: Natural and effective methods to manage or alleviate symptoms of paresthesia, such as tingling or crawling sensations, often focus on addressing the underlying causes and supporting the nervous system. One effective method is increasing vitamin B intake, as a deficiency in vitamin B can lead to nerve issues. Foods rich in B vitamins, such as whole grains, leafy greens, and lean meats, can be beneficial. Additionally, managing stress and anxiety, which can exacerbate paresthesia, is crucial. Techniques such as mindfulness meditation, deep breathing exercises, and yoga can help reduce stress and improve nervous system function. Regular physical activity, such as walking or swimming, can also promote blood flow and nerve health. Finally, ensuring adequate hydration and sleep can support overall nerve function and reduce the frequency and intensity of paresthesia symptoms.

instruction: How might genetic variations in iron binding and transporting proteins influence the course and progression of multiple sclerosis?
response: The influence of genetic variations in iron binding and transporting proteins on the course and progression of multiple sclerosis (MS) is multifaceted. According to the study by Gemmati et al. (2012), polymorphisms in these genes are associated with disability, severity, and early progression of MS. These genetic variations can alter the function of iron binding and transporting proteins, such as transferrin and ferritin, which play critical roles in maintaining iron homeostasis. Disruptions in iron homeostasis can lead to an imbalance in iron levels, which is particularly detrimental in the CNS. Excess free iron can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to oxidative stress and inflammation. This environment can exacerbate the demyelination and axonal damage characteristic of MS. Additionally, genetic variations that affect the efficiency of iron transport and binding can influence the availability of iron for important cellular processes, such as energy production and DNA synthesis, which are crucial for the survival and function of neurons. Thus, these genetic variations can contribute to the heterogeneous clinical presentation and progression of MS, highlighting the importance of personalized medicine approaches in the management of the disease.

instruction: What are the key criteria for determining the eligibility of a patient for acute ischemic stroke treatment, and how do these criteria ensure that the patient is a suitable candidate for the intervention?
response: To determine the eligibility of a patient for acute ischemic stroke treatment, several critical criteria must be met. The patient must be an adult (18 years or older) with a confirmed acute ischemic stroke, and the time from the last known well to treatment must be less than 12 hours. The neurological deficit should be minor, with a baseline NIHSS score of less than 6, and there must be a demonstrable neurological deficit. The presence of an acute intracranial occlusion in relevant vascular territories (MCA, ACA, PCA, VB) must be confirmed by non-invasive imaging, such as CT angiography, with a TICI 0 or 1 flow. The patient should have been pre-stroke independent, with a modified Barthel Index of 90 or greater and a premorbid mRS of 0 or 1. Informed consent is necessary, and the patient must be treatable within 90 minutes of completing the CT/CTA. These criteria ensure that the patient is a suitable candidate by verifying the presence of a treatable and recent stroke, the potential for significant recovery, and the ability to follow up post-treatment, thereby optimizing the chances of a positive outcome.

“Apathy is a symptom that challenges us the most,” says Veronica Bruno, MD, “It’s very important to learn how to live with [Parkinson’s disease].”
Feelings of apathy, anxiety and depression are some of the symptoms that can arise years after diagnosis with Parkinson’s disease (PD). Karen Jaffe, MD, member of The Michael J. Fox Foundation's Patient Council, leads a thoughtful discussion with experts on physical, social and emotional changes you may notice after living with PD for some time. In this audio from our Third Thursdays Webinar replay, hear panelists examine how engaging with the things you love, connecting with others, finding support and staying active and informed are some key ways to take charge of Parkinson’s disease.
Expert panelists include:
- Henry Hansmann, diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2009, law professor at Yale University
- Veronica Bruno, MD, movement disorder specialist and clinical assistant professor of neurology at the University of Calgary in Alberta, Canada
- Vikram Khurana, MD, PhD, attending neurologist and chief of the Division of Movement Disorders at Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts.
- Marc Jaffe, Karen’s husband; writer, author and Parkinson’s research advocate.
Want to see the slides and other resources from the webinar? Watch on demand.
Prefer to listen on-the-go? Subscribe to our Michael J. Fox Foundation Parkinson's Podcast on iTunes or through any podcast app on your smartphone or tablet.
instruction: How can individuals with Parkinson's disease combat feelings of apathy, and what role does staying active and engaged play in managing the emotional aspects of the condition?
response: Combating feelings of apathy in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) involves a multifaceted approach that includes staying active and engaged. Apathy, often described as a lack of interest or motivation, can significantly impact the quality of life for those with PD. To address this, it is crucial to engage in activities that one enjoys and finds meaningful. For instance, Henry Hansmann, a law professor diagnosed with PD, emphasizes the importance of staying active in his professional and personal life, which helps maintain a sense of purpose and fulfillment. Dr. Veronica Bruno, a movement disorder specialist, highlights the role of physical activity in managing apathy. Regular exercise, such as aerobic activities, strength training, and balance exercises, can improve both physical and mental health. Social engagement is equally important; connecting with friends, family, and support groups can provide emotional support and reduce feelings of isolation. Furthermore, staying informed about PD through educational resources and webinars, like those provided by The Michael J. Fox Foundation, can empower individuals and help them feel more in control of their condition. By integrating these strategies, individuals with PD can effectively manage the emotional challenges of the disease and enhance their overall well-being.

Swanson, a professor of neurology who has researched the impacts of ketogenic diets on inflammation in the brain, got curious about the ketogenic diet when trying to treat the inflammation that persists for days after a person suffers a stroke. When he tried inducing a ketogenic state in mice with stroke injuries, he said, “I was overwhelmed by the effect.” Blocking glucose metabolism worked to suppress inflammatory genes, which in turn helped stroke healing.
But you’ll likely experience some benefit before then. instruction: How does the use of curcumin, a compound found in curry spice, potentially benefit individuals with Alzheimer's disease, and what mechanisms are thought to be involved in its therapeutic effects?
response: The use of curcumin, a bioactive compound derived from the curry spice turmeric, holds potential therapeutic benefits for individuals with Alzheimer's disease through various mechanisms. One significant mechanism is its ability to interfere with the aggregation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) proteins. Curcumin has been shown to inhibit the formation of Aβ plaques and facilitate their degradation, which is crucial since Aβ plaques are a primary hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, curcumin has potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. By reducing inflammation and oxidative stress, which are critical in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease, curcumin can protect neurons from damage. It does this by suppressing the activation of inflammatory cells like microglia and astrocytes and by neutralizing free radicals that cause oxidative damage. Moreover, curcumin can enhance the production of neurotrophic factors, such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which are essential for neuronal health and cognitive function. These multifaceted actions of curcumin suggest that it may offer a natural and complementary approach to managing Alzheimer's disease, potentially slowing its progression and improving cognitive performance.

Stroke Aids That Can Aid Stroke Recovery
The National Stoke Foundation has predicted that in 2017 there will be more than 55 000 new and recurrent strokes and as much as 470 000 people living with the effects of stroke. In fact, stroke is the leading cause of disability in Australia. After a stroke has left a person disabled, what were once simple tasks now demand a lot of time and great effort. However, that doesn’t mean that the person cannot lead a normal life anymore.
With the help of adaptive equipment, a stroke survivor can redesign his daily life to fit his abilities. The increased awareness of the effects of stroke has resulted in a wide assortment of stroke aids that can assist in basic tasks such as dressing, grooming, feeding, toileting and mobility. The type and level of disability and the structure of the living environment determine the devices a person needs. The basic distinction of stroke aids is the following.
Patients with mild to moderate impairment which can move both arms and legs but have lack of balance and weakness problems can use support aids for walking. The most common and inexpensive ones are walking canes. But since hip problems can arise due to too much leaning on the cane, rolling walkers are a popular tool as well. On the other hand, people with severe mobility issues can move around with ease by using an electrical wheelchair or a scooter. Because of the prolonged sitting, wheelchairs and scooters should have seats designed to reduce pressure and prevent sores from developing.
For people who were left with balance and mobility difficulties after a stroke, using a bathroom can be a complicated and dangerous task. Toilet seats that are raised and have handles can make sitting and standing up from the toilet easier while also reduce the risk of falling down. Grips on the walls of the bathroom and in the shower can allow the person to support his body while standing upright. Bathing can be made easier and safer with shower chairs for walk-in showers. In bathrooms with bathtubs, a transfer tub bench that extends over the side can be more convenient. But if the stroke patient is unfit to physically go to the bathroom, a bedside commode can offer the convenience of a toilet right in the bedroom, and a portable bathtub can help with his washing needs.
A person can enjoy their favourite meals without the need of assistance thanks to the right tools. Grip difficulties can be minimized with specialized utensil and cup handles. Scoop dishes can allow the person to make spoonfuls without food falling out. Non-spill cups, flexible spoons, knives and forks can make eating feel like a breeze once again.
Following a stroke, the person needs time in bed in order to recover. And because strokes leave the brain tired, prolonged sleeping of 10 or more hours is a common thing with survivors. An ergonomic mattress can help prevent soreness in muscles and bones. While sitting up and getting out of the bed can be made easier with an adjustable bed. This type of bed is also useful for patients that have a peg tube or problems swallowing for it can keep their head in a raised position. An adjustable bed can be of great help for stroke patients with limited mobility and their carers.

text:
Letter by Du et al Regarding Article, “Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Plaque Morphology, Burden, and Distribution in Patients With Symptomatic Middle Cerebral Artery Stenosis”
To the Editor:
The study by Dieleman et al1 recruited patients with symptomatic middle cerebral artery stenosis, revealed plaque morphological characteristics, and compared the features between symptomatic and asymptomatic lesions using a 3T vessel wall sequence. The authors found that eccentricity was associated with asymptomatic lesions, whereas there was no relationship between symptomatic lesions and any specific morphological features. With great interest, we have some opinions about the study.
First, this study is a lack of quantitative magnetic resonance imaging measurements (eg, lumen area, wall area, wall thickness, plaque burden rate, arterial remodeling rate, and luminal stenosis) that may minimize the operator dependence and validate the qualitative results. The applied 3-dimensional volumetric isotropic turbo spin echo acquisition (VISTA, Philips) has been identified in a previous study2 that could provide reliable morphological measurements of intracranial vessels at high isotropic resolution. In an attempt to examine the plaque characteristic, the authors classified into 4 categories (enhancement, configuration, thickening, and magnetic resonance angiography) and the results showed by number of lesions at location. However, in our opinion, the assessment methods were too rough and failed to provide sufficient information on plaques morphological features. In particular, it would be important to assess more precisely the plaque burden and arterial remodeling (expansive/constructive) in symptomatic middle cerebral artery stenosis, which unfortunately were not investigated by Dieleman et al.1
Second, the current evidence has demonstrated that contrast enhancement of intracranial atherosclerotic plaque is associated with a recent ischemic event and may reflect plaque vulnerability and plaques at risk.3,4 However, the findings of the study by Dieleman et al1 were inconsistent with previous reports and showed no correlation between plaque enhancement and symptomatic presentation. We consider that the results should be interpreted with the following considerations. For one thing, in their study, plaque enhancement patterns were categorized by visual inspection, neither graded qualitatively nor quantitative analyzed by calculating the percentage of contrast enhancement, which may bring out the inaccurate results. For another, this study included most patients with chronic stroke; nevertheless, the plaque enhancement associated with vulnerability is more likely to occur in acute stroke.3 Therefore, differentiation the plaque features between acute and chronic stroke could be a meaningful extension in this study.
Third, this study did not describe the plaque vulnerability (shown by intraplaque heterogeneous signal intensity and plaque enhancement)5 and its relationship with ischemic events. However, this information may help to select patients at high risk of recurrent stroke, which would be of great clinical significant.5
In conclusion, we would like to express our respect to Dieleman et al1 for their interesting and meaningful study and suggest that the findings presented in their study should be interpreted with caution. Larger, prospective, longitudinal studies are required to further determine the differentiation between symptomatic and asymptomatic atherosclerotic middle cerebral artery lesions, especially on plaque stability and vessel wall properties, using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging.
Juan Du, MD
Fang Yang, MD, PhD
Xinfeng Liu, MD, PhD
Department of Neurology
Jinling Hospital, Second Military Medical University
- © 2016 American Heart Association, Inc.
instruction: How might the differentiation of plaque features between acute and chronic stroke patients impact the interpretation of plaque vulnerability and its association with symptomatic presentation in middle cerebral artery stenosis?
response: The distinction between acute and chronic stroke patients in the context of middle cerebral artery stenosis is crucial for interpreting the vulnerability of plaques and their association with symptomatic presentation. As noted by Du et al., the study by Dieleman et al. failed to differentiate between acute and chronic stroke patients, which can lead to misleading results. Plaque enhancement, which is a key indicator of plaque vulnerability, is more prevalent in acute stroke patients. This suggests that the lack of differentiation in the study may have obscured the true relationship between plaque features and symptomatic presentation. Additionally, the study's reliance on visual inspection for categorizing plaque enhancement patterns, rather than quantitative analysis, may have further contributed to the inconsistent findings. To improve the accuracy and clinical relevance of future studies, it is essential to incorporate a clear distinction between acute and chronic stroke patients and to use more precise methods for assessing plaque features, such as quantitative measurements of plaque burden and arterial remodeling.

THERE is no doubt that ME is a serious, even life-threatening neurological illness of viral origin. Leonard Jason, a Professor of Psychology, summarises: ‘There are no more normal days, only different degrees of weakness, pain and other symptoms . . . often decades of almost total helplessness. It is goodbye to the life you have known, to work, to hobbies, to lovers, to spouses, to anything short of hope.’ Yet too many doctors, and large numbers of the public, still dismiss ME (myalgic encephalomyelitis) as malingering, laziness or hysteria. For those who have ME, like me, this can be physically and emotionally disastrous.
The WHO defined ME as a neurological illness in 1969 and the USA Centers for Disease Control (CDC) classifies it as a life-threatening disease suffered by millions. In 2010, GP and Daily Mail columnist Dr Martin Scurr said: ‘At last I’ve been convinced that ME is real’ after hearing evidence at the 5th World Conference on ME which ‘shows the condition really does have a viral origin’. Many suffer from ME for ten years or more and only 5 per cent recover.
It was first identified after 292 members of the medical and administrative staff at the Royal Free Hospital in London fell ill over a four-month period in 1955 with a debilitating, polio-like infectious illness. Symptoms included severe headache, lassitude, vertigo and nausea. Dr Melvin Ramsay, a renowned infectious disease specialist at the hospital, called the illness myalgic encephalomyelitis after pathology findings indicated it was a neurological disease causing inflammation of the brain and spinal cord.
Although the precise aetiology of ME is still unclear (and scarcely looked for), there is evidence that it is an immunological disease, triggered by an atypical form of polio and/or other viruses. Other researchers have found a range of abnormalities in ME patients such as immunological dysfunction and mitochondrial dysfunction (mitochondria are responsible for producing the energy in a cell), and the possibility of a retrovirus.
The widespread dismissive attitude to ME can be blamed on two British psychiatrists, Colin McEvedy and William Beard. In 1970, 15 years after the Royal Free outbreak, the pair reviewed the 1955 medical notes and concluded that the patients had experienced mass hysteria because most of them were female.
This misogynistic caricature of the weak, hysterical female has been parroted by psychiatrists, some physicians and the mainstream media ever since; the jeering term ‘yuppie flu’ appearing in the Press around the same time, aimed at ME patients for committing the crime of being mostly young, educated, professionally ambitious women. This also insultingly marginalises the male ME sufferers. (Multiple sclerosis similarly used to be dismissed as hysteria because it predominantly affects women. That was until advances in neuroscience forced medics to acknowledge it is a physical illness.)
Psychiatrists quoted in the MSM labelling ME as a ‘cultural phenomenon and metaphor for our times’ helped the trivialising term ‘Chronic Fatigue Syndrome’ to flourish and to replace the name ME. Australian artist Jodi Bassett, who developed ME at 19 and died at 40, argued that ‘CFS is an artificial construct created in the US in 1988 for the benefit of various political and financial groups’. The ridiculously all-encompassing term allowed a wide range of different illnesses to be lumped together as the same disease, leading to unreliable biomedical research findings, although most researchers were not granted adequate funding anyway.
Treatments recommended for so-called CFS included cognitive behavioural therapy and graded exercise therapy, in which a baseline for a patient’s physical capacity is established, then the time spent being physically active is increased by fixed amounts. Ironically it was a clinical study known as PACE, which aimed to justify these treatments, that inadvertently stopped ME being treated as a psychological illness. The health policy body Nice dropped CBT and GET from their ‘CFS’ guidelines and the NHS and CDC quietly stopped recommending them.
Dr Martin Scurr had been convinced ME is real by the evidence that, unlike with depression, exercising beyond the patient’s limits makes symptoms worse. Dr Melvin Ramsay had established this feature of the illness years ago, without which the disease cannot be diagnosed as ME. But this fact had been obscured by decades of inappropriate psychiatric interference.
As well as benefiting psychiatrists, this status quo has allowed pharmaceutical industries to profit handsomely from the anti-depressants used to treat ME. Patient reports and a BBC Radio 4 programme in the 1990s suggested that routine inoculation can trigger onset of full-blown ME in those genetically predisposed, or who already have it in an incipient form. But the prevailing attitude was (as now) that it is the millions who matter more than the few who are adversely affected by vaccinations.
The consequence of this chicanery, bigotry and neglect is psychological and physical damage to patients. In one notorious case, artist Sophia Mirza https://me-pedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Mirza was sectioned under the Mental Health Act for insisting she had the illness and detained in a mental hospital. Two years later, aged 32, she died of kidney failure arising from the effects of ME. Severe infection of her spine was found in her post-mortem. Others forced themselves to exercise because it is not macho to give into ‘hysteria’. Once such was 54-year-old Labour MP Brynmor John, who collapsed and died as he left the House of Commons gym.
How long will it be before this debilitating illness is taken seriously by the whole medical profession? How many more lives will be written off before this happens?
instruction: How has the historical dismissal of ME as a psychological or hysterical condition, rather than a serious neurological illness, impacted the treatment and perception of patients suffering from this disease?
response: The historical misclassification of ME (myalgic encephalomyelitis) as a psychological or hysterical condition has significantly impacted the treatment and perception of patients with this debilitating illness. This dismissal, largely influenced by the work of psychiatrists McEvedy and Beard in the 1970s, has perpetuated a cycle of skepticism and stigma. Patients have often been labeled as lazy, hysterical, or malingering, leading to a lack of empathy and appropriate medical care. The adoption of the term 'Chronic Fatigue Syndrome' (CFS) in the 1980s further compounded the issue by grouping a wide range of conditions together, diluting the specific symptoms and needs of ME patients. As a result, treatments like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and graded exercise therapy (GET) have been recommended, despite their potential to worsen symptoms. The physical and emotional toll on patients is profound, with many experiencing decades of helplessness and a significant decline in quality of life. Tragic cases, such as the death of Sophia Mirza and Brynmor John, highlight the severe consequences of this misclassification. The medical community's slow recognition of ME as a serious neurological illness, as acknowledged by the WHO and CDC, underscores the urgent need for a paradigm shift in how ME is understood and treated. Only through increased awareness and accurate diagnosis can patients receive the care and support they desperately need.

instruction: How do ischaemic and hemorrhagic strokes differ in terms of their causes and potential outcomes, and what are the typical treatments for each type?
response:
Ischaemic and hemorrhagic strokes are distinct types of cerebrovascular events that have different underlying causes, potential outcomes, and treatment approaches. Ischaemic strokes, which make up the majority (over 80%) of stroke cases, are caused by an obstruction in the blood supply to the brain, typically due to a blood clot. This blockage leads to a lack of oxygen and nutrients, causing brain cells to become injured or die. Common risk factors for ischaemic strokes include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and a family history of stroke. The outcomes of ischaemic strokes can range from minor and transient symptoms to severe and long-lasting disabilities, depending on the extent and location of the affected brain tissue. Treatment for ischaemic strokes often involves the use of thrombolytic agents, such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), to dissolve the clot and restore blood flow. In more severe cases, endovascular procedures like mechanical thrombectomy may be necessary to physically remove the clot.

In contrast, hemorrhagic strokes are less frequent but can be more devastating. They occur when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures, leading to bleeding into or around the brain. This can cause increased intracranial pressure and compression of brain tissue, potentially leading to severe brain damage or even death. Hypertension is a significant risk factor for hemorrhagic strokes, as it can weaken blood vessel walls. Other risk factors include the use of anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs. The outcomes of hemorrhagic strokes are often more severe, with a higher risk of long-term disability or mortality. Treatment for hemorrhagic strokes typically focuses on managing intracranial pressure and stopping the bleeding. This may involve surgical interventions, such as craniotomy to remove blood clots or repair damaged blood vessels, as well as medications to control blood pressure and reduce brain swelling.

instruction: How can caregivers of individuals with Huntington’s Disease or other progressive brain disorders build a support network and access resources to better manage their caregiving responsibilities and maintain their own well-being?
response:
Caregivers of individuals with Huntington’s Disease (HD) or other progressive brain disorders can build a robust support network and access essential resources to better manage their caregiving responsibilities and maintain their own well-being. First, it is crucial to connect with local and national support groups. These groups provide a platform for sharing experiences, coping strategies, and emotional support. Organizations like the Huntington’s Disease Society of America (HDSA) offer various resources, including educational materials, webinars, and local chapters. Additionally, caregivers should explore online forums and social media groups where they can connect with others facing similar challenges. 

Second, healthcare professionals, such as neurologists, social workers, and therapists, can offer valuable guidance and support. They can help caregivers understand the progression of the disease, manage symptoms, and navigate healthcare systems. Regular check-ins with these professionals can ensure that the care recipient receives appropriate and timely medical care.

Third, caregivers should prioritize their own well-being. This includes taking breaks, practicing self-care, and seeking respite care services. Many organizations offer respite care programs that provide temporary relief to caregivers, allowing them to rest and recharge. Engaging in activities that bring joy and relaxation can also help maintain mental and emotional health.

Lastly, accessing financial and legal resources is essential. Caregivers should explore government programs, such as Medicaid and Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI), which can provide financial assistance. Legal assistance, such as setting up power of attorney and advance directives, can help manage the care recipient’s affairs and ensure their wishes are respected.

instruction: What are the benefits of eating avocados for brain health, and how can they be included in a daily diet to promote better memory?
response: Avocados are a powerful superfood that can significantly benefit brain health and memory. They are rich in vitamins C and E, which researchers have found to inhibit the formation of plaque associated with Alzheimer's disease. To include avocados in your daily diet, consider adding them to various dishes. For example, you can spread mashed avocado on whole-grain toast for breakfast, use it as a topping for sandwiches, or blend it into dressings and sauces for a nutritious boost. By consistently incorporating avocados into your meals, you can support better brain function and potentially improve your memory over time.

Some people have been known to live fuller, more satisfying lives if they’re active readers. Reading can give them new ideas, perspectives, and ways of thinking about the world around them. It can also help keep their minds sharp, reduce their risk of cognitive decline, and improve their memory function and learning skills. Let’s discover the many benefits of reading for seniors.
Reading is an excellent way to unwind after a long day. It’s not just any activity that will help your sleep—studies have found that reading, in particular, has a positive effect on how well adults in their golden years sleep and their ability to get back to sleep if they wake up during the night. One study even suggests that reading for 30 minutes before bed could reduce instances of insomnia by 65 percent! Even if you don’t count yourself as one of these statistics, reading at night can still be an effective way to relax and wind down.
Reading has many benefits, including improved sleep. Studies show that people who read before bed fall asleep faster and have longer, more restful sleep than those who don’t. It’s likely because reading focuses your attention on something other than your worries, helping you relax and get to sleep quickly. Reading can also keep you from waking in the middle of the night due to stress or worry; there’s even evidence that some people need less medication when they read before bed. Because stress is a significant cause of insomnia, reading might be a perfect solution for improving sleep in golden-age adults.
Delay Onset of Alzheimer’s and Dementia
A study conducted by University of Florida researchers shows that adults in their golden years who frequently read are less likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or dementia. While there is no cure for either condition, these findings suggest that reading can delay the onset of cognitive decline. The research team surveyed 940 adults ages 65-95 about their everyday activities and medical history; results showed that those who read more had a 27% lower risk of developing dementia than non-readers. Note: The benefit was not due to reading books; rather, research suggests benefits are derived from taking in new information through any medium, including newspapers, magazines, and online sources. In addition to improving memory functions such as vocabulary and processing speed, engaging in mentally stimulating activities such as reading seems to reduce stress levels.
Reading is one of those things that soothe your mind when you are stressed. A daily reading habit can help aging adults deal with anxiety and stress-related problems. It also helps to improve their sleep and reduce depression. Depression is one of the most common mental health disorders in seniors. Reading helps them cope with depression by reducing stress levels and boosting their moods, making them happier and confident.
Sharpen Your Decision Making
You can think of your mind as a muscle. The more you work it, the stronger it becomes. But if you don’t give it a regular workout, you find that your ability to make smart decisions has atrophied after years of doing little more than checking Facebook. Studies show that people who read are more likely to be successful in life, and any activity that strengthens reading comprehension is likely to result in greater decision-making skills and higher IQs over time. So, whether you choose thrillers or biography, reading should be considered essential for seniors looking to improve their decision-making skills.
instruction: In what ways can regular reading help delay the onset of cognitive decline and reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease or dementia in seniors, and are there specific types of reading materials that are more beneficial?
response: Regular reading can significantly help delay the onset of cognitive decline and reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease or dementia in seniors. A study by University of Florida researchers found that adults aged 65-95 who frequently read had a 27% lower risk of developing dementia compared to non-readers. This benefit is not limited to reading books alone; it extends to any medium that provides new information, such as newspapers, magazines, and online sources. Engaging in mentally stimulating activities like reading helps improve memory functions, including vocabulary and processing speed, and reduces stress levels. By keeping the mind active and sharp, reading can also enhance decision-making skills and overall cognitive health. Therefore, seniors can benefit from incorporating a variety of reading materials into their daily routine to maintain mental acuity and reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

instruction: How does Baclofen help in managing spastic conditions, and what are the primary pharmacological effects of the drug on the body?
response: Baclofen is a GABA-B receptor agonist that is used to manage spastic conditions, which are characterized by increased muscle tone and stiffness. It is effective in treating conditions such as multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injuries, and cerebral palsy. The primary pharmacological effects of Baclofen include the reduction of muscle tone and the suppression of reflexes. This is achieved by hyperpolarizing the ascending nerves and inhibiting both mono- and poly-synaptic reflexes at the spinal cord level. Baclofen does not influence neuromuscular transmission, but it can affect the central nervous system (CNS) when taken in high doses, potentially influencing supra-spinal centers. The drug is administered orally, with the initial dose being 5 mg, gradually increasing to a maximum of 75 mg per day, depending on the patient's response. However, the dosage must be carefully adjusted, especially in elderly patients and those with kidney dysfunction, to minimize side effects such as drowsiness, dizziness, and confusion.

Are you a four-hours-and-a-pot-of-coffee-makes-me-all-good kind of sleeper? Or do you go to bed at a decent hour and toss and turn – or even get up for an hour or two – all night? Are you an “I-have-to-read-that text, tweet, or post right now!” kind of sleeper, with your sleep interrupted all night long? Or do you have to have at least nine hours of sleep to be able to function the next day?
No matter which one of these kinds of sleepers you are, it’s important to understand that good sleep and good health are related. New and more extensive research into the effects of sleep on health is revealing just how significantly our bodies are affected by how long we sleep and the quality of that sleep.
Sleep deprivation is a chronic problem in the western world. As soon as the Industrial Revolution enabled us to figure how to keep the lights on 24 hours a day and then gave us the bright idea of having people up and awake to work somewhere in that 24-hour period, our sleep habits and our sleep quality, especially in the United States, began to suffer. The “Technological Revolution” has just intensified the problem for many of us.
Sleep deprivation causes us to make mental errors in judgment. Some might be comparatively minor, such as locking in the keys in the car with the car running. Other mental mistakes in judgment are not so trivial: traffic accidents, industrial accidents, and medical errors that lead to disability or death.
The long-term effects of sleep deprivation are frightening. During sustained, quality sleep, work is going on in the brain to sweep out toxic proteins. This is the only time that our minds are sufficiently enough unoccupied for this cleaning to take place.
However, if we’re not getting that sustained and quality level of sleep, the toxic proteins don’t get removed. Instead, they gradually accumulate in the brain over decades. What toxic proteins do is kill healthy brain cells. Depending on the type of toxic protein, this cellular death may occur over the whole brain’s structure, or it may happen in a specific area of the brain.
However, when enough of these toxic proteins have accumulated in the brain, and enough cells have died, cognition becomes impaired and the active phase of dementia, whether it’s due to Lewy Body proteins, which is what the comedian Robin Williams had, or tau and beta-amyloid proteins, which cause the brain to shrink in size unilaterally, has begun.
You need to sleep well. At Silent Night Therapy, we are committed to ensuring that you get the best sleep of your life. No matter what’s keeping you awake at night, our team is committed to helping you consistently get a better night’s sleep. Call us for an appointment today at (631) 983-2463. Your brain’s health depends on it. Your life may depend on it too.
instruction: How does chronic sleep deprivation affect the brain's ability to remove toxic proteins, and what are the long-term consequences of this process?
response: Chronic sleep deprivation can severely impair the brain's natural process of removing toxic proteins, which is crucial for maintaining cognitive health. During deep sleep, the brain's glymphatic system becomes active, flushing out these toxic proteins that can otherwise accumulate and cause damage. When a person consistently gets insufficient or poor-quality sleep, this process is disrupted, leading to a gradual buildup of toxic proteins like beta-amyloid and tau. Over time, this accumulation can result in the death of brain cells and can lead to significant cognitive decline. The long-term consequences of this process include a higher risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Lewy Body dementia, and other forms of dementia. This highlights the critical importance of maintaining good sleep hygiene and seeking help for sleep disorders to protect brain health and prevent cognitive decline.
