Dealing with Topamax Side Effects
The most frequent side effect numerically is the sensation of tingling (called paresthesias in medicalese) that can occur randomly on the face or fingers/toes. This is seen most often after a dosage change, particularly if the dose is changed too rapidly. There is a method to not have this side effect: keep dosage changes small (ie, by 25mg per change and only weekly or thereabouts). Many times doses are doubled and this can set you up for side effects. Another recently offered way to eliminate this side effect is to chew up some Tums or a similar type of calcium carbonate (3-4 per day). This seems to help. Dividing up the doses during the day may also be helpful.
One frequent “side effect” is that carbonated beverages taste metallic, tinny, or just plain terrible. This can be a good thing because many soda drinks contain calories that you may not need!
The most concerning side effect is that of possible cognitive difficulties while taking topiramate. Although the numbers are quite low in percentages, the idea of having difficulty remembering words (word-finding difficulties) bothers anyone on any medication. Again, the only safeguard is to keep dosage changes small and to allow plenty of time before moving on to a higher dose. Indeed, one may want to keep the daytime doses very low, compared to the late evening dosing. Or, the daytime dose could be eliminated altogether as topiramate has a long (21 hour) half-life. In my practice we have had about 8 patients experience word-finding difficulties out of all the people I have treated with this agent. Usually, reducing the dose or eliminating the daytime dose does the trick.
A relatively good “side effect” is that of weight loss. About 15% of patients will experience this. They say that food holds no interest for them or that they feel full after a small portion of what they might usually eat. This is thought to be due to the carbonic anhydrase inhibition that topiramate causes. One word of caution though: do not overlook taking in sufficient fluids, as dehydration can increase predisposition to kidney stones. These are seen to a very small degree (1.4% greater than in the population at large) in patients on topiramate, especially if they are dehydrated.
Otherwise, this is a nice agent to use for migraine prophylaxis and other clinical problems.
instruction: What are the potential cognitive side effects of taking Topamax, and what strategies can patients use to mitigate these effects while still benefiting from the medication?
response: Topamax, while effective for conditions like migraine prophylaxis, can have cognitive side effects such as word-finding difficulties, which can be distressing for patients. To mitigate these effects, it is important to follow a cautious dosing strategy. Gradual dosage changes, typically increasing by 25mg weekly, can help reduce the risk of cognitive side effects. Patients may also benefit from taking their Topamax dose primarily in the evening, as the medication has a long half-life and can be effective even with lower daytime doses. If cognitive issues arise, reducing the dosage or eliminating the daytime dose can often alleviate these symptoms. Regular communication with a healthcare provider is essential to monitor and manage side effects effectively.

text:
What will happen if the nerves in my legs and feet are damaged?
If diabetic neuropathy has damaged the nerves in your legs and feet, you may not be able to feel pain in those parts of your body. This is a problem because pain can be a useful signal. If you have no feeling in your feet, you could have an injury and not know it. In addition, your muscles might atrophy (decrease in size), and make it difficult for you to walk. The skin on your feet might crack and develop sores. If these sores do not heal or become infected, they might need to be treated at a hospital. In severe cases, you may need to have your foot amputated (removed). Because diabetes makes it harder for an injury to heal, it's important to take good care of your feet and prevent injuries in the first place.
Written by familydoctor.org editorial staff
instruction: What are the potential long-term effects of nerve damage in the legs and feet, and how can these effects impact daily life?
response: The long-term effects of nerve damage in the legs and feet can be quite debilitating and have a significant impact on daily life. One of the most notable effects is the loss of sensation, which means you might not feel pain, heat, or cold in your legs and feet. This loss of sensation can be particularly dangerous because pain is a critical warning mechanism that alerts you to injuries. Without this warning, you might not notice a cut, blister, or other injury, which can then become infected and lead to more serious health issues. Over time, nerve damage can also cause muscle atrophy, weakening the muscles in your legs and feet and making it difficult to walk or maintain balance. This can severely limit your mobility and independence. Additionally, the skin on your feet can become dry and prone to cracking, which can lead to sores and infections. Since diabetes impairs the body's ability to heal, these sores can become chronic and may require medical intervention. In the most severe cases, uncontrolled infections can lead to the need for amputation. Therefore, it is crucial to take proactive steps to manage and prevent nerve damage, including regular foot inspections, proper foot care, and seeking medical attention for any signs of injury or infection.

Location: Exhibit Hall located in Hall B, Level 2
Objective: To evaluate whether a novel outcome measure, Patient-Reported Outcomes in Parkinson’s disease (PRO-PD), correlates with disease duration, quality of life and established measures of PD severity.
Background: The PRO-PD is an outcome measure designed to capture disease status and severity in an inexpensive, clinically relevant, and comprehensive fashion. It was designed to require minimal time and instruction, while assessing patient perception of both motor and non-motor symptoms. The participant is asked to rate symptom severity, on average, over the previous seven days. The PRO-PD is the cumulative score of 33 slider bars. The goal was to create a continuous outcome measure that does not require a clinical exam, is not responsive to fluctuations in dopaminergic medications, takes only a few minutes to complete, and allows for stratification by symptom(s).
Methods: The PRO-PD is an outcome measure in three ongoing studies; the baseline data from these datasets was pooled and investigated. Symptom frequency and severity are described, Pearson’s correlation coefficients and regression analysis were used to determine whether PRO-PD scores increased as a function of time and correlated with established clinical outcome measures.
Results: Three studies provided 902 participants for analysis, 58 of whom were physically examined. The most frequently reported PD symptoms were impaired handwriting/ typing (91.8%), fatigue (91.2%), slowness (89.8%), daytime sleepiness (89.7%), muscle cramps (88.9%), forgetfulness (87.6%), impaired sense of balance (86.9%), and hyposmia (86.0%) Of the 33 variables, only tremor and nausea did not show a statistically significant increase over time. PRO-PD scores correlated with disease duration (r=0.388, P < 0.000), total UPDRS (r=0.446, P=0.008), patient-assessed Hoehn & Yahr (r=0.636, P <0.000), PDQ-39 (r=0.763, P<0.000), PROMIS Global quality of life question (r=-0.744, P<0.000), and the Timed Up and Go (TUG) (r=0.457, P<0.006). PRO-PD non-motor sub-score correlated with Non-Motor Symptom Scores (NMSS) (r=0.911, P<0.000).
Conclusions: PRO-PD correlates with other established exam-based measures of disease severity. This simple, open-access, patient-centered outcome measure may have utility for patients, providers, and researchers. Future validation efforts should evaluate test-retest reliability and change over time within individuals.

instruction: How might the use of patient-reported outcome measures like PRO-PD influence the management and treatment of Parkinson's disease in clinical settings?
response: The use of patient-reported outcome measures like PRO-PD can significantly influence the management and treatment of Parkinson's disease (PD) in clinical settings. PRO-PD is a comprehensive, inexpensive, and clinically relevant measure designed to capture both motor and non-motor symptoms over a recent seven-day period. By providing a continuous outcome measure that does not require a clinical exam and is not influenced by fluctuations in dopaminergic medications, PRO-PD offers several advantages. It allows for quick and consistent assessments, making it practical for regular use in clinical practice. The correlation of PRO-PD scores with disease duration, total UPDRS, patient-assessed Hoehn & Yahr, PDQ-39, PROMIS Global quality of life, and the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test indicates its reliability and validity. This measure can help healthcare providers better understand the patient's experience, tailor treatments to address specific symptoms, and monitor disease progression over time. Additionally, PRO-PD's focus on patient-reported symptoms can enhance communication between patients and providers, leading to more personalized and effective care.

instruction: What are the primary symptoms and diagnostic methods used to identify Myasthenia Gravis, and how do these symptoms differ from those of other neuromuscular disorders?
response:
Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disease that causes weakness in the skeletal muscles, which are responsible for breathing and moving parts of the body, particularly the eyes and face. The primary symptoms include muscle weakness that increases during periods of activity and improves after periods of rest. Common manifestations include ptosis (drooping eyelids), diplopia (double vision), difficulty speaking (dysarthria), trouble swallowing (dysphagia), and generalized weakness in the limbs.

Diagnosis of MG typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, laboratory tests, and electrophysiological studies. A physical and neurological examination can help identify muscle weakness and fatigue. Blood tests can detect the presence of autoantibodies, such as those against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or muscle-specific kinase (MuSK). Electromyography (EMG) can show abnormal muscle responses, and the edrophonium test can temporarily alleviate symptoms, confirming the diagnosis.

These symptoms and diagnostic methods can be distinguished from other neuromuscular disorders. For instance, in Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), symptoms often progress rapidly and include muscle weakness and paralysis, but not the fluctuating nature seen in MG. In Myotonic Dystrophy, muscle weakness is accompanied by myotonia, a delay in muscle relaxation after contraction, which is not a feature of MG. The specific autoantibodies and the characteristic response to edrophonium are key differentiators of MG from other neuromuscular conditions.

This project provides a catalogue of key dementia research and research gaps. It represents a great tool for all dementia researchers and is a major piece of research on its own.
The objective of the project was to develop a publication that provided a summary and catalogue of key dementia research for stakeholders that will underpin further research by identifying gaps in dementia research and support future systematic reviews of dementia research. In many parts of the world there is little information about the prevalence of the disease and while our understanding of the underlying pathology of dementia has progressed, our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of the disease remains incomplete.
A definitive diagnostic tool does not currently exist and hence diagnosis at an early stage of the disease is problematic and importantly, the currently available treatments are limited in their effectiveness. Understanding the experience and needs of people with dementia and their carers is still at a very early stage and further research that utilises qualitative as well and quantitative methods is warranted. Over the past years, important gaps have been identified and addressed, but many gaps remain. Dementia research is still a relatively young discipline compared to research into other areas such cardiovascular diseases or cancer which is at least a generation ahead.
This project was monumental in terms of its undertaking and required an extensive amount of work. The key components of the Dementia Research Map include the following:
Conclusion The Dementia Research Map provides an updated overview of important advances and persisting challenges in the field of dementia research. A Dementia Research Summary (16 pages) and the entire Dementia Research Map (220 pages) are attached.
instruction: How does the Dementia Research Map contribute to the understanding of dementia research gaps and support the advancement of future studies, particularly in comparison to more established fields like cardiovascular diseases or cancer?
response: The Dementia Research Map plays a crucial role in advancing dementia research by systematically cataloguing key studies and identifying significant research gaps. This comprehensive resource is particularly valuable because dementia research is a relatively young field compared to more established areas like cardiovascular diseases or cancer. The map provides a detailed overview of the current state of dementia research, which is essential for researchers, policymakers, and stakeholders. It highlights critical areas where more research is needed, such as the lack of a definitive diagnostic tool, limited understanding of the underlying mechanisms of the disease, and the early stage of research into the experiences and needs of people with dementia and their carers. By addressing these gaps, the Dementia Research Map helps to ensure that future research efforts are more focused and effective. This, in turn, can lead to more rapid advancements in the field, ultimately improving the lives of those affected by dementia and bringing the research community closer to the level of progress seen in more mature research areas.

The following discussion is for general informational purposes only and is not meant to provide the reader with specific medical advice. Please consult with your personal physician, or with a neurologist, for specific advice, guidance and information regarding your particular circumstances.
Botox, the best known form of Botulinum toxin, has been increasingly used in Neurology practice since its first approval by FDA in 1989. In addition to its popular role for cosmetic purpose, it has been used in multiple neurological conditions including: migraine; tension headache; tilted neck (torticollis or cervical dystonia); chronic neck and back pain; facial and eye lid twitches (facial and blepharospasms); limb spasticity after stroke, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis or spinal cord lesions; hyperhydrosis; temple-mandibular joint dysfunction (TMJ) and tremors.
Botox works by blocking the neurotransmitter release from nerve endings to muscle, allowing the muscle to relax. As a result, abnormal movements or muscle contractions are decreased.
Individual response to Botox treatment varies. Overall the treatment success rate is very high and majority of patients who receive this treatment are pleased with the benefit. But it is not a cure. On average, its effects last about 3 months and frequently repeat treatment is required.
Botox treatment is not without side effects, but they are extremely rare and transient. After long term use of Botox, there is a slight chance developing resistance and the treatment appears less effective. The other widely used Botulinum Toxin is Myobloc, which is equally effective and it has special value in patients who developed resistance to Botox.
For torticollis, spasticity, and other dystonias, most insurances including Medicare cover the treatment. For other indications, it varies and frequently a pre-authorization from the insurance company is needed. This question can be addressed during consultation in our Botox Clinic.
instruction: What are the potential side effects and long-term considerations of using Botox for treating neurological conditions, and how do these factors influence the decision to use it as a treatment option?
response: Botox, a form of Botulinum toxin, is commonly used to treat various neurological conditions such as migraine, tension headache, cervical dystonia, and spasticity. While it is generally well-tolerated and effective, it does come with potential side effects and long-term considerations. Common side effects include pain at the injection site, muscle weakness, and temporary drooping of the eyelid or brow. These side effects are usually mild and transient, resolving within a few days to weeks. In rare cases, more serious side effects can occur, such as difficulty swallowing, breathing, or speaking, which require immediate medical attention. Long-term use of Botox may lead to the development of antibodies against the toxin, reducing its effectiveness over time. This can be managed by adjusting the dosage or using alternative forms of Botulinum toxin, such as Myobloc. The decision to use Botox as a treatment option depends on the patient's specific condition, the potential benefits, and the likelihood of side effects. Regular monitoring and follow-up with a healthcare provider are essential to ensure the treatment remains effective and to address any emerging concerns.

“Dementia” describes a set of characteristic symptoms that may include memory loss and trouble with thinking, problem-solving, and/or language. The International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition refers to dementia as “Neurocognitive Disorder.” There are actually several types of dementia based on both how the symptoms were brought about and what particular symptoms are displayed.
Each person will experience dementia somewhat differently. Generally, the symptoms often are mild in intensity and often subtle at the outset of the disease progression and can intensify over time. A person with dementia will frequently have some combination of the following cognitive and emotional symptoms:
- Memory Loss
- Trouble Concentrating or Organizing Activities
- Language Impairment – such as trouble following a conversation or finding the right words to say
- Impaired Visuospatial Skills – for instance, trouble judging distances, navigating stairs or seeing objects in three dimensions
- Impaired Orientation – for example, losing track of the day, date, or where they are
- Changes in Mood – such as becoming frustrated or irritable, growing anxious or withdrawn or becoming unusually sad
- Changes in Perception – for instance, experiencing delusions or hallucinations
As was mentioned previously, this disease is often progressive. In later stages, there can be physical symptoms and gradual deterioration in the body and functioning including muscle weakness, weight loss, reduced appetite, impaired sleep patterns, and swallowing difficulty.
There are several sub-types of dementia including Alzheimer’s disease, Vascular, Lewy Body, and Frontotemporal dementia. The symptoms are readily apparent and can be easily detected with available medical examination and imaging. For example, the Vascular type is typically caused by a stroke and symptoms are characterized by where in the brain the stroke occurred. However, other types, like Alzheimer’s disease, are not as easy to pinpoint a cause. Dementia is often diagnosed through a combination of medical examination and confirmatory evaluation by a neuropsychologist.
If you have questions about this or would like to schedule a consultation, please Contact Us or set an appointment on this website.
instruction: How do the symptoms of dementia typically progress over time, and what are some of the physical symptoms that may appear in the later stages of the disease?
response: Dementia symptoms typically evolve over time, starting with mild and often subtle cognitive and emotional issues that become more pronounced as the disease progresses. Initially, individuals may experience memory loss, difficulty concentrating or organizing tasks, language difficulties (such as trouble following conversations or finding the right words), and impaired visuospatial skills (like difficulty judging distances or navigating stairs). They may also exhibit changes in mood, such as increased irritability, anxiety, or sadness. As the disease advances, cognitive symptoms can worsen, leading to significant memory loss, severe language impairment, and the potential for delusions or hallucinations. In the later stages of dementia, physical symptoms become more apparent, including muscle weakness, weight loss, reduced appetite, disrupted sleep patterns, and difficulties with swallowing. These physical symptoms can significantly impact the individual's ability to perform daily activities and may require specialized care. The progression of dementia can vary depending on the type, such as Alzheimer’s disease, Vascular dementia, Lewy Body dementia, or Frontotemporal dementia, but the overall trend is a progressive decline in cognitive and physical function.

instruction: How does Guillain-Barre Syndrome impact the lives of individuals, and what are the common challenges faced by those diagnosed with this neurological disorder?
response: Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS) is a neurological disorder characterized by the immune system attacking the peripheral nerves, leading to muscle weakness and paralysis. This condition can profoundly affect the lives of individuals in multiple dimensions. Physically, the rapid onset of symptoms can result in a loss of mobility and independence, requiring extensive medical care and rehabilitation. For example, Dr. Paul Steingard, a team physician for the Phoenix Suns, experienced significant weakness in his arms and legs, necessitating hospitalization and a prolonged recovery period. Emotionally, GBS can be extremely challenging, causing anxiety, depression, and a sense of vulnerability. The sudden change in physical health can be overwhelming, especially for those who were previously healthy and active. Socially, the disorder can lead to isolation and stigma. Shaya Van Horn, a young girl diagnosed with GBS, faced social challenges at school, feeling uncomfortable and stigmatized by her peers. The recovery process is often lengthy and unpredictable, adding to the stress and uncertainty. Furthermore, the potential for long-term effects, such as residual weakness or chronic pain, can impact an individual's quality of life and ability to return to their previous activities. Despite these challenges, many individuals, like Dr. Steingard, are expected to make a full recovery, although it may take weeks or months.

instruction: How do auras manifest before neurological episodes, and what are their typical characteristics and duration?
response: Auras are sensory or perceptual phenomena that occur shortly before a neurological episode, such as an epileptic seizure or a migraine attack. They act as a precursor or warning sign, indicating that a significant neurological event is imminent. Auras can manifest in various forms, including visual disturbances (phosphenes, zigzag lines, or flashing lights), auditory sensations (ringing in the ears), olfactory sensations (unusual smells), or somatosensory symptoms (tingling, numbness, or a feeling of heaviness). They can also involve more complex experiences, such as cognitive changes or emotional shifts. The duration of auras is typically brief, lasting from a few seconds to several minutes, and they provide valuable time for individuals to prepare for the upcoming neurological episode.

London, Jan 29 : Women, please take note. Women are twice more likely to suffer from severe depression after a stroke than men, as researchers have found that 20 per cent of women suffered from severe depression compared to 10 per cent of men.
The study also found varying patterns of symptom progression; that long-term increased symptoms of depression are associated with higher mortality rates; and that initially moderate symptoms in men tend to become worse over time.
"...we can't pinpoint exactly why depression is more common among women...," said lead author Salma Ayis from the School of Population Health and Environmental Sciences at King's College London in UK.
"What is common to both sexes is the dramatic decrease in the likelihood of survival as depression symptoms increase.
We believe, therefore, that by monitoring symptoms of depression in stroke survivors and acting accordingly, clinicians may be able to provide better long-term care."
For the study, published in the European Journal of Neurology, the research team followed the progress of symptoms over five years after stroke onset in 2,313 people (1,275 men and 1,038 women).
Patients who had their first-ever stroke between 1998 and 2016 were recruited to the study and were monitored until July 2017.
Participants' mental health was assessed and cross-referenced with their physical health and socio-demographic data.
Stroke is a life-threatening medical condition that occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked.
An estimated, one in six people worldwide will have a stroke in their lifetime and there are more than 100,000 strokes in the UK every year.
Although severity and symptoms are wide-ranging, about a third of all survivors experience depression following their stroke: approximately 400,000 people in the UK today.
instruction: What strategies can healthcare providers implement to effectively monitor and manage depression symptoms in stroke survivors to improve their long-term care and survival outcomes?
response: To effectively monitor and manage depression symptoms in stroke survivors, healthcare providers should adopt a comprehensive and multidisciplinary approach. One key strategy is to conduct routine screening for depression using validated tools, such as the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), at regular intervals post-stroke. This is especially important given the higher prevalence of severe depression in women and the association between increased symptoms and higher mortality rates. Another important strategy is to implement early intervention for patients showing moderate symptoms, as these tend to worsen over time, particularly in men. Healthcare providers should also collaborate with mental health professionals to provide integrated care, including medication management and psychotherapy. Furthermore, incorporating lifestyle modifications, such as regular physical activity and a healthy diet, can have a positive impact on both physical and mental health. Finally, providing access to support groups and educational resources can help stroke survivors and their families better manage the challenges of recovery and reduce the risk of depression.

All US Kmart Pharmacies to Offer Free Memory Screenings During Alzheimer’s Awareness Month in November
NEW YORK, Nov. 03, 2017 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The Alzheimer’s Foundation of America (AFA) and Kmart Pharmacy are teaming up to expand access to free, confidential memory screenings throughout the month of November, which is Alzheimer’s Awareness Month and National Memory Screening Month. All Kmart Pharmacy locations in the US will serve as memory screening sites, where individuals can get screened free of charge during normal business hours.
“Memory screenings should be a regular part of an individual’s annual wellness routine; it’s important that people get regular checkups for their brains, just as they do for other parts of their bodies,” said Charles J. Fuschillo, Jr., President & CEO of the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America. “We are grateful to Kmart Pharmacy for once again helping us make memory screenings more accessible and enabling thousands of people to take advantage of this important health service.”
“Kmart Pharmacy understands the critical impact this would have on our patients," said Jennifer Speares Lehman, RPh, Kmart Pharmacy’s Senior Director of Compliance and Administration. “As part of our 'Care Beyond the Counter' approach, and our quest to continue our award winning service levels, Kmart Pharmacy more deeply connects with our patients on issues that matter to them most. Free Memory Screenings is definitely one of them.”
A memory screening is a simple, non-invasive test to check cognitive health. The screening, which often takes as little as 10 minutes, consists of questions and tasks designed to gauge memory, language and thinking skills. A screening is not a diagnosis; however, if a person scores below the normal threshold, he or she will be referred to a primary care physician for a full evaluation. It is important to keep in mind that not all memory problems are indicative of Alzheimer’s disease. Other sources of memory problems include vitamin deficiencies, thyroid issues and depression, which are treatable and in some cases, curable.
If a memory problem does turn out to be Alzheimer’s, benefits to early detection include affording an individual to participate in developing his care plan, as well as take part in legal and financial planning conversations. Early detection can also allow someone to take advantage of treatments that can slow the progression of symptoms or to participate in a clinical trial.
AFA and Kmart have partnered on the program in the past, enabling over 15,000 people to get screened. Since its inception in 2003, AFA’s National Memory Screening Program has screened over 3.5 million people.
Individuals wishing to get screened can locate the nearest Kmart Pharmacy by visiting pharmacy.kmart.com. AFA’s National Memory Screening Program also offers additional sites, both during November and throughout the year, which can be found by visiting www.alzfdn.org.
About Alzheimer’s Foundation of America (AFA):
The Alzheimer’s Foundation of America, based in New York, is a non-profit organization that unites more than 2,600 member organizations nationwide with the goal of providing optimal care and services to individuals living with dementia, and to their caregivers and families. Its services include a national, toll-free helpline (866-232-8484) staffed by licensed social workers, educational conferences and materials, a free quarterly magazine for caregivers, the National Memory Screening program, and “AFA Partners in Care” dementia care training for healthcare professionals. For more information about AFA, call 866-232-8484, visit www.alzfdn.org, follow us on Twitter, or connect with us on Facebook or LinkedIn.

Participate in Research Advancing our understanding and treatment of motor impairment
NeuRA has secured significant funding to expand research into motor impairment, a problem that arises from many diseases and aging, and a growing public health challenge.
Everything the human body does requires movement, but our muscles—and our brain and nerves that control them—are often the first tissues attacked by a long list of disorders that includes stroke, spinal cord and brain injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, musculoskeletal injury and cerebral palsy.
Prof Simon Gandevia is an expert in the brain’s control of human movement at NeuRA (Neuroscience Research Australia) and will spearhead the nearly $7 million multidisciplinary program of study, funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia.
“Motor impairment encompasses muscle weakness and paralysis, reduced movement at our joints, diminished sensation across the body and a loss of balance. Motor impairments can arise because of many different diseases, making it a major cause of disability world-wide,” Prof Gandevia said.
“We know about some forms of impairment, but nothing about others. This is an under-researched area of medicine and this grant will allow us to fill gaps in our knowledge and develop and trial new treatments,” Prof Gandevia said.
Motor impairments affect a large number of Australians, and as our population ages, incidence is predicted to grow. For example, 1 in 3 elderly people fall each year, often because of problems with mobility and their balance and sensory systems.
However, another leading causes of motor impairment is stroke. Around 4 million Australians will suffer a stroke in their lifetime and half will go on to develop disabling muscle stiffening and problems in their affected arm or leg.
Current muscle therapies for these stroke survivors are limited and improving our understanding and treatments for motor impairments such as these will bring huge benefits.
“We will focus on both scientific and clinical outcomes. Our team will begin by studying everyday functions that people take for granted, such as standing, balancing and using our hands. We will study these abilities in people suffering different diseases and develop therapies to help restore function and improve quality of life,” Prof Gandevia concluded.
Follow @MotorImpairment on Twitter to receive updates from the research team and learn more about this field.
- Prof Simon Gandevia is the Deputy Director of NeuRA and an expert in clinical neurophysiology.
- Prof Stephen Lord is a research leader in accidental falls and ageing; his book on falls in older people is considered the seminal text on the subject.
- Prof Rob Herbert has pioneered the use of randomized control studies to assess the effectiveness of physical therapies in people recovering from motor impairment.
- Assoc Prof Janet Taylor is an expert in human motor physiology and fatigue.
instruction: What are the primary causes of motor impairment, and how do these conditions impact the quality of life for individuals affected by them?
response: The primary causes of motor impairment include a variety of neurological and musculoskeletal conditions such as stroke, spinal cord and brain injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, musculoskeletal injury, and cerebral palsy. These conditions can lead to muscle weakness, paralysis, reduced joint movement, diminished sensation, and loss of balance. For instance, stroke is a leading cause of motor impairment, affecting around 4 million Australians, with half of those experiencing muscle stiffness and mobility issues in their affected limbs. Spinal cord injuries can result in paralysis and loss of sensation, while multiple sclerosis can cause muscle weakness and coordination problems. Parkinson’s disease leads to tremors, stiffness, and balance issues, and cerebral palsy can affect muscle tone, posture, and motor skills. These impairments significantly impact the quality of life for individuals by limiting their ability to perform daily activities, reducing independence, and increasing the risk of falls and injuries. For example, 1 in 3 elderly people fall each year, often due to motor impairments, which can lead to further health complications and decreased mobility.

text:
Paracetamol and Migraine-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms: Relief Strategies
Personal experience with migraine attacks and associated gastrointestinal symptoms often leads individuals to seek effective relief strategies. One common treatment option for migraine attacks is paracetamol, also known as acetaminophen. Paracetamol has been widely used for its pain-relieving properties, but what role does it play in alleviating migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
Understanding Migraine-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms
Migraine attacks can come with a range of symptoms, and gastrointestinal symptoms are frequently reported by migraine sufferers. There is a clear link between migraine attacks and gastrointestinal symptoms, although the precise underlying mechanism is still being studied. During migraine attacks, individuals may experience nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, which can significantly impact daily activities and overall well-being.
For example, individuals with migraine attacks may experience severe nausea that can lead to vomiting. This can make it difficult to keep food or medications down, including paracetamol, which can limit its effectiveness in relieving both pain and gastrointestinal symptoms.
The Role of Paracetamol in Migraine Treatment
Paracetamol is commonly used as an over-the-counter medication for migraine pain relief. It works by inhibiting prostaglandin production, which helps reduce pain signals in the brain. While paracetamol can effectively alleviate migraine pain, its effectiveness in addressing accompanying gastrointestinal symptoms is limited.
It is important to note that paracetamol primarily targets pain pathways in the brain and may not directly affect the gastrointestinal system. Thus, its ability to provide relief for nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain during migraine attacks may be limited compared to medications specifically designed to target these symptoms.
Strategies for Maximizing Relief Provided by Paracetamol
Optimal Timing of Paracetamol Intake During a Migraine Attack
Taking paracetamol at the earliest sign of a migraine attack can help maximize its effectiveness in reducing pain. Instead of waiting for the headache to become severe, prompt administration can potentially prevent the development of severe gastrointestinal symptoms.
For example, if you experience warning signs or prodromal symptoms of a migraine, such as visual disturbances or aura, taking paracetamol immediately can help address both pain and potential gastrointestinal symptoms before they worsen.
Regularly monitoring symptom changes during a migraine attack is crucial. If the initial dose of paracetamol does not provide adequate relief, it may be necessary to follow up with additional doses as directed by a healthcare provider, ensuring that the recommended maximum daily dosage is not exceeded.
Combining Paracetamol with Other Medications
When treating migraine attacks with associated gastrointestinal symptoms, it may be beneficial to combine paracetamol with other medications. Antiemetics, which are drugs commonly used to control nausea and vomiting, may enhance the overall relief achieved. Consultation with a healthcare provider is essential to evaluate the potential benefits of combination therapy and identify suitable options.
For example, combining paracetamol with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide may provide more comprehensive relief for both migraine pain and gastrointestinal symptoms. Metoclopramide works by increasing the movement of the stomach and intestines, reducing nausea and promoting better digestion.
Some combination medications may already include paracetamol as one of the active ingredients. However, it is important to follow dosage instructions carefully and avoid exceeding the recommended maximum daily dosage of paracetamol to minimize the risk of liver damage.
Addressing the Impact of Gastrointestinal Symptoms on Paracetamol Absorption
Migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms can affect the absorption and effectiveness of orally administered paracetamol. Taking paracetamol with food or beverage can help minimize gastrointestinal discomfort and improve absorption. However, keep in mind that the presence of food may delay the onset of paracetamol’s action, so timing is crucial.
Exploring alternative formulations or delivery methods of paracetamol, such as rectal suppositories or intravenous administration, may be considered for individuals with severe gastrointestinal symptoms or those who experience difficulties with oral intake during migraine attacks. Consultation with a healthcare provider is necessary to explore these options.
Alternative Treatment Options for Migraine-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms
In addition to paracetamol, there are alternative treatment options for managing migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms. These options include non-pharmacological approaches and prescription medications for severe symptoms.
Incorporating non-pharmacological approaches into migraine management can help alleviate gastrointestinal symptoms. Relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or meditation, can reduce stress levels and ease gastrointestinal discomfort. Dietary modifications, like identifying trigger foods and making appropriate changes, may also help prevent symptom exacerbation.
For example, certain foods and beverages, such as caffeine, alcohol, and processed foods, are known to trigger migraine attacks and gastrointestinal symptoms in some individuals. Avoiding these triggers and maintaining a balanced diet with plenty of hydration can offer relief and reduce the frequency of both migraine attacks and associated gastrointestinal symptoms.
Prescription Medications for Severe Symptoms
For individuals experiencing severe migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, prescription medications may be necessary. Antiemetic drugs, such as metoclopramide or ondansetron, can help control nausea and vomiting more effectively than over-the-counter options. It is crucial to work closely with a healthcare provider to identify and utilize appropriate prescription medications based on individual symptoms and medical history.
These medications are specifically designed to target and alleviate symptoms of nausea and vomiting. They can provide more potent relief when gastrointestinal symptoms are severe and significantly affecting quality of life during migraine attacks.
Addressing migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms is an important aspect of comprehensive migraine management. While paracetamol can effectively relieve migraine pain, its ability to alleviate accompanying gastrointestinal symptoms is limited. By maximizing the relief provided by paracetamol through strategic use and considering alternative treatment options, individuals can work towards better managing their migraine attacks and associated symptoms. Consulting healthcare providers for personalized guidance is highly recommended to develop an individualized treatment plan.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. Can paracetamol completely eliminate migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
No, paracetamol primarily targets pain pathways in the brain and may not directly address gastrointestinal symptoms. While it can help alleviate pain during a migraine attack, additional treatment options may be necessary to manage gastrointestinal symptoms effectively.
2. Are there any specific antiemetics recommended for migraine-related nausea and vomiting?
Several antiemetics, such as metoclopramide and ondansetron, are commonly prescribed to manage nausea and vomiting during migraine attacks. The choice of medication depends on individual symptoms and medical history, and consultation with a healthcare provider is necessary to determine the most suitable option.
3. Can I take paracetamol with other over-the-counter pain relievers during a migraine attack?
It is generally not recommended to combine multiple over-the-counter pain relievers during a migraine attack, as they often contain similar active ingredients, including paracetamol. Exceeding the recommended dosage of paracetamol can increase the risk of liver damage. Consultation with a healthcare provider is advised before combining medications.
4. Can relaxation techniques alone provide relief for migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
While relaxation techniques can help reduce stress levels and ease gastrointestinal discomfort, they may not provide complete relief for all individuals. Incorporating other treatment strategies, such as dietary modifications or medications, may be necessary for comprehensive management.
5. Can alternative formulations of paracetamol, such as suppositories, be more effective for migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
Alternative formulations of paracetamol, such as suppositories or intravenous administration, may be considered for individuals with severe gastrointestinal symptoms or difficulties with oral intake. These options require consultation with a healthcare provider to determine suitability and proper administration.
6. Are there any dietary changes that can specifically target migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
While dietary modifications can help prevent trigger foods and reduce the frequency of migraine attacks, the impact on gastrointestinal symptoms may vary among individuals. Identifying and avoiding trigger foods, along with maintaining a balanced diet and hydration, can contribute to overall symptom management.
7. Can paracetamol be safely used for migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms during pregnancy?
It is essential to consult a healthcare provider before using any medications, including paracetamol, during pregnancy. The appropriate use of medications during pregnancy depends on factors such as trimester and individual health circumstances.
8. Can I take paracetamol regularly to prevent migraine attacks and associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
Regular use of paracetamol for migraine prevention is not recommended without the guidance of a healthcare provider. There are other preventive medications available, and a comprehensive management plan should be discussed with a healthcare provider for long-term usage.
9. How long does it typically take for paracetamol to provide relief during a migraine attack?
Paracetamol usually starts to take effect within 30 minutes to an hour after ingestion. However, individual responses may vary. It is important to follow recommended dosages, timing, and consult a healthcare provider if relief is not achieved.
10. Can paracetamol be used alongside other prescription medications for migraine-associated gastrointestinal symptoms?
Consultation with a healthcare provider is crucial when considering the use of paracetamol with other prescription medications. Drug interactions and potential contraindications need to be assessed to ensure safety and efficacy.
instruction: How can the timing and method of paracetamol administration be optimized to maximize its effectiveness in relieving both migraine pain and gastrointestinal symptoms?
response: To maximize the effectiveness of paracetamol in relieving both migraine pain and gastrointestinal symptoms, focus on the following key strategies: 1. **Early Intake**: Administer paracetamol at the first sign of a migraine to prevent the exacerbation of pain and gastrointestinal symptoms. 2. **Combining with Antiemetics**: Use paracetamol in conjunction with antiemetic medications like metoclopramide or ondansetron to better control nausea and vomiting. 3. **Regular Monitoring**: If the initial dose of paracetamol does not provide sufficient relief, consider additional doses as recommended by a healthcare provider, being cautious not to exceed the maximum daily dosage. 4. **Alternative Delivery Methods**: For severe gastrointestinal symptoms, explore alternative formulations such as rectal suppositories or intravenous administration, which can improve absorption and effectiveness. 5. **Complementary Approaches**: Implement non-pharmacological methods like relaxation techniques, dietary modifications, and hydration to enhance overall symptom management. Always consult a healthcare provider for personalized advice and to create a comprehensive treatment plan tailored to your specific needs.

Marin General Hospital has received recertification from the Joint Commission for its stroke program, and for the second year in a row, it received the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association’s Get With The Guidelines®-Stroke Gold Plus Quality Achievement Award. Both programs are voluntary processes intended to elevate the standard of care for stroke programs and instill confidence in the community served.
“Studies have shown there’s an extremely small window of time in which stroke treatment results in the best outcomes,” said Dr. John Panagotacos, a neurologist and fellowship-trained stroke specialist at Marin General Hospital. "Both designations demonstrate the efforts of our EMS team, the emergency department staff and our imaging and laboratory services to work together to maximize speed to treatment while ensuring the highest quality care. It also recognizes the commitment of our dedicated nurses, therapists, social workers and case managers who take over once recovery and discharge begin."
To receive the Get With The Guidelines award, a hospital must achieve 85 percent or higher adherence to all indicators for two or more consecutive 12-month intervals and 75 percent or higher compliance with six of 10 Get With The Guidelines-Stroke Quality Measures. These measures include aggressive use of medications that have been shown to improve patient outcomes, such as tPA, antithrombotics, anticoagulation therapy, DVT prophylaxis, cholesterol reducing drugs and smoking cessation. All are aimed at reducing death and disability and improving the lives of stroke patients.
Hospitals receiving the award have been measured over two or more 12-month intervals on their adherence to the guidelines and stroke quality achievement indicators developed by the AHA’s American Stroke Association division. These measures include aggressive use of medications, such as tPA, antithrombotics, anticoagulation therapy, DVT prophylaxis, cholesterol reducing drugs and smoking cessation, all aimed at reducing death and disability and improving the lives of stroke patients.
“Our aim is not only to save lives, but to maximize recovery,” said Dr. Panagotacos. “Each one of us is well aware that every minute lost can result in brain damage. That’s why we invest so much time and effort in the Get With The Guidelines program.”
“Marin General Hospital is to be commended for its commitment to implementing standards of care and protocols for treating stroke patients,” said Lee H. Schwamm, M.D., chair of the Get With The Guidelines National Steering Committee and director of the TeleStroke and Acute Stroke Services at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. “The full implementation of acute care and secondary prevention recommendations and guidelines is a critical step in saving the lives and improving outcomes of stroke patients.”
The Get With The Guidelines-Stroke program calls for hospitals to use the time soon after a patient has had a stroke—when they’re most likely to be receptive to guidance—as a “teachable moment.” This is the ideal time to advise patients about how to manage their risk factors. The AHA/ASA provides customized patient education materials that are made available at the point of discharge, based on patients’ individual risk profiles. They’re written in an easy-to-understand format and are available in English and Spanish.
The Joint Commission Advanced Certification program was developed in collaboration with the American Stroke Association and launched in 2003, It is based on the Brain Attack Coalition's "Recommendations for the Establishment of Primary Stroke Centers." Certification is available only to stroke programs in Joint Commission-accredited acute care hospitals.
The risk of stroke roughly doubles every decade after age 50,” said Dr. Panagotacos. “Especially here in Marin, we face a wave of aging Baby Boomers and we know we need to be focused on continually improving the quality of stroke care.”
According to the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association, stroke is one of the leading causes of death and serious, long-term disability in the United States. On average, someone suffers a stroke every 40 seconds; someone dies of a stroke every four minutes; and 795,000 people suffer a new or recurrent stroke each year.
instruction: What specific strategies and educational materials do hospitals use during the critical 'teachable moment' immediately after a stroke to help patients manage their risk factors and prevent future strokes?
response:
During the critical 'teachable moment' immediately after a stroke, hospitals like Marin General Hospital implement several strategies and educational materials to help patients manage their risk factors and prevent future strokes. These strategies are based on the Get With The Guidelines-Stroke program and include:
1. **Personalized Educational Materials**: Hospitals provide customized patient education materials that are tailored to each patient's specific risk factors. These materials are written in an easy-to-understand format and are available in multiple languages to ensure accessibility.
2. **Medication Management**: Aggressive use of evidence-based medications is a key component of the program. This includes thrombolytics like tPA, antithrombotics, anticoagulants, DVT prophylaxis, cholesterol-lowering drugs, and smoking cessation aids. These medications are essential in reducing the risk of recurrent strokes.
3. **Interdisciplinary Care Teams**: A multidisciplinary team, including nurses, therapists, social workers, and case managers, works collaboratively to provide comprehensive care. They focus on educating patients and their families about risk factor management and the importance of adhering to treatment plans.
4. **Secondary Prevention Protocols**: Hospitals follow strict guidelines for secondary prevention, which involve educating patients on lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, and smoking cessation. These protocols are designed to reduce the risk of future strokes and improve long-term outcomes.
5. **Timely and Effective Education**: The 'teachable moment' is used to provide immediate and effective education to patients. This includes discussions about the importance of medication adherence, regular follow-up appointments, and making necessary lifestyle changes to manage risk factors effectively.

by Steven Ertelt
November 7, 2005
Seoul, South Korea (LifeNews.com) — Human cloning researchers in South Korea have been flooded with thousands of requests to participate in a new stem cell research program aimed at helping patients with Parkinson’s disease or spinal cord damage.
The day registration for the program opened, 3,000 people signed up and the applications continue to come in heavily even though only 100 applicants will be chosen to participate in the clinical trials.
Those chosen will be subjected to test experiments whereby scientists collect stem cells from the patients and clone them. The patients will then begin stem-cell therapies.
The research project, headed by Ahn Cu-rie of the Seoul National University’s Medical School, builds upon work by cloning pioneer Dr. Hwang Woo-suk, and will be conducted at 9 separate research facilities based in South Korea and abroad.
"About 100 patients suffering from neurological illnesses including spinal cord damage and Parkinson’s disease will be selected," Cu-rie said.
Patients will be chosen according to the extent of their illness or damage, how long ago their symptoms or injuries began, and whether or not they are likely going to benefit from the therapies.
Once cloned, the stem cells will be used in a series of tests on primate to determine if they will be useful. Patients will then begin their own therapies.
Those who don’t get picked to participate will get a phone call explaining why. Each patient must be approved by an ethics board.
Adult stem cell research has already proven successful in treating patients with spinal cord injuries.
Korean scientists have used umbilical cord blood stem cells to restore feeling and mobility to a spinal cord injury patient, according to a report published in Cythotherapy.
The patient is a woman who has been paraplegic from an accident for more than 19 years. She had surgery and also an infusion of umbilical cord blood stem cells.
Not only did the patient regain feeling, but "41 days after [stem cell] transplantation" testing "also showed regeneration of the spinal cord at the injured cite" and below it.

The program, spearheaded by Dr. Ahn Cu-rie from Seoul National University’s Medical School, focuses on patients with neurological conditions such as spinal cord damage and Parkinson’s disease. The criteria for selecting patients include the severity of their condition, the duration of their symptoms or injuries, and their likelihood of benefiting from the stem cell therapies. Out of the thousands of applicants, only 100 will be chosen to participate. Each selected patient must also be approved by an ethics board, ensuring that the research adheres to high ethical standards. Additionally, the stem cells collected from the patients will be tested on primates to determine their efficacy before being used in human trials. This comprehensive approach not only ensures that the treatments are targeted towards those who stand to gain the most but also maintains the integrity and safety of the research process.

instruction: How does mild cognitive impairment differ from age-related memory decline and early-stage Alzheimer's disease, and what are the key indicators that distinguish these conditions?
response:
Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a cognitive condition that lies between the normal cognitive decline associated with aging and the more severe cognitive decline seen in dementia, including early-stage Alzheimer's disease. Age-related memory decline, or benign senescent forgetfulness, is characterized by minor memory lapses and cognitive changes that are typical of the aging process and do not significantly impact a person's daily functioning. These changes are generally mild and do not interfere with the ability to perform routine tasks.

MCI, however, involves a more noticeable decline in cognitive abilities that is greater than what is expected for a person's age and education level. While individuals with MCI may still be able to function independently, they often experience memory problems and other cognitive difficulties that are more pronounced than those seen in age-related decline. MCI can be a precursor to more severe cognitive conditions, such as Alzheimer's disease, but it is not always a guarantee that it will progress to dementia.

Early-stage Alzheimer's disease is a more severe and progressive form of cognitive decline. It is marked by significant memory loss, difficulty with language and communication, impaired judgment, and changes in mood and behavior. These symptoms are more severe and persistent than those seen in MCI and can begin to affect a person's ability to perform daily activities and maintain social relationships. Unlike age-related memory decline and MCI, early-stage Alzheimer's is a more definitive and irreversible condition that will continue to worsen over time.

To distinguish between these conditions, healthcare providers often use a combination of cognitive assessments, medical history, and neurological exams. Key indicators that may help in the diagnosis include the severity and persistence of memory and cognitive symptoms, their impact on daily life, and the presence of other neurological signs or risk factors.

Know an unsung hero? Nominate for Stroke Awards
THE Stroke Foundation is seeking to uncover the inspirational unsung heroes making life better for Australia's stroke community.
Nominations for the 2016 Stroke Awards are now open, shining a light on the thousands of people working tirelessly to improve the lives of survivors, their families and carers in the community.
Stroke Foundation director of communications Mary Orgill said the awards recognised the outstanding Australians dedicated to supporting and advocating for stroke survivors and the broader stroke community.
"One in six people will have a stroke in their lifetime and there is one stroke in this country every 10 minutes. Its effects can be devastating. Helping stroke survivors and their families and carers negotiate the days, weeks and months after a stroke is vital work in our community,'' Ms Orgill said.
"We want to acknowledge the amazing individuals who carry out this important work and celebrate the stroke survivors, carers, health professionals and volunteers who improve the state of stroke in our country," she said.
"In holding the awards, we also want to raise awareness of stroke and the challenges faced by stroke survivors, their families and carers."
Nominations for the eighth annual awards open on March 29 and close on May 31.
There are five award categories, each highlighting an area where people are working to improve the lives of people affected by stroke.
This year will see the introduction of the Courage Award, recognising the indomitable spirit of survivors and carers facing tough recoveries after stroke.
Ms Orgill encouraged Australians to nominate people in their community.
making a difference.
"Every day we see incredible examples of people going above and beyond to lessen the significant burden stroke places on our community," she said.
"The Stroke Awards are one of the ways people can encourage support for stroke survivors, their families and carers, and increase awareness of how we can work together in the fight against stroke.
"I would encourage people to nominate the stroke champions in their community."
To nominate for the 2016 Stroke Awards, go to www.strokefoundation .com.au.
instruction: What are the key challenges faced by stroke survivors and their families, and how can community efforts and initiatives like the Stroke Awards help address these challenges?
response: Stroke survivors and their families face a multitude of challenges, including physical disabilities, cognitive and emotional issues, and the need for continuous care and support. Physically, survivors may struggle with mobility, speech, and other bodily functions, which can significantly impact their quality of life. Emotionally, the trauma of a stroke can lead to depression, anxiety, and social isolation. The burden on family members and carers is also substantial, often requiring them to take on new roles and responsibilities. Community initiatives like the Stroke Awards play a crucial role in addressing these challenges by acknowledging and celebrating the efforts of individuals who support stroke survivors. These awards not only provide recognition but also inspire others to contribute to the community. By highlighting the stories of survivors and their supporters, the Stroke Awards help to raise awareness, reduce stigma, and foster a more compassionate and supportive environment for those affected by stroke.

instruction: What factors are considered when deciding whether to prescribe anticonvulsants after a first seizure, and how does the diagnosis of epilepsy influence this decision?
response: The decision to prescribe anticonvulsants after a first seizure is a nuanced one, influenced by multiple factors. Key considerations include the cause of the seizure, the patient's overall health, and the likelihood of recurrence. For instance, if the seizure was triggered by a transient factor like a high fever or alcohol withdrawal, it may not recur once the trigger is removed, and anticonvulsants might not be necessary. On the other hand, if the seizure is unprovoked and the patient has risk factors such as a family history of epilepsy, a history of head trauma, or neurological abnormalities, anticonvulsants may be prescribed to prevent future seizures. The diagnosis of epilepsy, which is established after two or more unprovoked seizures at least 24 hours apart, plays a crucial role in this decision. In such cases, anticonvulsants are typically recommended to manage the condition and reduce the risk of additional seizures. Given that anticonvulsant therapy can be a long-term commitment, the decision must be carefully weighed to ensure that the benefits justify the potential side effects and long-term use.

Anyone can suffer a stroke, but there are several factors that put you at higher risk. Family health history, blood pressure and ethnicity are all factors that impact your chances of having a stroke.
What happens when you have a stroke?
Strokes happen when a blood vessel in your brain bursts or is blocked, starving your brain of oxygen. Because brain damage can occur within minutes of a stroke, seeking emergency medical care right away is vital and can decrease your risk of long-term effects or death.
What are the signs of a stroke?
The symptoms of a stroke include face drooping, slurred or confused speech, and weakness in one arm. Call 911 right away if you or someone around you shows any of these signs. Learn more about the signs and symptoms of a stroke.
Where can you go for stroke care?
The first step to stroke care is calling 911 immediately if someone displays the signs of a stroke. Even if you're not positive that a stroke is the cause, seek medical care without delay.
Some emergency rooms, like those at TriPoint and West medical centers, are certified by the Joint Commission as Primary Stroke Centers. Lake Health's Primary Stroke Centers offer a full range of care by a staff of experts, including Emergency Department physicians, neurologists and specially trained nurses who are dedicated to quick response, advanced treatment and comprehensive rehabilitation.
instruction: What are the primary risk factors that increase the likelihood of someone having a stroke, and how do they affect the brain's health?
response: Several key risk factors increase the likelihood of someone having a stroke, including family health history, blood pressure, and ethnicity. Family health history is crucial because it can indicate a genetic predisposition to conditions like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes, all of which are significant risk factors for stroke. High blood pressure, in particular, is a leading cause of stroke because it weakens and damages the blood vessels in the brain, making them more vulnerable to rupture or blockage. Ethnicity also influences stroke risk, with some groups, such as African Americans and Hispanic Americans, experiencing higher rates of stroke due to a combination of genetic and socioeconomic factors. During a stroke, a blood vessel in the brain either bursts or is blocked, cutting off the supply of oxygen to the brain. This oxygen deprivation can lead to the rapid death of brain cells, causing brain damage and potentially severe long-term disabilities or death. Immediate medical attention is critical to minimize the extent of brain damage and improve the chances of recovery.

instruction: What are the potential long-term health risks associated with the recreational use of nitrous oxide, and how do these risks vary depending on the frequency and environment of use?
response: The recreational use of nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, can lead to a range of long-term health risks, which can vary significantly depending on the frequency and environment of use. Olivia Golding, a 24-year-old from Bristol, shared her personal experience of becoming paralyzed after inhaling nitrous oxide. Research shows that diet plays an important role in cognitive health and the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine has developed new dietary guidelines for the prevention of Alzheimer’s disease. The guidelines are similar to a heart healthy diet and include adding certain vitamins and avoiding excess metals such as iron and copper.
Good nutrition the best medicine
Alzheimer’s disease strikes nearly half of Americans who live to at least the age of 85. According to the American Academy of Neurology, the proportion of people affected by Alzheimer’s is expected to triple in the next forty years. The Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine, a nonprofit organization that conducts clinical research and advocates good nutrition as preventive medicine, doesn’t want to let that happen.
The PCRM presented their guidelines in a report titled “Dietary Guidelines for Alzheimer’s Prevention” at the International Conference on Nutrition and the Brain held in Washington DC in July.
“The current generation of clinicians is in a battle over food — especially Alzheimer’s-promoting foods, such as those which contain saturated and trans fats,” said Neal Barnard, MD, PCRM president and lead author of the guidelines. “We potentially have the capabilities to prevent a disease that is poised to affect 100 million people worldwide by 2050. Why wait?”
Eating for Alzheimer’s prevention
Research has shown that a heart healthy diet is also good for the brain. Studies have produced evidence that preventive measures including certain foods and regular exercise can reduce the risk of getting Alzheimer’s disease by 50 percent or more. The PCRM recommends avoiding saturated and trans fats, framing the diet around plant-based foods, adding sources of vitamin E and B and avoiding potentially harmful metals.
According to the guidelines, diet staples should include vegetables, legumes (beans, peas, and lentils), fruits, and whole grains. The diet is built upon foods that have little or no saturated fat or trans fats and are rich in vitamins, such as folate and vitamin B6, that play protective roles for brain health.
Get your vitamins
Vitamin E is an antioxidant associated with reduced Alzheimer’s risk found in many foods, particularly nuts and seeds. Other good sources include mangoes, papayas, avocadoes, tomatoes red bell peppers spinach, and fortified breakfast cereals.
Three B-vitamins—folate, B6, and B12—have been proven essential for cognitive function. These vitamins work together to reduce levels of homocysteine, an amino acid linked to cognitive impairment. Good folate sources include leafy greens, such as broccoli, kale, and spinach. Other sources include beans, peas, citrus fruits, and cantaloupe. Vitamin B6 is found in green vegetables in addition to beans, whole grains, bananas, nuts, and sweet potatoes.
According to the PCRM, iron and copper are essential nutrients most people get plenty of from everyday foods. Excessive iron and copper intake has been linked to cognitive problems and the committee recommends using multivitamins without added metals. Avoiding the use of cookware, antacids, baking powder, or other products that contribute dietary aluminum is also recommended.
In addition to documenting the foods to indulge in as well as avoid, the PCRM recommends engaging in aerobic exercise equivalent to at least 40 minutes of brisk walking 3 times per week.
Cause and effect
Medical and Alzheimer’s experts commenting on the PCRM guidelines cautioned that the recommendations are supported merely by correlations that have been found between diet and cognitive health, not hard evidence that eating certain foods will ensure mental acuity in old age. However, there is certainly no harm in eating a healthy diet and getting plenty of exercise. The cause and effect of taking better care of yourself can be observed every day of your life.
instruction: How can a diet rich in plant-based foods and specific vitamins contribute to the prevention of Alzheimer’s disease, and what are some practical ways to incorporate these dietary recommendations into daily meals?
response: A diet rich in plant-based foods and specific vitamins plays a crucial role in the prevention of Alzheimer’s disease. The Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine (PCRM) has outlined dietary guidelines that emphasize the importance of a heart-healthy diet for cognitive health. Key recommendations include avoiding foods high in saturated and trans fats and focusing on plant-based foods, such as vegetables, legumes, fruits, and whole grains. These foods are low in harmful fats and rich in essential vitamins that support brain health. Vitamin E, an antioxidant, can be obtained from nuts, seeds, mangoes, papayas, avocados, tomatoes, red bell peppers, and spinach. Vitamin E has been associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Additionally, three B-vitamins—folate, B6, and B12—are vital for cognitive function. Folate can be found in leafy greens like broccoli, kale, and spinach, as well as beans, peas, citrus fruits, and cantaloupe. Vitamin B6 is present in green vegetables, beans, whole grains, bananas, nuts, and sweet potatoes. To incorporate these recommendations into your daily meals, you can start with a breakfast of fortified cereal and a smoothie made with spinach, banana, and nuts. For lunch, try a quinoa salad with chickpeas, cherry tomatoes, and a variety of colorful vegetables. Dinner could be a vegetable stir-fry with tofu, served over brown rice. Snacks can include fresh fruits, mixed nuts, and whole-grain crackers. Along with these dietary changes, engaging in regular aerobic exercise, such as 40 minutes of brisk walking three times a week, can further support cognitive health and potentially reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

Overview on Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia (HSP) Treatment
HSP is a group of inherited conditions whose primary feature is progressive gait disorder. It presents with contraction and spasticity of the lower limbs. Though the condition has no cure, it can be managed. Regular physical therapy is important to improve and maintain the muscle strength and range of movement.
