By Tom Nugent, Pure Matters
First, you burned breakfast. Then, you were late for work. And on your way home, the car had a flat tire, making you miss your daughter's softball game.
Now you've got this throbbing headache that has gone from a minor annoyance to a major jackhammer pounding away in your skull.
And this jackhammer crew keeps busy: An estimated 45 million Americans suffer from chronic headaches, according to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) and the American College of Physicians. In fact, for half that number, that pounding pain will be severe and possibly disabling.
For most of us, though, relief is as close as the medicine cabinet: About 90 percent of all headaches are harmless episodes that can be treated with over-the-counter (OTC) painkillers—alone or together with rest, ice packs, or relaxation techniques.
Just what is a headache?
Most often, that pain is caused by one of two things:
- An inflammation, spasm, or stretching in the scalp, in the membranes that cover the brain, and in the muscles of the face and jaw.
- A temporary distortion of the blood vessels that supply the brain. They tighten, then relax and expand. The enlarged blood vessels press against nerves, causing pain. A shortage of serotonin, a chemical in the brain, can cause the vessels to constrict.
In general, headaches fall into three classes: tension, migraine, and cluster.
instruction: How do tension, migraine, and cluster headaches differ, and what are some effective treatment options for each type?
response:
Tension, migraine, and cluster headaches are distinct in their symptoms, causes, and treatment approaches. Tension headaches are the most prevalent and are often described as a constant, dull ache or pressure that feels like a tight band around the head. They can be triggered by stress, muscle strain, or poor posture. Over-the-counter pain relievers such as ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and aspirin are effective for most people, along with relaxation techniques like deep breathing, meditation, and physical therapy to address muscle tension.

Migraines are more severe and can be highly disruptive. They are characterized by intense, throbbing pain, often on one side of the head, and can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. Migraines can be triggered by various factors, including hormonal changes, certain foods, and environmental stimuli. Treatment options include prescription medications like triptans and anti-nausea drugs, as well as preventive measures such as beta-blockers, anticonvulsants, and lifestyle modifications to avoid triggers.

Cluster headaches are the least common but the most painful, featuring intense, one-sided pain around the eye, often with tearing and nasal congestion. They typically occur in clusters, lasting for weeks or months. Oxygen therapy is a highly effective treatment, providing rapid relief, while medications like sumatriptan can also be used. Preventive strategies include corticosteroids and nerve blocks to reduce the frequency and severity of attacks.

New Epilepsy Gene Discovered in Dogs May Help Humans
Dogs are not only man’s best friend, they also suffer many of the same diseases as their human companions, and what we learn about a condition in one species often can help the other. Such may be the case with a new epilepsy gene discovered in dogs.
Epilepsy is common in some dog breeds
Epilepsy syndrome can be divided into genetic (idiopathic) epilepsies, structural/metabolic (symptomatic) epilepsies, and epilepsies of unknown cause. Idiopathic epilepsy occurs in up to 3% of dogs, according to the Dog Owner’s Home Veterinary Handbook, and is responsible for up to 80% of recurrent seizures.
The common thread among the three main types of epilepsy is recurring seizures, which can appear in various forms and are divided into two main types: focal and generalized. Focal (partial) seizures are electrical disturbances that occur in a limited area of the brain, while generalized seizures affect the entire brain.
Both dogs and people can experience either type of seizure, and both types can occur in Belgian Shepherds, the dog breed that was the focus of a recent study by Professor Hannes Lohi and his team from the University of Helsinki and the Folkhalsan Research Center. Their discovery of a chromosome region associated with the most common form of epilepsy in dogs is a major breakthrough.
Although previous research had uncovered several genes involved in the development of symptomatic epilepsies, the genetic foundation of idiopathic epilepsies was unknown. Lohi and his colleagues compared the genome of dogs with epilepsy and healthy controls and found a gene region in chromosome 37 which, if homozygous, increases the risk of developing epilepsy by sevenfold. (Homozygous means having identical DNA coding on a specific location on a chromosome for a single trait.)
The discovery is exciting because this is the first time epilepsy genes have been identified in this chromosome region, so this new find will reveal a new epilepsy gene in dogs and perhaps also in humans. “I believe that the ongoing analyses will help us to discover the specific epilepsy gene,” noted Lohi.
In addition, Lohi explained that their discovery will “give us a better understanding of the disease mechanisms and provide us with new diagnostic tools for the disease.” Continuing research into epilepsy is important for all dogs, and especially those that tend to inherit the condition, including Beagles, Dachshunds, Keeshonden German Shepherds, Belgian Shepherds, and others.
Eija Seppala, PhD, first author of the new research article, explained they are trying to “identify the specific mutation for genetic testing” at chromosome 37 and possibly other chromosomes. Seppala described the need for a gene test as “urgent” because up to 20% of Belgian Shepherds are believed to have epilepsy.
Epilepsy in dogs
Epileptic seizures in dogs usually occur in three phases: aura, grand mal seizures, and postseizure state. During the aura, dogs typically become restless, cry, demand affection, or try to be alone. The seizure itself usually causes the dog to collapse and the legs to become rigid. Dogs become unconscious, may stop breathing for 10 to 30 seconds, and may have jerking legs, chewing or drooling behavior, and loss of bladder and bowel control.
As the dog regains consciousness, he or she enters the postseizure stage, characterized by staring, stumbling while walking, and confusion, which may last several minutes or up to several hours.
Epilepsy is the most common nervous system disorder in dogs, and different types of genetic epilepsies are seen in dozens of dog breeds. According to the Dog Owner’s Home Veterinary Handbook, it’s important to identify which dogs are carriers of genes for epilepsy before they are bred, as “no dog known to seizure from suspected epilepsy should be bred.”
Thus the discovery of a new gene for epilepsy in dogs is an important step in identifying which dogs have the seizure disorder, and it may also prove helpful in better understanding the more than 50 million people in the world who also have epilepsy.

instruction: How might the discovery of a new epilepsy gene in dogs contribute to our understanding and treatment of epilepsy in humans?
response: The discovery of a new epilepsy gene in dogs, specifically in Belgian Shepherds, holds significant promise for advancing our understanding and treatment of epilepsy in humans. Professor Hannes Lohi and his team's identification of a chromosome region on chromosome 37 that increases the risk of epilepsy by sevenfold is a major breakthrough. This region has not been previously associated with epilepsy, making it a novel finding that could lead to the discovery of a new epilepsy gene. The genetic basis of idiopathic epilepsy, which is common in both dogs and humans, has been largely unknown until now. By understanding the specific genetic mutations and mechanisms involved in canine epilepsy, researchers can apply this knowledge to human epilepsy. This can lead to the development of more accurate diagnostic tools and more effective treatments. Moreover, the ongoing research by Lohi and his team, aimed at identifying the specific mutation for genetic testing, could provide a valuable resource for both veterinary and medical practitioners. The urgent need for a gene test in dogs, especially in breeds like Belgian Shepherds where up to 20% of the population may have epilepsy, underscores the importance of this discovery. Ultimately, this research can contribute to better management and potentially even prevention of epilepsy in both dogs and humans.

Joe Swash, 38, is the cheeky chappy who’s shown TV audiences his vast array of talents. The star won a place in the nation’s heart when he played the character of Mickey Miller in the soap EastEnders back in 2003. Since then, Joe has had a string of appearances in presenting roles including becoming a permanent fixture on I’m A Celebrity Get Me Out Of Here. However it’s his latest appearance and fancy footwork that has seen many fans love him even more.
- Paddy McGuinness health: Presenter’s shock diagnosis at the age of 44
To say Joe has had a tough time of late is an understatement.
The star was taken to hospital for the second time after suffering an ear injury earlier in the week when he was kicked in the head with an ice skate.
The ghastly wound left his dream of competing in the final hanging in the balance.
Joe underwent surgery a few days ago to help drain his ear of the buildup of ‘goo’ caused by the injury after it became infected.
Speaking on Instagram and giving his fans an update of his ordeal, Joe said: “I went to hospital and my ear swelled up again and they had to drain it, which was honestly the worst feeling in the world.
“But the worst feeling in the world is that I think the bandage has got bigger.”
Joe has been sporting a rather large bandage around his head lately much to the amusement of his partner Stacey Solomon.
Despite the seriousness of Joe’s condition, the Loose Women presenter found the funny side after Joe returned home wearing the protective headgear following his operation.
Continuing on Instagram, Joe added: “I thought we’d get the elephant out of the room and talk about this stupid, ridiculous bandage on my head.
“So basically what happened was me and Al were doing disco dad and her skate kicked me in the ear which gave me cauliflower ear.
“Then it got infected which meant last night I had to get rushed to the hospital and have an operation on it and cut it open and drain out all the gooey stuff. “
- Freddie Flintoff health: Cricket star’s health battle
Sadly for Joe, serious health conditions are something he has experienced before.
At 23, Joe was struck down by a sudden case of viral meningitis. The serious condition causes the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord to become inflamed.
The condition is potentially life-threatening and left untreated, it could lead to brain swelling and cause permanent disability, coma and even death.
Symptoms of the condition include nausea, muscle pain, fever, cold hands or feet, confusion and severe headaches.
For Joe it was back to basics after recovering from meningitis. “I had to learn coordination and my speech was slurred.
“It felt like my tongue was too big for my mouth. And I had terrible headaches,” the actor recalled.
After gruelling physiotherapy sessions, Joe made a full recovery and was back to his old ways.
Ever the fighter, Joe is feeling much better and was given the OK to skate in the final by a doctor earlier today.
Joe will be taking his fighting spirit on the ice competing against Libby Clegg and Mark Hanretty, and Perri Kiely and Vanessa Bauer to see who’s the ultimate dancer.

instruction: What are the potential long-term effects of viral meningitis, and how does recovery from such a condition typically involve physical and cognitive rehabilitation?
response: The long-term effects of viral meningitis can vary widely, but they often include cognitive and physical challenges that require rehabilitation. Joe Swash, who battled viral meningitis at 23, experienced significant issues such as slurred speech, difficulty with coordination, and severe headaches. His recovery involved intensive physiotherapy to rebuild his physical strength and coordination, as well as speech therapy to improve his speech clarity. Additionally, cognitive rehabilitation might be necessary for patients to regain memory, concentration, and other cognitive functions. The recovery process is typically multifaceted, combining physical and cognitive therapies to ensure a comprehensive return to normal functioning. For many, the road to recovery is challenging but ultimately rewarding with the right support and interventions.

Multiple Sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system. Mostly it strikes between the ages of 20 and 40, but can be exhibited at any age.
More women have the disease than men, and it may have a genetic connection. Health officials think it may be related to a virus that lies dormant in cells.
MS is caused by damage to the myelin sheath, the protective covering that surrounds nerve cells. When covering is damaged, nerve signals slow down or stop.
Nerve damage is caused by inflammation that occurs when the body’s immune cells attack the nervous system. This can occur along any area of the brain, optic nerve and spinal cord. Scar tissue develops where the myelin is damaged and this is what disrupts nerve messages.
Symptoms may abate ,and remissions last for months or years. More damage is done with each episode.
No cure has been found, but therapies can slow the disease’s progress. Treatment can control symptoms. Treatments include drugs to reduce muscle spasms and urinary problems; antidepressants and drugs to reduce fatigue.
Diagnosing MS often is a tedious process of eliminating other possibilities. A CT scan and an MRI may help physicians decide the symptoms are MS-related, along with a lumbar puncture to test spinal fluid.
Symptoms can be across a broad spectrum, including loss of balance, muscle spasms, abnormal reflex responses, numbness, weakness and tremors.
Physical therapy can help strengthen muscles and retrain muscles affected by the disease.
It is estimated 2.5 million people are living with MS, about 400,000 in the United States.

instruction: What are the common methods used to diagnose Multiple Sclerosis, and why is the process often described as tedious and complex?
response: The diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is often described as tedious and complex due to the variability and nonspecific nature of its symptoms. Common diagnostic methods include a detailed clinical assessment, where a healthcare provider evaluates the patient's medical history and performs a physical examination to identify symptoms such as balance issues, muscle spasms, and sensory disturbances. Imaging techniques, particularly MRI scans, are crucial for detecting lesions in the brain, optic nerve, and spinal cord that are indicative of MS. CT scans can also be used, though MRI is more sensitive. A lumbar puncture (spinal tap) is another key diagnostic tool, as it allows for the analysis of cerebrospinal fluid for the presence of oligoclonal bands, which are a hallmark of MS. The process is often lengthy because it requires ruling out other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, such as Lyme disease, viral infections, and other autoimmune disorders. This comprehensive approach ensures a more accurate diagnosis but adds to the complexity and duration of the diagnostic journey.

Cardiology jobs involve treating patients with cardiovascular disease as well as patients who are at risk for a stroke or who have already suffered a stroke. Most readers will be familiar with the largest risk factors for stroke: age, elevated blood pressure, smoking, and having diabetes. However, there are additional risk factors that only a cardiologist or other qualified physician can diagnose: left ventricular hypertrophy and atrial fibrillation (two types of abnormal heart function). Normally, patients with controllable risk factors like smoking, diabetes, being overweight, etc., can reduce the risk to their health by controlling their diabetes, reducing their weight, exercising, and being treated by a qualified physician.
The most basic way to understand a stroke is by thinking of all the blood vessels that connect the heart with the brain (the vessels that connect these two organs are called arteries). The human brain is like the central command center of the body, and each of the arteries brings blood (and oxygen!) to a specific part of the brain. When a stroke occurs, one of these arteries is either blocked, or it bursts, causing an area of the brain to lose access to the nourishment it would normally receive. This cutoff from its usual supply of blood causes the deprived part of the brain to die.
The effects on the patient depend in large part upon which area of the brain is deprived of oxygen. For example, the general areas of the brain that can be affected by stroke include the areas that govern speech, motor function, sensory function, hearing, language comprehension, emotions, vision, and balance. An interesting detail about the way that the brain controls the body is that the right and left hemispheres of the brain control opposite sides of the body – so, for instance, the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body and is associated with figuring out science problems, math, and with number skills. The right hemisphere is associated with artistic skills, creativity, and other features.
An ischemic stroke is the term used when a blood clot blocks an artery, thereby cutting off the flow of oxygen-rich blood to a part of the brain. This type of stroke is the most common, but unfortunately, it is also the type where survivors are most likely to have problems using certain parts of their bodies. The second type of stroke is called a hemorrhagic stroke, and occurs when a blood vessel in the brain bursts and spills blood into the brain. Brain aneurysms and high blood pressure can cause these types of stroke to occur.
There are several ways to reduce the risk of a stroke. For one, patients should monitor their own blood pressure and make sure that their doctor does as well – high blood pressure is an important risk factor for stroke. Second, patients should consult a qualified cardiologist if they have atrial fibrillation (and irregular heartbeat that can make blood pool or form clots more easily). Patients who smoke should try to quit as soon as possible, and those that drink should do so only in moderation. Overweight patients or those with high cholesterol should work on lowering their total cholesterol numbers as well as their body weight; diabetic patients should keep their disease under control as much as they are able. Eating a balanced diet with plenty of fruits and vegetables along with including plenty of exercise are recommended as well for all patients.
instruction: What are the primary differences between ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes, and how do these differences affect the treatment and potential outcomes for patients?
response: The primary differences between ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes lie in their mechanisms and the resulting impacts on brain function and patient outcomes. An ischemic stroke is caused by a blockage in an artery, usually due to a blood clot, which cuts off the supply of oxygen-rich blood to a specific part of the brain. This type of stroke is the most prevalent and often results in long-term disabilities, especially in areas controlled by the affected part of the brain, such as speech, motor skills, and sensory function. Treatment for ischemic strokes typically involves the administration of thrombolytic medications to dissolve the clot, antiplatelet agents to prevent new clots, and lifestyle changes to reduce risk factors. In contrast, a hemorrhagic stroke occurs when a blood vessel in the brain bursts, leading to bleeding into the brain tissue. This can cause significant swelling and increased intracranial pressure, which can be life-threatening. Treatment for hemorrhagic strokes focuses on managing blood pressure, reducing intracranial pressure, and sometimes surgical procedures to stop the bleeding or repair the ruptured vessel. The outcomes for hemorrhagic stroke patients can be more severe, with higher mortality rates and a greater likelihood of severe brain damage.

instruction: How can recognizing and responding quickly to stroke symptoms potentially improve the outcome for someone experiencing a stroke?
response: Quickly recognizing and responding to stroke symptoms is crucial for improving the outcome of a stroke. The F.A.S.T. method—Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call 911—helps in identifying stroke symptoms promptly. When these symptoms are detected early, it allows for immediate medical intervention, which is essential for effective treatment. Early treatment can prevent further brain damage, reduce the severity of the stroke, and lower the risk of long-term complications. For instance, administering thrombolytic drugs like tPA within the first few hours of symptom onset can dissolve blood clots and improve blood flow to the brain. This timely action can lead to better functional outcomes and a higher likelihood of recovery for the patient.

instruction: How does alcoholic neuropathy compare to other forms of neuropathy in terms of symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment options, and what unique challenges does it present for healthcare providers?
response:
Alcoholic neuropathy is a type of peripheral neuropathy that results from chronic alcohol abuse and is characterized by damage to the peripheral nerves. Symptoms of alcoholic neuropathy can include numbness, tingling, burning pain, muscle weakness, and coordination issues, particularly in the extremities. In severe cases, it can also affect the autonomic nervous system, leading to issues such as incontinence and sexual dysfunction. Diagnosis of alcoholic neuropathy typically involves a thorough medical history, physical examination, and sometimes nerve conduction studies and blood tests to rule out other causes. Treatment often includes pain management, physical therapy, and addressing nutritional deficiencies, particularly thiamine deficiency, which is common in alcoholics.

Compared to other forms of neuropathy, such as diabetic neuropathy, alcoholic neuropathy can have a more variable and sometimes rapid onset of symptoms. Diabetic neuropathy, which is caused by high blood sugar levels over time, usually develops more gradually and is often associated with other complications of diabetes. The diagnosis of diabetic neuropathy typically involves blood glucose testing and monitoring. Treatment for diabetic neuropathy focuses on controlling blood sugar levels, which can help slow the progression of nerve damage. Both conditions can benefit from lifestyle modifications, such as a healthy diet and regular exercise, but the underlying causes and specific treatment approaches differ.

Healthcare providers face unique challenges when treating alcoholic neuropathy, including addressing the underlying alcohol abuse and managing potential comorbidities such as liver disease and nutritional deficiencies. Effective treatment often requires a multidisciplinary approach, involving addiction specialists, nutritionists, and pain management specialists, to address the complex needs of the patient.

text:
Content and Effectiveness of Interventions Focusing on Community Participation Poststroke: A Systematic Review
© 2019 American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine Objective: To investigate the content and effectiveness of interventions that address poststroke community participation. Data Sources: EMBASE, PsycINFO, PubMed, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health (CINAHL) were searched using 3 indexing terms and respective thesaurus: stroke, social participation, and clinical trials. Filters for English, publication dates (January 2001-May 2017), and publication types were used. The search also included checking references from relevant systematic reviews. Study Selection: Studies conducted with adults with stroke, evaluating interventions addressing community participation, having a comparison group, and reporting at least 1 of 3 outcomes (participation, depression, and health-related quality of life) were selected. Retrieved articles were screened by 2 reviewers. After substantial agreement was achieved using interrater reliability, reviewers screened articles independently. Eighteen of 1130 articles were included. Data Extraction: Characteristics of participants, key elements of intervention, comparator, and results were independently extracted by 2 reviewers. Intervention content was categorized based on 9 categories from the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health Activities and Participation domains. Risk of selection, performance, attrition, and reporting bias were evaluated. Data Synthesis: Two intervention categories were identified: leisure participation and community integration. Three leisure and 4 community integration interventions showed significant group differences favoring the intervention group in the target outcomes. The majority of interventions addressed the leisure, interpersonal relations, and community life categories of International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health with few focusing on political life, education, assisting others, and religion. Conclusions: A limited number of studies showed an effect on participation, depression, and health-related quality of life outcomes. There were gaps in intervention content indicating that current community participation interventions fall short in addressing full inclusion and citizenship of people with stroke. Future interventions should focus on civic- and societal-level participation and community activities beyond leisure.
Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
Lee, Danbi; Heffron, Jenna L.; and Mirza, Mansha, "Content and Effectiveness of Interventions Focusing on Community Participation Poststroke: A Systematic Review" (2019). Faculty Articles Indexed in Scopus. 152.
instruction: What are the main categories of interventions that have been found to be effective in improving community participation for individuals post-stroke, and what specific outcomes have these interventions targeted?
response: Effective interventions for improving community participation in individuals post-stroke can be broadly categorized into two main types: leisure participation and community integration. These interventions have aimed to enhance outcomes such as participation, depression, and health-related quality of life. Among the studies reviewed, three leisure participation interventions and four community integration interventions demonstrated significant improvements in the target outcomes. The interventions primarily focused on the ICF domains of leisure, interpersonal relations, and community life. However, there were notable gaps in addressing areas such as political life, education, and religious activities. This suggests that current interventions are not fully inclusive and may not promote comprehensive societal engagement. Future research should aim to develop and evaluate interventions that target a broader range of participation domains to better support the full integration and citizenship of individuals post-stroke.

instruction: What are the potential side effects of tramadol on the central nervous system, and how do they compare to those of other common analgesics?
response: Tramadol can cause a range of side effects on the central nervous system, including initial stimulation with excitement, delusions, and convulsions, followed by more severe symptoms such as increased respiration, a rise in blood pressure, and ultimately paralysis with cold extremities, weak pulse, and respiration, leading to coma. Muscular twitching, which is not prevented by division of motor nerves, is another potential side effect. These effects are generally dose-dependent and can be quite serious. In comparison, other common analgesics like NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) and acetaminophen have milder central nervous system effects. NSAIDs can cause drowsiness and dizziness, while acetaminophen is generally well-tolerated with minimal CNS side effects. Opioids like morphine can cause sedation, respiratory depression, and cognitive impairment, which are more pronounced than those seen with tramadol. However, the risk of these severe CNS effects with tramadol is still significant, especially at high doses or in individuals with pre-existing conditions.

instruction: What are the key considerations and preparations that should be made in the workplace to ensure the safety and well-being of an employee with epilepsy, particularly in the event of a seizure?
response: To ensure the safety and well-being of an employee with epilepsy in the workplace, several key considerations and preparations should be made, particularly in the event of a seizure. First, the employee should be asked to provide detailed information about their condition, including the type of epilepsy, frequency of seizures, and any specific triggers. This information can help tailor the workplace environment to minimize risks. For instance, the workplace should be arranged to minimize potential hazards such as sharp objects, heavy machinery, or heights. A designated safe area should be identified where the employee can go if they feel a seizure coming on, ensuring privacy and a clear, uncluttered space. This area should have a comfortable mat and be equipped with any necessary medical supplies, including emergency medication. The employee's care plan should be readily accessible, and all relevant staff should be aware of it, including instructions on what to do if a seizure lasts longer than a specified time. A trained first aider should be available to assist during and after a seizure, and the employee should be given the option to have a buddy or designated member of staff accompany them. Additionally, the workplace should have a clear protocol for contacting emergency services and the employee's named contacts. Regular rest breaks and reasonable adjustments, such as flexible working hours, should be considered to help the employee manage their condition effectively. Finally, the employee should have the option to inform their colleagues about their epilepsy, and a supportive and understanding workplace culture should be fostered.

What age does dementia usually start?
Dementia is more common in people over the age of 65, but it can also affect younger people.
Early onset of the disease can begin when people are in their 30s, 40s, or 50s.
With treatment and early diagnosis, you can slow the progression of the disease and maintain mental function..
Can early dementia be seen on MRI?
MRI can detect brain abnormalities associated with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and can be used to predict which patients with MCI may eventually develop Alzheimer’s disease. In the early stages of Alzheimer’s disease, an MRI scan of the brain may be normal.
Can a brain scan show memory loss?
A UCLA-led study has found that MRI scans can help doctors distinguish whether a person’s memory loss is being caused by Alzheimer’s disease or by traumatic brain injury. The study, which also involved researchers at Washington University in St.

What should you not say to someone with dementia?
Avoid asking the person questions about the past; rather, tell your own stories that don’t involve the person’s input (Ex. “I remember I loved chocolate ice cream when I was little.”) Avoid distractions. Don’t try to converse with a person with dementia if the environment is loud and/or chaotic.
Do you see a neurologist for memory loss?
He or she may also order blood tests and brain-imaging tests that can help identify reversible causes of memory problems and dementia-like symptoms. You might be referred to a specialist in diagnosing dementia or memory disorders, such as a neurologist, psychiatrist, psychologist or geriatrician.
What is the 30 question cognitive test?
The Mini–Mental State Examination (MMSE) or Folstein test is a 30-point questionnaire that is used extensively in clinical and research settings to measure cognitive impairment. It is commonly used in medicine and allied health to screen for dementia.
Can dementia get worse suddenly?
Symptoms of vascular dementia are similar to Alzheimer’s disease, although memory loss may not be as obvious in the early stages. Symptoms can sometimes develop suddenly and quickly get worse, but they can also develop gradually over many months or years.
Can dementia be seen on a brain scan?
Dementia brain scans Brain scans are often used for diagnosing dementia once the simpler tests have ruled out other problems. Like memory tests, on their own brain scans cannot diagnose dementia, but are used as part of the wider assessment.
How does peanut butter detect Alzheimer’s?

How quickly can dementia progress?
Rapidly progressive dementias (RPDs) are dementias that progress quickly, typically over the course of weeks to months, but sometimes up to two to three years. RPDs are rare and often difficult to diagnose. Early and accurate diagnosis is very important because many causes of RPDs can be treated.
instruction: What are some common medical conditions that can be mistaken for dementia, and how can they be distinguished from true dementia?
response: Several medical conditions can be mistaken for dementia due to overlapping symptoms. For instance, head trauma, which can occur from falls or accidents, may lead to cognitive impairment that mimics dementia. Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is another condition where the buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain can cause symptoms like memory loss, difficulty walking, and incontinence. Vision and hearing problems can also be misdiagnosed as dementia, as individuals might struggle with communication and understanding. Cardiovascular issues, such as heart and lung diseases, can reduce blood flow to the brain, leading to cognitive symptoms. Liver and kidney diseases can cause toxin buildup, affecting brain function. Hormonal imbalances, such as thyroid disorders, can also mimic dementia. Infections, particularly those affecting the brain like encephalitis or meningitis, can cause cognitive impairment. To distinguish these conditions from true dementia, a comprehensive evaluation is necessary, including detailed medical history, physical examination, cognitive tests, and brain imaging like MRI or CT scans. Blood tests and other diagnostic procedures can also help identify specific causes.

instruction: What are the potential benefits and limitations of using a gluten-free diet as a management strategy for epilepsy, and how effective is it in reducing seizure frequency?
response: The use of a gluten-free diet (GFD) in managing epilepsy has gained attention due to its potential benefits, but it also comes with certain limitations. Studies suggest that GFD can be effective in reducing seizure frequency in about 53% of cases. This reduction in seizures may be attributed to the diet's impact on reducing inflammation and improving gut health, which can affect the brain's function. For individuals with gluten sensitivity or celiac disease, GFD can be particularly beneficial. However, the effectiveness of GFD varies among individuals, and it is not a universal solution for all cases of epilepsy. The diet can be challenging to adhere to, as it requires careful monitoring and avoidance of gluten-containing foods, which can be socially and practically difficult. Moreover, there is a lack of extensive long-term studies to fully understand the sustained benefits and potential side effects of GFD in epilepsy management. Therefore, while GFD can be a helpful adjunct to traditional treatments, it should be implemented with the oversight of a healthcare professional and tailored to the individual's specific needs.

Night leg cramps are described as painful muscle contractions or tightening, which appear during the night. They are defined as sudden muscle spasms, usually felt in the lower leg, but you can also feel them in the thighs and feet.
The pain can be very sharp, which usually causes the person to wake up. It can last from a few seconds to few minutes. When the pain is gone, you can still feel the muscles sore. This condition may continue during the whole night and the next day. Men and women older than 50, are usually affected by this syndrome.
What’s the difference between leg cramps and restless leg syndrome?
It is true that both these conditions occur at night when in bed, but they are actually very different. Restless leg syndrome is a neurological disorder. When experiencing it, you have an uncontrollable urge to move your legs. While doing that, you feel an instant relief. The leg cramps are totally different. Certain medications, standing on concrete floors, pregnancy, alcoholism, sedentary position for longer period of time, bad sitting posture, and some exercises can be the risk factors for the occurrence of leg cramps.
Preventing leg cramps: What to do?
- The best thing you can do is taking a hot bath before going to bed.
- Perform water exercises to build and shape the leg muscles.
- Make sure you always stretch your legs before bedtime.
- Get enough intake of potassium and magnesium.
- Use horse chestnut to improve blood circulation.
- It’s important to wear ergonomic shoes.
- Put a heating pad to the affected area.
How to relieve the spasms?
- Start by putting your legs in front of you and then sit on the ground. After that, bend the knees and position the toes toward the knees.
- It’s important to get up slowly and then turn around a bit. To stimulate the blood flow, shake your legs.
- By making circular motions, rub the area gently.
- Take a teaspoon of yellow mustard.
instruction: How do leg cramps differ from restless leg syndrome in terms of symptoms and underlying causes, and what are some common risk factors for each condition?
response:
Leg cramps and restless leg syndrome (RLS) differ significantly in their symptoms and underlying causes. Leg cramps are characterized by sudden, painful muscle contractions or spasms that typically occur in the lower leg, thighs, or feet. These cramps often wake a person up at night and can last from a few seconds to several minutes, leaving the muscles sore afterward. The pain and soreness can persist for hours or even the next day. Leg cramps are more common in individuals over 50 and can be triggered by factors such as certain medications, standing on concrete floors, pregnancy, alcoholism, prolonged sedentary positions, poor sitting posture, and specific exercises.

On the other hand, restless leg syndrome is a neurological disorder that causes an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, often accompanied by uncomfortable or painful sensations. Moving the legs provides temporary relief. RLS typically occurs during periods of rest, especially at night, and can significantly disrupt sleep. The exact cause of RLS is not fully understood, but it is often associated with genetic factors, iron deficiency, and certain medical conditions such as Parkinson's disease, kidney failure, and diabetes.

Common risk factors for leg cramps include age (over 50), certain medications, prolonged standing on hard surfaces, pregnancy, alcohol consumption, and sedentary lifestyles. For RLS, risk factors include a family history of the condition, low iron levels, chronic diseases like Parkinson's and kidney failure, and pregnancy.

instruction: How does the consumption of Monosodium Glutamate (MSG) affect cognitive function and brain health, and what are the potential long-term implications for individuals exposed to high levels of MSG in their diet?
response: The consumption of Monosodium Glutamate (MSG) has been shown to have significant effects on cognitive function and brain health, particularly in the context of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative conditions. Studies in animal models, such as the double transgenic mice App/PS1, have demonstrated that oral administration of MSG can accelerate the development of AD-like pathophysiology. Specifically, MSG administration led to increased levels of amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau phosphorylation (p-tau) in the hippocampus, a brain region crucial for memory and learning. These changes were associated with increased Cdk5-p25 activity and impaired long-term potentiation, which are critical for synaptic plasticity and memory formation. Furthermore, cognitive deficits were observed in the Hebb-Williams maze test, indicating that MSG can negatively impact cognitive function. The long-term implications of high MSG consumption may include an increased risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases, particularly in individuals with genetic predispositions to AD.

It is estimated that there are more than 350 cases of stroke in Gosford City per year and, during Stroke Week, the Central Coast Local Health District is raising awareness of the impact that time has on a stroke.
Stroke kills more women than breast cancer and more men than prostate cancer, and is a leading cause of disability. District Neurologist and Stroke Staff Specialist, Dr Bill O’Brien, said that a speedy reaction not only infl uences the treatment path for a person having a stroke but also their recovery. “Most treatments for stroke are time sensitive, as around 1.9 million brain cells are lost per minute during a stroke’, he said. Erina woman, Ms Barbara Ardas, 69, suffered a massive stroke while out for a walk with her husband, Tony, in May. If not for the quick reaction of neighbours, Barbara’s stroke could have ended in tragedy. “I was just walking along and then all of a sudden I couldn’t breathe and got wobbly,” she said.
My husband asked if I was ok and the next minute I collapsed onto the footpath,” she said. Neighbours rushed to the aid of the pair, recognising that Barbara was having a stroke and immediately calling an ambulance to rush her to Gosford Hospital. At the time Barbara couldn’t speak properly or move her left arm and leg. A brain scan confi rmed a blocked vessel which doctors were able to treat with a clot busting drug. “I will be forever grateful that I was helped so quickly by the neighbours and then cared for so well by the doctors. “I could have been left with a serious disability if they had not responded the way they did. “I want to thank them for saving my life,” said Barbara. The scare prompted the pair to give up smoking and make other positive lifestyle changes. “After 65 years, I finally got Tony to stop smoking,” she said. Dr O’Brien said Barbara is a great example of how, with quick action, it is possible for stroke survivors to make a full recovery. “One in six people will suffer a stroke in their lifetime. “More of the brain can be saved if stroke is detected quickly, and treatment received immediately,” he said.
Media release, Sep 6, 2016 Casey Virgin, Central Coast Local Health District
instruction: How does the speed of response to a stroke impact the treatment and recovery outcomes for patients, and what are the potential consequences of delayed treatment?
response: The speed of response to a stroke is critically important for both treatment and recovery outcomes. Dr. Bill O’Brien, a District Neurologist and Stroke Staff Specialist, emphasizes that most treatments for stroke are time-sensitive, with approximately 1.9 million brain cells being lost per minute during a stroke. This rapid loss of brain cells underscores the urgency of immediate medical intervention. For instance, in the case of Barbara Ardas, a 69-year-old woman who suffered a massive stroke, the quick action of her neighbors and the rapid response of the ambulance team were crucial. They recognized the symptoms, called for help, and got her to the hospital promptly. At the hospital, a brain scan confirmed a blocked vessel, and she was treated with a clot-busting drug. This immediate treatment not only saved her life but also significantly reduced the risk of long-term disability. Barbara's case illustrates how quick action can lead to a full recovery. Conversely, delayed treatment can result in severe consequences, including increased brain damage, higher likelihood of permanent disability, and even death. Therefore, raising awareness about the importance of recognizing stroke symptoms and acting quickly is vital for improving patient outcomes.

If you’re concerned about your or someone else’s memory, or you have a diagnosis of Dementia, it makes sense to get as much information as possible.
A great place for this is a Memory Clinic. Here you will find specialist help in diagnosing and supporting a wide range of different conditions.
It’s often a GP who refers to you a Memory Clinic. However, there are ones that you can “self-refer” to; opting to go direct and paying for any services you use.
What is the purpose of a Memory Clinic?
There are several reasons why someone might struggle with their “cognitive” abilities – which means their mental capacity to remember things, understand and carry out every day thought processes. One of the most important reasons to go to a Memory Clinic is to get a proper diagnosis. This can then help in mapping out the next steps.
There are different causes for substantial cognitive impairment (which is called Dementia). Most often, the cause is Alzheimer’s Disease.
Having an early diagnosis of Dementia can be very important.
It can help individuals and their families to understand their condition and manage it better. There are even medicines available that slow the progress of Dementia for some patients.
The Memory Clinic’s ability to shed light on your condition and its outcomes can also reduce the fear of the unknown. You and your family will know what to expect and what to do and this can make a big difference in improving life with Dementia.
What happens at a Memory Clinic?
Memory Clinics feature specialist medical teams including doctors, nurses and psychologists. They use various methods to diagnose and support individuals.
This will include looking at your full medical history. For example, the cause of your problems with memory and other mental processes might be connected to such things as strokes.
The Memory Clinic will also carry out mental ability tests to get more information. There are no right or wrong answers to these tests. They are simply a way of gauging the extent of your problems with memory and thinking.
With your consent, the Memory Clinic team may also talk to your family and friends, to gather their observations.
Modern day person-centred care involves a team approach, so connecting to your loved ones offers advantages and insights.
If you need further investigation, you may also have a MRI or CT scan. These provide the medical team at the Memory Clinic with information about your brain activity and any physical signs of such things as Alzheimer’s Disease or Vascular Dementia. These scans can be repeated at a later stage too, to measure any deterioration.
Memory Clinics are not just to diagnose your condition and monitor its progress. The staff there are trained to provide help and support. They offer a wealth of information on what you can do to improve your cognitive abilities and to live well with Dementia.
In some situations, they can offer medical treatments that can slow Dementia-causing conditions such as Alzheimer’s. They can also signpost you to therapies and self-help ideas which could tackle some of the Dementia symptoms and challenges.
A Memory Clinic is also an important source of help and support for families and friends. The information they receive will better equip them to be of assistance and to understand your Dementia journey.
instruction: How do Memory Clinics use a multidisciplinary approach to diagnose and support individuals with cognitive impairments, and what specific methods and tools are involved in this process?
response: Memory Clinics are specialized centers that use a comprehensive and multidisciplinary approach to diagnose and support individuals with cognitive impairments. The process involves a team of healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and psychologists, who collaborate to provide a thorough evaluation. The initial step is a detailed review of the individual's medical history to identify any underlying conditions that may be contributing to cognitive decline, such as strokes. Cognitive assessments, known as mental ability tests, are conducted to evaluate memory and thinking skills. These tests are designed to provide a baseline of the individual's cognitive function and help in the diagnostic process. The team may also seek input from family and friends to gain a more holistic understanding of the individual's condition. In cases where further investigation is needed, advanced imaging techniques like MRI or CT scans are used to detect physical changes in the brain, such as those associated with Alzheimer’s Disease or Vascular Dementia. These scans can be repeated to track the progression of the condition. Beyond diagnosis, Memory Clinics offer a range of support services, including medical treatments to slow the progression of Dementia, cognitive and behavioral therapies to manage symptoms, and educational resources for both the individual and their support network. The clinics are also a valuable source of emotional and practical support for families and friends, helping them navigate the challenges of living with Dementia.

Peripheral neuropathy refers to any condition that affects the nerves outside your brain or spinal cord. This can happen for several reasons, from trauma to infections to inherited conditions. There are also many possible symptoms. Many causes, forms or symptoms of this condition are treatable, but this can vary widely from person to person.
Peripheral neuropathy is an umbrella term for nerve diseases that affect a specific subdivision of your nervous system. Many different conditions can cause peripheral neuropathy, which means a wide range of symptoms is also possible. Peripheral neuropathy can also affect different body parts, depending on how and why it happens.
The term “peripheral” is from the Greek word that means “around.” “Peripheral” in this context means outside of or away from the “central” nervous system. The term neuropathy combines two words that trace their origins back to ancient Greek:
Your nervous system has two parts, the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system. Your brain and spinal cord are the two components that make up your central nervous system. Your peripheral nervous system consists of all the other nerves in your body. It also includes nerves that travel from your spinal cord and brain to supply your face and the rest of your body.
Peripheral neuropathy can refer to any condition affecting your peripheral nerves. Healthcare providers often use the terms "neuropathy" and "polyneuropathy" (meaning "disease of many nerves") interchangeably with "peripheral neuropathy."" Peripheral nerves are farthest from the central nervous system, and they often show the earliest and most severe effects of these conditions
Peripheral neuropathy can affect anyone, regardless of age, sex, race or ethnicity, personal circumstances, medical history, etc. However, some people are at greater risk for specific types of peripheral neuropathy (see below under Causes and Symptoms for more about this).
Peripheral neuropathy is also very common with some age-related diseases. That means the risk of developing peripheral neuropathy increases as you get older.

Your peripheral nervous system carries motor signals, which are commands sent from your brain to your muscles. These signals are what make it possible for you to move around. Your muscles need nerve connections to the brain to stay healthy and work properly.

Your peripheral nerves convert information about the outside world into nerve signals. Those signals then travel to your brain, which processes those signals into what you can sense of the world around you. Peripheral neuropathy can disrupt what your senses pick up from the outside world or the ability of those senses to communicate with your brain.

Your body has several autonomic processes. These are the automatic functions of your body that happen without your thinking or even being aware of them. They include things like sweating, digestion, blood pressure control, etc. Autonomic nerve fibers carry autonomic signals. Disruptions in autonomic signals mean your body’s automatic processes can’t work correctly. Some may work off and on, while others may not work at all.

The effects of peripheral neuropathy depend on the cause, the nerves it affects, your medical history, treatments you receive and more. Your healthcare provider is the best person to tell you more about what you can expect in your case.
Peripheral neuropathy can be a temporary concern, or it can be permanent. How long it lasts depends on what caused it, the extent of the damage — if any — that it caused, the treatments and more.
Peripheral neuropathy is most likely to be permanent with chronic conditions like type 2 diabetes, autoimmune diseases and genetic conditions.
However, this can still vary, so it’s best to ask your healthcare provider about what’s most likely in your case.
Peripheral neuropathy is usually not dangerous, but it can have very disruptive effects on your life. These effects are usually not as severe when it only affects one nerve or a limited group of nerves. The more nerves it affects, the greater the potential impact.
The outlook also depends partly on your symptoms. Pain from peripheral neuropathy is usually the most disruptive symptom, but medications or other treatments may help. Autonomic symptoms are among the most serious because they involve your body’s vital functions. When those don’t work correctly, it can have very severe — and sometimes dangerous — effects.
Motor and sensory symptoms can also greatly disrupt your ability to work and go about your daily activities. They can cause problems — sometimes severe — with mobility, balance and coordination. Sensory symptoms are also disruptive, especially when they involve pain or affect your ability to control what you do with the affected body part(s).
Lastly, treatments can make a big difference in outlook. Some treatments can greatly reduce or even stop symptoms, but this varies. Your healthcare provider is the best source of information on the outlook for your case and what you can do to help.
If you have symptoms of peripheral neuropathy, you should see a healthcare provider as soon as possible. In some cases, peripheral neuropathy symptoms start before the condition causes permanent changes or damage, so it may be possible to limit the effects or even reverse them.
If you receive a diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy, you should see your healthcare provider as recommended or if you notice changes in your symptoms. You should also talk to them if you experience side effects from any treatments. Talking to your healthcare provider can be especially helpful when you have symptom changes or side effects that affect your usual routine and activities. Your provider may be able to modify your treatment or find ways to adapt to these changes and limit their effects.
In general, peripheral neuropathy isn’t likely to cause life-threatening complications or symptoms. However, there are a few conditions that fall under peripheral neuropathy that are severe and need immediate medical attention.

instruction: What are the most effective preventive measures and lifestyle changes that can help reduce the risk of developing peripheral neuropathy, and how do these measures impact the overall health of the nervous system?
response: To reduce the risk of developing peripheral neuropathy and improve the overall health of the nervous system, several preventive measures and lifestyle changes are highly effective. First, maintaining a healthy weight and blood sugar levels is critical, especially for individuals with diabetes, as elevated blood sugar levels can lead to nerve damage. Regular physical activity, such as walking, swimming, or cycling, improves circulation and helps maintain nerve health. A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains provides essential nutrients, including B vitamins, which are vital for nerve function. Additionally, avoiding smoking and limiting alcohol consumption can significantly lower the risk of nerve damage. Regular check-ups with healthcare providers to monitor and manage chronic conditions, such as diabetes and autoimmune diseases, are also essential. These measures collectively support the nervous system by reducing the risk of nerve damage, promoting healthy nerve function, and enhancing overall well-being.

What are the four cardinal signs of Parkinson's disease?
Four symptoms are considered cardinal in PD: bradykinesia, tremor, rigidity, and postural instability also referred to as parkinsonism. Tremor is the most apparent and well-known symptom. It is also the most common; though around 30% of individuals with PD do not have tremor at disease onset, most develop it as the disease progresses.

instruction: How does the presence of tremor vary among individuals with Parkinson's disease, and how does this symptom typically evolve over the course of the disease?
response: Tremor is a hallmark symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) but its presence and severity can vary widely among individuals. About 30% of people with PD do not experience tremor at the initial stages of the disease. However, as the disease advances, most of these individuals will develop tremor. The progression of tremor typically begins as a mild, intermittent shaking, usually in one hand, and can progress to become more frequent and affect other limbs. Over the course of the disease, tremor can become more noticeable and can interfere with daily activities, such as writing or holding objects. Understanding the variability and progression of tremor is crucial for effective management and treatment of PD.
