When people think of miracles, they are usually referring to an occurrence so wonderful that words can not explain. And for Martha Rotelli, the miracle began unexpectedly at a Madison bookstore back in January.
“I was standing looking at books and, all at once, I wondered what I put in my pocket because it was so heavy,” she says. “I took my hand out of my pocket and realized three of my fingers were completely numb. Once I realized the numbness wasn’t going away I went to a manager and requested an ambulance. He asked what was wrong and I said, ‘I think I’m having a stroke.’”
Martha knew at the time the words she uttered were exactly what she needed to say, but to this day she’s still not sure exactly how she knew what was happening to her.
“I listen to my radio in the car all the time and they have these PSAs and I listen to all those things and I think that’s what told me the symptoms of stroke,” says Rotelli.
Thanks to her quick thinking, Martha arrived via ambulance at the Dean & St. Mary’s Stroke Center at St. Mary’s Hospital in less than an hour of the onset of her symptoms. That’s important because drugs used to reverse the damage caused by stroke, in most cases, can only be administered within the first three hours after stroke symptoms start. With these treatments, 50-70 percent of survivors are able to lead a normal life. Up to 30 percent of people, however, are permanently disabled.
“A stroke means there’s an obstruction to the blood vessels going to the brain,” says Dr. Charles Miley, Medical Director of the Dean & St. Mary’s Stroke Center. “Because blood is not able to flow, brain tissue is starved of oxygen and glucose and it becomes damaged. That can lead to a loss of function, loss of movement in your arms and legs, or blurry vision and dizziness (?).”
Breast cancer may be most women’s number one health concern, but the reality is two times as many women die from stroke each year compared to breast cancer. And a new study shows among people age 45-54, stroke is two to three times more common in females than in males. This is particularly the case for women in this age group who are obese.
But nobody is immune. In fact, stroke is the number three killer of all people in the U.S., and strikes more than 100,000 African Americans per year. Of those who have and survive a stroke, about 40 percent will suffer another within 5 years.
“In the 45-54 year old age group, strokes are generally pretty uncommon,” says Dr. Miley. “But once you reach a certain age, nobody is immune from serious health problems. It’s estimated as many as 80 percent of all strokes are preventable. So you have to work on risk factors to prevent stroke.”
Risk factors include a family history of stroke, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, being overweight and not exercising. Additionally, in women, the risk for stroke increases for those who take birth control pills, are pregnant, use hormone replacement therapy, have high triglycerides or suffer from migraines.
Minimizing your risk factors is very important but so is recognizing and reacting to the signs and symptoms of stroke.
Martha was treated with interarterial TPA which is essentially an injection that dissolves the clot to open back up the artery. It works best within the first three hours of stroke, with new research suggesting it may be able to be used up to 4.5 hours after the first signs. The Dean & St. Mary’s Stroke Center also has a device called the Merci Retriever which is a mechanical means of removing a stroke. It can be used when a clot is found in certain parts of the brain. In some cases, a new treatment option called the Penumbra is used like a mini vacuum cleaner to suck out the clot. But again, in order for any of these to be effective, it’s important for people to call 9-1-1 at the first signs of stroke.
“We know from experience people can and do live normal lives following a stroke,” says Dr. Miley. “But I cannot stress how important it is to seek medical assistance right away. Just a few hours of waiting can lead to permanent damage that cannot be reversed.”
It’s been a few months now since Martha Rotelli had her stroke and recovery is going well. For the most part, feeling is back in her hand and the only real way to even tell she’s had a stroke is her minor memory lapses.
“My memory isn’t exactly right but I know how to get around that,” she jokes. “I just laugh and tell people I forgot what I was going to say.”
Martha’s husband, Leo, says her positive attitude through all of this combined with following doctor’s orders have been the keys to her success.
“We kid one another a lot and you have to have that. We have a lot of fun,” he says.
Martha agrees and says she’s thankful to everyone who helped make her treatment and recovery happen. She hopes through sharing her story others who find themselves in the same situation will be able set recovery goals and achieve those goals using the same positive attitude she has.
“All in all, I know this happened and I don’t look at it as something bad that happened. This was my miracle and we all deserve at least one,” she says.
And her words of advice to others? Pay close attention to what your body is telling you.
“Most people are in denial when they have symptoms,” she says. “It isn’t fine. You have to pay attention to it. And I think that’s what saved me.”
Signs You’re Having a Stroke
With stroke, time is of the essence. Call 9-1-1 if you are having:
- numbness or weakness in your face, arms or legs
- sudden confusion or trouble seeing
- difficulty walking
- having a severe headache that comes on without warning
According to the National Stroke Association, women also can have unique symptoms of stroke including:
- sudden face and limb pain
- general weakness
- chest pain
- shortness of breath
- rapid heart beat
Did You Know?
May is Stroke Awareness Month. Stroke is the number three killer in the U.S. causing the death of twice as many women each year compared to breast cancer. Of those who survive one stroke, 40 percent will have another within the next five years. It’s important to realize your risk factors and know the symptoms.
- Someone has a stroke in the U.S. every 45 seconds
- Stroke is the number three killer in the U.S.
- Stroke is the leading cause of long-term disability
- 14% of people who survive a stroke have another within one year
Breakout: Risk Reduction
- Control your blood pressure
- Quit smoking
- Maintain a healthy weight
- Exercise 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week
- Keep diabetes under control
instruction: What are the key steps individuals should take to recognize and respond to the signs of a stroke, and why is immediate action critical for effective treatment?
response:
Immediate recognition and response to the signs of a stroke are essential for effective treatment and can significantly influence the outcome. Here are the key steps individuals should take:
1. **Recognize the Symptoms**: Familiarize yourself with the signs of stroke, which can include numbness or weakness in the face, arms, or legs, especially on one side of the body; sudden confusion or trouble speaking; trouble seeing in one or both eyes; difficulty walking or loss of balance; and a severe headache with no known cause. Women may also experience additional symptoms such as sudden face and limb pain, general weakness, chest pain, shortness of breath, and a rapid heartbeat.
2. **Call 9-1-1 Immediately**: If you suspect a stroke, do not delay. Call emergency services right away. Early intervention is crucial because treatments like intravenous thrombolysis with tPA (tissue plasminogen activator) are most effective when administered within the first 3-4.5 hours of symptom onset.
3. **Provide Clear Information**: When calling for help, clearly communicate that you suspect a stroke. This can expedite the response and ensure that the medical team is prepared to provide the necessary treatment.
4. **Stay Calm and Safe**: While waiting for medical help, remain calm and avoid giving the person anything to eat or drink. Ensure they are in a safe and comfortable position.
5. **Follow Medical Advice**: After receiving initial treatment, follow the advice of healthcare professionals. This may include rehabilitation and lifestyle changes to reduce the risk of future strokes.
Immediate action is vital because the brain is highly sensitive to the lack of blood flow and oxygen. Delaying treatment can lead to irreversible brain damage, resulting in severe disability or death. By acting quickly, you can help minimize the damage and improve the chances of a successful recovery.

Postural instability is one of the cardinal features in Idiopathic Parkinson's disease. It is a significant factor of disability in Parkinson's disease. We aimed to examine the physical activity levels in patients with Parkinson's disease comparing with healthy subjects and their association with the postural stability. Fifty-six Parkinson's disease patients and 58 healthy subjects were involved. The disease-specific disability of patients was determined by using Modified Hoehn and Yahr Scale and Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale. The physical activity levels of participants were evaluated using SenseWear Arm Band activity monitor. The participants used the activity monitor for seven consecutive days. The postural stability was assessed using NeuroCom Balance Master system. The Parkinson's disease group was found to take fewer steps and to have shorter duration of sleep and sedentary behavior but a higher level of energy expenditure than the healthy control group (P < 0.05). In Parkinson's disease group, the data obtained from the activity monitor were found to be in correlation with disease-specific disability and the parameters of NeuroCom Balance Master system (P < 0.05). We found that the physical activity levels of patients with a mild or moderate stage of Parkinson's disease were lower compared to healthy subjects and were affected by the disease-specific symptoms, dynamic postural instability, and walking function. To increase the activity level in Parkinson's disease, these factors should be aimed to improve, as well as designing the personalized physiotherapy programs starting from the early-mid stage.
instruction: How does postural instability in Parkinson's disease impact physical activity levels, and what measures can be taken to improve these levels through personalized physiotherapy programs?
response: In patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), postural instability is a critical factor that significantly affects physical activity levels. The study found that PD patients exhibit lower physical activity levels, characterized by fewer steps taken, shorter sleep duration, and increased sedentary behavior, compared to healthy individuals. These changes are strongly correlated with the severity of postural instability and other disease-specific symptoms. To combat these effects and enhance physical activity, personalized physiotherapy programs are essential. These programs should be tailored to the individual's specific needs and can include exercises to improve postural stability, balance, and walking function. Early intervention, particularly during the mild to moderate stages of the disease, is crucial to maximize the benefits of physiotherapy. By addressing postural instability and other symptoms, these programs can help PD patients maintain higher levels of physical activity, which is vital for their overall health and well-being.

Epilepsy is mostly a chronic neurological disorder associated with occasional seizures. It is estimated that there are approximately 40 different types of seizures. Still, in the majority of patients an epileptic attack is characterized by a consistent patter of symptoms.
Based on certain characteristics seizures are classified as partial seizures and generalized seizures. In case of partial seizures localized muscle contractions occur due to abnormal electrical activity of a small part of the brain while generalized seizures are characterized by contraction of the entire body due to uncontrollable spread of many electrical impulses across the entire cortex of the brain.
Partial Seizures Clinical Characteristics
Partial seizures are further divided into simple partial seizures and complex partial seizures. The only difference between the two is loss of consciousness which occurs in complex partial seizures. Patients suffering from simple partial seizures remain fully conscious during the entire attack.
Patients with simple partial seizures may experience changes regarding senses, déjà vu, a tingling sensation in the extremities, a sudden intense emotion, stiffness of muscles in the arms or legs, localized twitching of certain body parts etc.
On the other hand, it is normal for complex partial seizures to induce lip smacking, hand rubbing, making random noises, moving the extremities (especially arms) around, maintaining the abnormal posture etc.
After a complex seizure patients do not remember anything that have happened.
Generalized Seizures Clinical Characteristics
Generalized seizures are divided into 6 subtypes.
The first one are absent seizures. They predominantly affect children and cause loss of awareness for approximately 20 seconds. The affected child may stare, flutter his/her eyes and smack lips.
Myoclonic jerks are a type of generalized seizures affecting the arms, legs and upper back. The affected individual behaves as if he/she received an electric shock. Myoclonic seizures may occur in a combination with some other types of seizures and never last longer than a few seconds.
Clonic seizures resemble myoclonic jerks but they last much longer and may be accompanied by loss of consciousness.
Atonic seizures, interestingly, induce sudden muscle relaxation. Because of that patients commonly end up falling to the ground and may easily get injured.
Tonic seizures cause sudden stiffness of all the muscles in the body and are also associated with different injuries, especially head injury.
Tonic-clonic seizures always go through two phases, the first one characterized by stiffness of the arms and legs and the second one when the body starts twitching. Loss of consciousness and urine or fecal incontinence are a few more characteristics of this subtype of generalized seizures. This is the most common type of seizures affecting around 60% of all patients.
Finally, many patients have a distinctive feeling that the attack is about to happen. This is a so called aura which may be in different forms such as noticing a strange smell/taste, experiencing a sense of fear or anxiety, having a feeling of déjà vu etc. Such warning signs may be of major help and inform the patients and nearby people that the attack will soon take place. By recognizing the attack and being prepared for it, people may help the affected individuals and prevent some serious injuries such as head injury caused by a sudden fall.
instruction: What are the different subtypes of generalized seizures, and what specific symptoms and behaviors are associated with each subtype?
response: Generalized seizures are classified into six subtypes, each with distinct symptoms and behaviors. Absence seizures primarily affect children, causing a brief loss of awareness for about 20 seconds, often accompanied by staring, eye fluttering, and lip smacking. Myoclonic seizures involve sudden, brief jerks of the arms, legs, and upper back, as if the person has received an electric shock, lasting only a few seconds. Clonic seizures are similar to myoclonic jerks but last longer and may involve loss of consciousness. Atonic seizures cause a sudden loss of muscle tone, leading to falls and potential injuries. Tonic seizures result in sudden muscle stiffness, often causing injuries, especially to the head. Tonic-clonic seizures, the most common type, involve two phases: initial stiffness of the arms and legs followed by twitching of the body, along with loss of consciousness and possible incontinence.

A stroke happens when blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted because a blood vessel in the brain is blocked or bursts open. Brain cells deprived of blood and oxygen can die, causing permanent damage resulting in weakness or paralysis of an arm or leg or problems with speech. Stroke is the third leading cause of death in the United States.
A stroke is a medical emergency. Immediate treatment can save lives and reduce disability. A person experiencing the symptoms of a stroke should have a complete physical and neurological exam. CT and MR imaging and nuclear medicine techniques are used to determine the type, location and cause of the stroke and to help rule out other disorders.
How does molecular imaging help people with a stroke?
SPECT imaging with the radiopharmaceutical Tc-99m is the most frequent nuclear medicine technique used for stroke detection.
In addition to detecting acute stroke, SPECT is also used in the evaluation of patients who have had a stroke and/or transient ischemic attack (TIA). During a TIA, which is also known as a mini-stroke, an individual experiences stroke-like symptoms that last from minutes up to several hours. Although TIAs do not typically result in permanent brain damage, physicians often use SPECT to determine which parts of the brain may be at risk.
instruction: How does immediate medical intervention, such as imaging techniques, play a crucial role in the treatment and recovery of stroke patients?
response: Immediate medical intervention, particularly through the use of imaging techniques, is crucial in the treatment and recovery of stroke patients. A stroke is a medical emergency where blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted, leading to the death of brain cells due to lack of blood and oxygen. This can cause permanent damage, including weakness, paralysis, or speech problems. CT (Computed Tomography) and MR (Magnetic Resonance) imaging are essential tools used to determine the type, location, and cause of the stroke, as well as to rule out other potential disorders. These imaging techniques allow healthcare providers to quickly and accurately diagnose the stroke, which is critical for initiating appropriate treatment. For example, if a stroke is caused by a blood clot, immediate administration of clot-dissolving drugs can be life-saving and reduce the extent of brain damage. Early diagnosis and intervention significantly improve the chances of a better recovery and reduced disability.

Disabled sports, also adaptive sports or parasports, are sports played by persons with a disability, including physical and intellectual disabilities.
Hypertonia is a term sometimes used synonymously with spasticity and rigidity in the literature surrounding damage to the central nervous system, namely upper motor neuron lesions.
The International Paralympic Committee (IPC; Internationales Paralympisches Komitee) is an international non-profit organisation and the global governing body for the Paralympic Movement.

instruction: What are the primary symptoms of ataxia and athetosis, and how do these conditions affect an individual's ability to participate in sports and daily activities?
response: The primary symptoms of ataxia include a lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements, which often manifests as gait abnormalities and difficulty with balance and coordination. This can make it challenging for individuals to perform activities that require precise movements, such as walking, running, or engaging in sports that demand agility and balance. Athetosis is characterized by slow, involuntary, and writhing movements, typically affecting the fingers, hands, toes, and feet, but sometimes extending to the arms, legs, neck, and tongue. These movements can disrupt voluntary control and fine motor skills, making it difficult to perform tasks that require precision, such as writing or using tools. Both conditions can significantly limit participation in sports and daily activities. For instance, in sports, ataxia can hinder performance in track and field events due to poor balance and coordination, while athetosis can affect sports that require fine motor control, such as archery or table tennis. In daily life, ataxia can make it hard to walk without assistance, and athetosis can make it challenging to perform tasks like dressing or eating without support.

1. Royal families have used CBD
Despite being stigmatized and restricted today, cannabis derivatives like CBD have been used throughout history.
One notable example is that of Queen Victoria, who ruled England from 1837 to her death in 1901.
Today, we have preliminary scientific evidence and plenty of anecdotes attesting to CBD’s usefulness as a pain reliever.
The queen seemed to know that too, as she used cannabis high in CBD to help with menstrual cramps.
2. Hemp is one of the world’s oldest crops
Hemp – the CBD rich variant of the cannabis genus – may have been perfected thanks to modern agriculture, but it’s far from new.
In fact, archaeologists traced it back as far as the emergence of agriculture, between 12,000 to 10,000 years ago.
The late astronomer and marijuana advocate, Carl Sagan, proposed in 1977 that hemp may have actually been the first cultivated crop, although this is yet to be fully confirmed.
3. Medical cannabis was prescribed in ancient Greece
While it’s safe to say that he Greeks didn’t require a doctor’s note and a medical marijuana card, this doesn’t mean that it wasn’t regarded as a prescription medication.
Claudius Galen, a Greek doctor (among other things), often gave cannabis “juice” as a remedy for pain – a classic example of CBD’s analgesic effects.
In Galen’s words, “Some people, pulling out the juice from it when it is not ripe, use it against ears’ pains due to an occlusion, as I believe.”
Galen got his idea from what historians believe to be the first recorded text about marijuana as an official medicine, the De Materia Medica.
Written by Pedanius Dioscorides around 65-70 CE, the third volume states: Kannabis; is a plant of much use in this life for the twisting of very strong ropes, it has leaves like to the Ash, of a bad scent, long stalks, empty, a round seed, which being eaten of reduces sexual activity, but being juiced when it is green is good for the pains of the ears.”
Since then, cannabis spread as a medicine to other civilizations, like the Romans and the Byzantine Empire.
4. CBD may actually fight cancer
Although research is still ongoing, a study by the National Cancer Institute indicates that not only is CBD (along with THC) effective in helping with various symptoms associated with cancer treatment, but it might also have properties that hinder or destroy tumor cells, specifically breast cancer in this case.
It explains that “CBD inhibited the survival of both estrogen receptor–positive and estrogen receptor–negative breast cancer cell lines, inducing apoptosis in a concentration-dependent manner while having little effect on nontumorigenic mammary cells.”
In layman’s terms, this means that the CBD stifled cancerous cell growth while leaving healthy (“nontumorigenic”) cells intact.
5. CBD in all forms is illegal in Canada (without a prescription)
While it’s easy to ship CBD derived from hemp to various parts of the world, our neighbors to the North aren’t so permissive.
Despite the inevitable country-wide legalization of marijuana planned by the Trudeau government in the next two or three years, CBD oil of any sort is a Schedule II drug.
This means that you can’t obtain it without a prescription and, so far, it’s unavailable as a hemp extract.
Those with prescriptions can get CBD oil from licensed medical marijuana companies as medicine created from marijuana, not hemp.
The problem is that Canada’s laws haven’t separated CBD hemp oil and CBD oil derived from marijuana.
They fall under the same umbrella, and are treated accordingly.
While it’s certainly possible to have CBD oil and other products mailed to Canada, there’s a small chance of it being intercepted by customs and either sent back or destroyed.
Fines and criminal charges could also be levied against importers at the discretion of the Canada Border Services Agency.
6. People have gone to great lengths to get CBD
“Medical tourism” is a phrase a lot of people use.
Americans often travel to Canada to get cheaper prescription medications, but that’s nothing compared to the Forde family, who went all the way from Ireland to Colorado.
Their son, Tristan, suffers from Lennox Gastaut Syndrome, which causes frequent seizures.
Conventional treatments failed to help. After starting on CBD, Tristan’s parents noticed a major improvement in his condition.
Unfortunately, it’s not legal in Ireland, leaving them no choice but to travel 4,000 miles to obtain this critical medicine.
7. CBD might help improve brain function
We’ve heard it from parents, teachers and in health class – “pot makes you stupid” (even though CBD isn’t technically “pot”).
Regardless, research now suggests the complete opposite.
Following an accident that left Debbie Wilson with a variety of neurological issues, including PTSD, epilepsy, migraines and memory problems, she turned to medical cannabis for help.
Initially, Wilson used (and still uses) THC-rich dry herb for her seizures; however, when she tried an oil consisting of 22% CBD and 1% THC, she noticed a major improvement.
According to Wilson: “I know for a fact that I’m now accessing file drawers in my memory bank that were shut for more than 20 years.
My story has not ended yet, I’ve been able to retire my seizure alert dog, my helmet, my diapers and over a dozen central nervous system depressants, pain relievers and antidepressants.
So many areas of my body have been helped that it’s not even like I’m the same person.”
Research seems to back up Debbie’s claims.
A study on pigs published in the U.S. National Library of Medicine found that “…administration of CBD…reduced short-term brain damage and was associated with extracerebral [non-neurological] benefits.”
8. CBD has been shown to reduce stress
Stress has become a normal part of life for virtually everyone in the world.
But CBD appears to be a promising alternative to prescription medications that are used to handle stress-related health problems.
While CBD certainly isn’t a “cure-all” for every stress-related ailment, it’s been found to be helpful as a mood-stabilizer and antidepressant.
According to Samir Haj-Dahmane of Buffalo University, CBD and other cannabinoids can “…restore normal endocannabinoid function [to] potentially help stabilize moods and ease depression.”
9. CBD may reverse brain damage from alcohol
Alcoholism is a terrible addiction.
Even if people are able to eventually quit, it could be too little, too late for the human brain – until now.
A study by the University of Kentucky found that administering CBD gel through the skin “…resulted in a 48.8% reduction in neurodegeneration…”
This is really promising for those trying to recover from addiction to alcohol and hopefully live normal lives.
10. CBD might support addiction recovery
There are a lot of drugs out there, both legal and illegal, that can cause severe dependency or even death.
But research suggests that CBD acts as an inhibitor to control addictive behaviors.
According to a study in the U.S. National Library of Medicine, “CBD has been shown to be an agonist of 5-HT1a serotoninergic receptors and to regulate stress response and compulsive behaviors.”
In other words, it blocks the serotonin receptors responsible for the pleasurable brain response when using certain drugs, while mitigating stress reactions that drive people to use drugs.
Specifically, the researchers looked at a variety of addicting substances, including opioids, alcohol, tobacco and – ironically – marijuana (THC).
instruction: What are the potential benefits of CBD in treating neurological conditions, and how does it compare to traditional treatments in terms of effectiveness and side effects?
response: CBD has shown potential benefits in treating various neurological conditions, including reducing the frequency and severity of seizures in conditions like Lennox Gastaut Syndrome, as seen in the case of Tristan Forde. Additionally, it may help improve brain function and reduce short-term brain damage, as supported by research involving pigs. CBD has also been found to reduce stress and potentially reverse brain damage caused by alcohol, offering a promising alternative for addiction recovery. Compared to traditional treatments, CBD often has fewer side effects. For example, conventional anticonvulsants can cause drowsiness, dizziness, and cognitive impairment, whereas CBD is generally well-tolerated with minimal side effects such as mild fatigue or changes in appetite. However, more research is needed to fully understand its long-term effects and optimal dosing.

Imagine what it would be like if the screaming pain of neuropathy didn’t keep you from doing everything you love… if you didn’t have to wonder when the next intense sensation would attack.
Neuropathy strikes in unexpected ways. Sometimes, it will plague you with pins and needles… other times, your feet may go numb, making it virtually impossible to walk comfortably. One moment you may feel like your toes are on fire, and the next your hands could feel unbearably itchy.
Mainstream “solutions” for this never-ending problem just don’t seem to make the pain stop. Worse, they might bring on new discomforts to add to your distress. And there doesn’t seem to be anything your doctor can do that will really make a difference.
That leaves you stuck suffering every day and night. Out of desperation, you start looking for natural ways to at least turn down the volume on your pain… but everything you’ve tried before has left you disappointed and living in agony.
You don’t have to live like that anymore. Not when you find the right botanical to help turn things around. Because nature provides exactly what you need to feel your best – if you know where to look –so you won’t be stuck wishing for your neuropathy to fade away.
Migraine “weed” helps soothe the nerves
It’s known as bachelor’s buttons, midsummer daisy, flirtroot, and featherfoil… but natural healers know it best as feverfew. This daisy-like “weed” grows wild throughout Europe and the United States, and it’s been a staple of folk medicine for generations.
Its most common name – feverfew – comes from febrifugia, Latin for fever reducer, because it was primarily used to defeat “hot inflammation.” And a plant that’s known for quieting burning heat and inflammation could play a soothing role in neuropathy.
Though this flowering herb most widely used to by people with migraines, it’s also been used traditionally to treat fevers, toothaches, rheumatoid arthritis, insect bites, allergies, and painful spasms (like foot cramps).
Researchers have discovered a wealth of plant chemicals with wide-ranging capabilities in feverfew. Its known properties include:
Thanks to several human clinical trials (mainly focused on headaches), we know that feverfew works safely and effectively to thwart pain and inflammation. That’s mainly thanks to a unique plant chemical found in the herb, one that holds a lot of promise for nerve health.
Potent plant chemical targets pain signals
Most medicines get their start in the plant kingdom. That’s because nature provides everything we need to stay healthy… even if many medical professionals have forgotten that.
Feverfew is chockfull of biologically active compounds, including plant chemicals such as
- sesquiterpene lactones
- volatile oils
- polyphenolic acids
Some of these you may have heard of (like camphor and quercetin), while others will be unfamiliar. But the most studied – and the most powerful – is a sesquiterpene lactone known as parthenolide. This potent plant compound tackles pain and inflammation in some very important ways, including interrupting the NF-kB pathway, which can unleash a dangerous inflammatory cascade.
Another way feverfew can help ease the agony of neuropathy: Parthenolide also targets a special pain-signaling channel called TRPA1. When TRPA1 is stimulated, it causes sensations like heat, cold, itchiness, and pain. But parthenolide acts directly on that channel, muting those signals and reducing their effects.
Researchers have also found that parthenolide from feverfew:
- makes skin less sensitive to touch… so you won’t have to worry about pain when you go to put socks on
- reduces neuropathic pain… so everything you do won’t be colored by throbbing, stinging, burning agony
- inhibits the production of several inflammatory compounds, including TNF-a (tumor necrosis factor alpha) and IL-1B (interleukin one beta)… so your nerves have a chance to calm down and stop sending the wrong signals
All of those capabilities help explain why feverfew works so well to quiet the excruciatingly painful sensations brought on by neuropathy… and there are many studies that highlight just how effectively it can do that.
Taming neuropathic pain and regenerating healthy nerves
While the lion’s share of human clinical studies on feverfew focused on headaches, other research has been discovering just how much this healing plant can do for nerve health. The results have been truly astounding, as scientists learn exactly how well feverfew and its powerful components can turn the tables on neuropathy.
One study found that feverfew relieved neuropathic pain in diabetic lab rats in a way “comparable to clinically used antihyperalgesic drugs,” according to the researchers. That effectiveness was traced back to parthenolide, one of the key plant chemicals found in feverfew. And the researchers also noted that rats getting feverfew treatment didn’t show any signs of behavioral side effects or changes in coordination.
Another animal study found that feverfew reduced sensitivity in inflamed paws similarly to standard pain relievers. Researchers discovered that injecting a feverfew extract significantly increased the animals’ pain threshold within just 30 minutes. Animals with neuropathy (brought on by either injury or chemotherapy) got substantial pain relief from that feverfew extract. That led the researchers to conclude that feverfew extract could have an effect on many different kinds of pain, including neuropathy.
And some very exciting research shows us that feverfew can do more than just ease some painful symptoms… it may also help encourage healthy nerve regeneration. And pristine healthy nerve cells don’t send mixed up signals. In a groundbreaking study, scientists learned that parthenolide nearly doubles axonal regrowth – and axons are the parts of nerves responsible for sending messages. Basically, feverfew helped speed up nerve repair in animals with nerve damage.
Now, these are all animal studies, but they’ve consistently had such promising results that scientists believe feverfew could have equally remarkable effects on people. Just imagine what it might be able to do for you!
Feverfew PLUS additional soothing ingredients for complete nerve support
On its own, feverfew – powered by parthenolide – offers the anti-inflammatory and nerve-regenerating support your nerves need to stop sending mixed up pain signals. And when it’s combined with three other high-quality traditional herbs in a proprietary blend, its powers go even further.
You’ll find that unique blend of four premium herbal extracts in an effective nerve formula called Nerve Renew, along with six essential healthy-nerve nutrients you need to say goodbye to the agonizing discomfort. Now, these aren’t just regular off-the-shelf nutrients that you could find in any old multi-vitamin… they’re specialized, highly bioavailable forms that work differently and better… so you can feel like yourself again in no time at all.

Additionally, feverfew has been shown in animal studies to promote nerve regeneration, potentially leading to long-term improvements in nerve health. This holistic approach not only helps manage pain but also supports the body’s natural healing processes, making it a promising alternative to conventional treatments.

What are the long term effects of a seizure?
Long lasting seizures, or status epilepticus, may also cause brain damage or death.
People with epilepsy are eight times more likely than people without it to experience certain other chronic conditions, including dementia, migraine, heart disease, and depression..
What should you eat after a seizure?
The modified Atkins diet and the ketogenic diet include high-fat foods such as bacon, eggs, mayonnaise, butter, hamburgers and heavy cream, with certain fruits, vegetables, nuts, avocados, cheeses and fish.
What are the 3 main phases of a seizure?
Seizures take on many different forms and have a beginning (prodrome and aura), middle (ictal) and end (post-ictal) stage.
Does your body hurt after a seizure?
The seizure episode typically lasts for less than a minute and is followed by period of lethargy (sluggishness) and temporary confusion. Often muscles are very sore after a generalized seizure.
How long does it take to feel normal after a seizure?
The postictal state is the altered state of consciousness after an epileptic seizure. It usually lasts between 5 and 30 minutes, but sometimes longer in the case of larger or more severe seizures, and is characterized by drowsiness, confusion, nausea, hypertension, headache or migraine, and other disorienting symptoms.
How do you feel better after a seizure?
Stay Calm; Most Seizures Only Last a Few Minutes If the first person remains calm, it will help others stay calm too. Talk calmly and reassuringly to the person during and after the seizure – it will help as they recover from the seizure.
Is it OK to sleep after a seizure?
After the seizure: they may feel tired and want to sleep. It might be helpful to remind them where they are. stay with them until they recover and can safely return to what they had been doing before.
What should you do after a seizure?
Hold the person down or try to stop their movements. Put something in the person’s mouth (this can cause tooth or jaw injuries) Administer CPR or other mouth-to-mouth breathing during the seizure. Give the person food or water until they are alert again.
Should I go to ER after seizure?
Call 911 or seek emergency medical help for seizures if: A seizure lasts more than five minutes. Someone experiences a seizure for the first time. Person remains unconsciousness after a seizure ends.
What should you not do after a seizure?
Do not hold the person down or try to stop his or her movements.Do not put anything in the person’s mouth. This can injure teeth or the jaw. … Do not try to give mouth-to-mouth breaths (like CPR). … Do not offer the person water or food until he or she is fully alert.
Can a seizure change your personality?
When epilepsy affects you for long periods, you may notice changes in your behavior, your feelings, and in how you see the world. Feelings of depression or anxiety are especially common. A few people with epilepsy experience psychosis (losing contact with reality).
What are the symptoms after a seizure?
SymptomsA scream. Some people may cry out at the beginning of a seizure.Loss of bowel and bladder control. This may happen during or following a seizure.Unresponsiveness after convulsions. Unconsciousness may persist for several minutes after the convulsion has ended.Confusion. … Fatigue. … Severe headache.Feb 24, 2021
instruction: What are the potential long-term health impacts of experiencing frequent seizures, and how do they affect a person's quality of life?
response: Experiencing frequent seizures can lead to a variety of long-term health impacts that can severely affect a person's quality of life. These impacts include the potential for brain damage, particularly if seizures are prolonged or if they occur in the form of status epilepticus. Individuals with epilepsy are also more likely to develop other chronic conditions, such as dementia, migraine, heart disease, and depression. These comorbidities can exacerbate the challenges of living with epilepsy, leading to cognitive impairment, chronic pain, and emotional difficulties. Moreover, the post-ictal symptoms, such as muscle soreness, confusion, and fatigue, can make it difficult for individuals to engage in daily activities, further diminishing their quality of life.

instruction: What are the primary treatment options for managing atypical neuropathy, and how do they address the various symptoms associated with this condition?
response: Managing atypical neuropathy involves a multi-faceted approach that includes medications, physiotherapy, and surgery, tailored to the specific symptoms and severity of the condition. Medications are a cornerstone of treatment, with anticonvulsants like gabapentin and pregabalin being effective for neuropathic pain. Antidepressants, such as duloxetine and amitriptyline, can help manage pain and improve mood, which is often affected in neuropathy patients. Pain killers, ranging from over-the-counter NSAIDs to prescription opioids, are used for severe pain. Physiotherapy is crucial for improving muscle strength and function, which can help alleviate symptoms like weakness and numbness. It often involves tailored exercises to enhance flexibility, balance, and coordination. In more severe cases, surgery may be considered to address issues like nerve compression or structural abnormalities that contribute to the neuropathy. Additionally, managing underlying conditions such as diabetes or HIV/AIDS is essential to prevent further nerve damage and to control symptoms. For example, maintaining stable blood sugar levels in diabetes and preventing the transmission of HIV can significantly impact the progression of atypical neuropathy. By combining these treatment modalities, healthcare providers can effectively manage the diverse symptoms of atypical neuropathy and improve the patient's overall well-being.

Blocking dPerk in the intestine suppresses neurodegeneration in a Drosophila model of Parkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterised by selective death of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the midbrain and motor function impairment. Gastrointestinal issues often precede motor deficits in PD, indicating that the gut-brain axis is involved in the pathogenesis of this disease. The features of PD include both mitochondrial dysfunction and activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase involved in the recycling of defective mitochondria, and PINK1 mutations cause early-onset PD. Like PD patients, pink1 mutant Drosophila show degeneration of DA neurons and intestinal dysfunction. These mutant flies also lack vital proteins due to sustained activation of the kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (dPerk), a kinase that induces the UPR. Here, we investigated the role of dPerk in intestinal dysfunction. We showed that intestinal expression of dPerk impairs mitochondrial function, induces cell death, and decreases lifespan. We found that suppressing dPerk in the intestine of pink1-mutant flies rescues intestinal cell death and is neuroprotective. We conclude that in a fly model of PD, blocking gut-brain transmission of UPR-mediated toxicity, is neuroprotective.
Acknowledgements: We thank the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Centre and Vienna Drosophila RNAi Centre for fly stocks. We also thank the Fly Facility, Department of Genetics, University of Cambridge for generating the transgenic lines. We thank Dr G. Fedele for guidance with laboratory experiments.
instruction: What role does the gut-brain axis play in the development of Parkinson's disease, and how might understanding this relationship inform new treatment strategies for the condition?
response: The gut-brain axis is increasingly recognized as a crucial factor in the development and progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). In a study using a Drosophila model of PD, researchers found that gastrointestinal issues often precede motor symptoms, highlighting the involvement of the gut-brain axis in the disease's pathogenesis. The study focused on the kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (dPerk), which is part of the unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway and is activated in response to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In pink1 mutant flies, which exhibit features of PD such as dopaminergic (DA) neuron degeneration and intestinal dysfunction, the sustained activation of dPerk leads to impaired mitochondrial function and cell death. By suppressing dPerk specifically in the intestine, the researchers observed a rescue of intestinal cell death and neuroprotection. This finding suggests that targeting the gut to block the transmission of UPR-mediated toxicity could be a promising new approach for treating PD. Understanding the gut-brain axis and its role in PD could lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies that focus on the gastrointestinal tract to prevent or slow the progression of neurodegeneration.

instruction: What are some common physical sensations, such as tingling and numbness, that can be triggered by anxiety, and how can they be distinguished from more serious medical conditions like a stroke or TIA, especially in younger individuals?
response: Tingling and numbness are common physical sensations that can be triggered by anxiety, often due to heightened stress and muscle tension. These symptoms can be distressing, especially for individuals with a history of hypochondria. In your case, the tingling in your right hand and the numbness in your leg that resolved quickly are more likely related to anxiety rather than a serious medical condition like a stroke or TIA. Here’s how you can distinguish these symptoms: 1. **Age and Risk Factors**: At 16, the risk of a stroke or TIA is very low. These conditions are more common in older adults, particularly those with risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, and a history of cardiovascular disease. 2. **Duration and Nature of Symptoms**: Anxiety-related symptoms are often transient and resolve quickly, as you experienced. In contrast, stroke or TIA symptoms typically persist and may worsen over time. They can include sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body; confusion; trouble speaking or understanding speech; vision problems; dizziness; and loss of balance. 3. **Context and History**: Your history of multiple visits to the emergency room for anxiety-related symptoms suggests that these experiences are often anxiety-driven. It’s important to have a healthcare provider who understands your history and can provide appropriate support and reassurance. If you continue to experience these symptoms or if they become more frequent or severe, a medical evaluation can help rule out any underlying conditions. However, given your history and the nature of your symptoms, it is likely that they are anxiety-related. Managing anxiety through techniques such as deep breathing, mindfulness, and cognitive-behavioral therapy can be beneficial in reducing the frequency and intensity of these symptoms.

instruction: What are the key modifiable risk factors for stroke, and how can healthcare providers and patient advocates effectively educate and implement healthy habits to reduce these risks in at-risk populations?
response: The key modifiable risk factors for stroke are hypertension, physical inactivity, poor diet, smoking, alcohol consumption, psychosocial stress, and diabetes. These factors are significant because they are associated with a high proportion of stroke cases. For example, a study in The Lancet found that nearly 91% of strokes could be prevented by addressing these risk factors. To effectively educate and implement healthy habits, healthcare providers and patient advocates should focus on several strategies. First, they can provide patient education on the importance of blood pressure control, including regular monitoring and adherence to prescribed medications. Second, they can encourage physical activity by recommending tailored exercise plans and community programs that promote movement. Third, they can promote a healthy diet, emphasizing the benefits of a Mediterranean diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. Fourth, they can offer smoking cessation programs and resources, such as nicotine replacement therapy and counseling. Fifth, they can provide education on the risks of excessive alcohol consumption and offer guidance on safe drinking limits. Additionally, they can address psychosocial factors by providing mental health support and stress management techniques. By implementing these strategies, healthcare providers can empower patients to make lifestyle changes that reduce their risk of stroke.

Aspirin highly effective in mini-strokes: Lancet Study
Taking aspirin immediately after minor strokes could substantially reduce the risk of major strokes in patients who have minor 'warning' events, a team of European researchers has found.
Writing in the journal Lancet, the researchers said that immediate self-treatment with aspirin when patients experience stroke-like symptoms would considerably reduce the risk of major stroke over the next few days.
Aspirin is already given to people who have had a stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA often called a 'mini stroke') to prevent further strokes after they have been assessed in hospital and in the longer term, reducing the subsequent stroke risk by about 15 percent.
However, based on a previous study, the team suspected that the benefits of more immediate treatment with aspirin could be much greater.
"The risk of a major stroke is very high immediately after a TIA or a minor stroke (about 1,000 times higher than the background rate), but only for a few days," said lead researcher Peter Rothwell, stroke expert from the University of Oxford.
The team revisited the individual patient data from twelve trials (about 16,000 people) of aspirin for long-term secondary prevention that is, to prevent a further stroke and data on about 40,000 people from three trials of aspirin in treatment of acute stroke.
They found that almost all of the benefit of aspirin in reducing the risk of another stroke was in the first few weeks, and that aspirin also reduced the severity of these early strokes.
Rather than the 15 percent overall reduction in longer-term risk reported previously in these trials, aspirin reduced the early risk of a fatal or disabling stroke by about 70-80 percent over the first few days and weeks.
"Our findings confirm the effectiveness of urgent treatment after TIA and minor stroke and show that aspirin is the most important component. Immediate treatment with aspirin can substantially reduce the risk and severity of early recurrent stroke," Rothwell said.
"This finding has implications for doctors, who should give aspirin immediately if a TIA or minor stroke is suspected, rather than waiting for specialist assessment and investigations," Rothwell noted.
instruction: What are the potential benefits of immediately taking aspirin after experiencing symptoms of a minor stroke or TIA, and how does this compare to the long-term benefits of aspirin therapy?
response: The potential benefits of immediately taking aspirin after experiencing symptoms of a minor stroke or TIA are significant and well-documented. A study published in the Lancet found that the risk of a major stroke is about 1,000 times higher in the immediate aftermath of a TIA or minor stroke, but this risk can be reduced by 70-80 percent in the first few days and weeks with immediate aspirin use. This immediate reduction is much more substantial than the long-term benefits of aspirin therapy, which typically reduces the risk of subsequent strokes by about 15 percent. The study also found that aspirin not only reduces the risk of another stroke but also lessens the severity of these early recurrent strokes. Therefore, the immediate use of aspirin is crucial for minimizing the risk and severity of major strokes, and doctors are advised to prescribe aspirin immediately upon suspicion of a TIA or minor stroke.

instruction: What are the key differences and similarities between dementia and Alzheimer's disease, and how do these conditions affect the cognitive abilities of elderly individuals?
response: Dementia and Alzheimer's disease share several similarities, including their impact on cognitive abilities in elderly individuals, such as memory loss, reduced concentration, and difficulty in processing information. Both conditions often result in social withdrawal, denial, and a need for constant care and support from caregivers. However, there are key differences between the two. Dementia is an umbrella term that encompasses a variety of cognitive disorders, which can be caused by different factors such as brain injuries or other diseases. Alzheimer's disease is a specific type of dementia characterized by the presence of beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain, leading to the progressive degeneration of brain cells. While the symptoms may overlap, Alzheimer's disease typically follows a more predictable and gradual progression. Effective management of both conditions involves a combination of medication, psychological support, and a supportive care environment, often provided by specialized centers and committed practitioners.

instruction: How do changes in attention and working memory with aging or disease impact the daily lives of individuals, and what are some of the key research areas being explored to address these changes?
response:
The impact of changes in attention and working memory with aging or disease, such as Parkinson's, can be profound and multifaceted. These cognitive declines can affect an individual's ability to perform daily tasks, maintain social relationships, and manage their health. For instance, reduced attention can lead to difficulties in concentrating on work, following instructions, or engaging in conversations. Working memory impairments can make it challenging to remember important information, follow multi-step tasks, and make decisions, which can result in a decline in independence and overall well-being.

Several key research areas are being explored to mitigate these effects:
1. **Cognitive Rehabilitation Programs**: These programs focus on training and exercises designed to improve attention and working memory. They often include computerized tasks, cognitive games, and real-life activities to enhance cognitive skills.
2. **Neurostimulation Techniques**: Research is being conducted on the use of non-invasive brain stimulation methods, such as TMS and tDCS, to enhance neural plasticity and improve cognitive functions.
3. **Drug Therapies**: Scientists are investigating both new and existing medications to treat cognitive decline. This includes drugs that target specific neurotransmitter systems, such as dopamine, which is particularly relevant in Parkinson's disease.
4. **Lifestyle Interventions**: Studies are exploring the benefits of physical exercise, a healthy diet, and adequate sleep on cognitive health. These interventions aim to support brain function and potentially slow down cognitive decline.
5. **Technological Solutions**: There is growing interest in developing assistive technologies, such as smartphone apps and wearable devices, that can help individuals manage their cognitive symptoms and improve their daily functioning.

These research areas are crucial for developing effective strategies to support individuals with cognitive impairments and enhance their quality of life. By addressing these challenges, researchers hope to provide practical solutions that can make a significant difference in the lives of those affected by aging and neurological conditions.

According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control & Prevention, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death in the United States and is a major cause of adult disability. The Visiting Nurse Association (VNA) Space Coast, a not-for-profit home health agency serving all of Brevard County, provides in-home health care to support patients and their family caregivers as they recover from a stroke.
Linda Shelby, RN, is the director of the VNA’s home health services. She explains that her staff of nurses, therapists and home health aides care for patients who have experienced strokes of various types and severities. Hemorrhagic strokes, which may lead to the most severe complications, result from the rupture of a blood vessel and are often caused by uncontrolled high blood pressure. Ischemic strokes occur when a blood vessel becomes blocked by a clot of some type. A transient ischemic attack, often called a “TIA” or “mini-stroke,” is caused by a temporary blockage and may cause less severe symptoms that go away with no residual effect.
Linda explains that most VNA home health patients are seen after they’ve suffered a TIA. “We work with those patients,” she explained. “To address the underlying health condition that contributed to the stroke. A TIA can be a precursor to a major stroke, so we’re really trying to help patients prevent a second, more serious and potentially debilitating stroke.”
Often, this means teaching patients and their family how to manage chronic health conditions like hypertension, high cholesterol, or atrial fibrillation along with related medications such as anti-coagulants and blood thinners. The VNA can also provide in-home telemonitoring to keep an eye on patients’ vital signs and symptoms.
Sometimes, however, patients suffer more severe strokes and need rehabilitative therapy to help them regain the ability to walk, speak, or even swallow. They may also need instruction on how to adapt to life when using a cane, walker or wheelchair. In these instances, the VNA’s therapy team steps in. Amy Fulmer, PT, the VNA’s primary physical therapist in Brevard County, explains that the VNA’s physical, speech, and occupational therapists help patients regain the highest level of function possible after a stroke. Many patients become frustrated at the perceived slow pace of their recovery. “They worry that their level of function won’t return to normal,” she said. “So we’re there to reassure them and provide them with coping techniques to help them practice patience as they recover.”
Patients who experience severe debility after a stroke need ongoing assistance from a family or professional caregiver. Eileen Petrie, RN, the VNA’s patient care manager, explains that the VNA can help family caregivers navigate seemingly daunting challenges like how to properly move the patient, prevent skin ulcers in bed-bound patients, or even administer tube feedings. “Our patients didn’t need us before a stroke,” she said. “I always tell them we’ll get them to the point that they can get along without us, regardless of how much education and support is required.”
In-home care provided by the VNA’s nurses, therapists, home health aides and social workers is generally covered by Medicare and commercial insurances; Linda Shelby says she’s surprised at how many people don’t realize that in-home care is a covered Medicare benefit.
VNA medical director James Kearney, M.D., agrees, “I have seen firsthand the benefit of home health care therapy in the long-term recovery in patients with stroke,” he said. “It is important for patients to work closely with healthcare providers to identify early onset of symptoms.”
For more information about VNA home care services, please call (321) 752-7550 or visit VNAtc.com License
instruction: What are the key strategies and educational approaches used by home health care providers to help patients and their families manage the risk of a second, more serious stroke after a TIA?
response: Home health care providers, like the VNA Space Coast, employ several key strategies and educational approaches to help patients and their families manage the risk of a second, more serious stroke after a TIA: 1) **Education on Chronic Condition Management**: Patients and families are taught how to manage conditions like hypertension, high cholesterol, and atrial fibrillation, which are significant risk factors for stroke. This includes detailed instructions on medication adherence, particularly for anti-coagulants and blood thinners. 2) **Telemonitoring for Continuous Care**: In-home telemonitoring systems are used to keep a close watch on patients' vital signs and symptoms, enabling early detection and intervention for potential issues. 3) **Rehabilitation Services**: For those with more severe strokes, physical, speech, and occupational therapists provide comprehensive rehabilitation to help patients regain as much function as possible and adapt to any new physical challenges. 4) **Emotional and Psychological Support**: Providers offer emotional support and coping techniques to help patients deal with the frustration and anxiety that often accompany the recovery process. 5) **Family Caregiver Training**: Home health care providers educate family caregivers on essential skills, such as proper patient handling, preventing skin ulcers, and managing complex care tasks like tube feedings, ensuring that patients have the necessary support for their ongoing recovery.

instruction: What are the potential neurological abnormalities that can occur in the setting of metabolic coma, and how do they typically present?
response: In the setting of metabolic coma, several neurological abnormalities can occur, including decerebrate rigidity, which is a severe and dramatic posturing characterized by extension of the limbs, plantar flexion of the feet, and internal rotation of the arms. This condition is often a sign of severe brainstem dysfunction and can be seen in cases of profound and prolonged hypoglycemia. Other potential neurological abnormalities include decorticate posturing, characterized by flexion of the arms and extension of the legs, and various levels of consciousness impairment, ranging from stupor to coma. These abnormalities typically present as changes in muscle tone, reflexes, and level of consciousness, and they can be reversible if the underlying metabolic disturbance is promptly corrected, as demonstrated in the case of a patient who fully recovered from decerebrate rigidity associated with hypoglycemic coma.

Why Do Dementia Patients Remember Some Care Givers?
It is possible that the person’s ability to perceive themselves or their friends, family, and partner may become reduced. It may also be due to them believing they are in a different era, which makes it very difficult for family and friends.
Why Do Dementia Patients Remember Some Things And Not Others?
Recent memories, plus the ongoing availability of new information, are at a disadvantage when living with Alzheimer’s. It takes longer for a person to process, remember, or recall specific events from childhood or later.
Do Dementia Patients Remember People?
Confusion and loss of memory. people with Alzheimer’s, they may forget a number of familiar objects or people. When a child has memory loss or confusion, it is extremely difficult for caregivers and families to come to terms with it. The need to communicate and understand is immense.
What Do Dementia Patients Remember?
While people with dementia may forget the details of an event even if they forgot them, they have no memory of how they felt about it anyway. Some may not be able to remember the location of their summer vacation, or their trip had been gone when a friend visited, however they will still enjoy it later on.
Do Dementia Patients Remember Family?
Memory loss has a significant impact on people with dementia who don’t remember their parents or even close friends. This shouldn’t be an issue for you. Over time, dementia causes this type of memory loss.
What Helps Dementia Patients Remember?
To be more positive, say, “Do it again. Let’s try it.” rather than, “Don’t do it.”
Don’t forget to respect and talk to them respectfully as if you didn’t hear from them, did not know their names or understand them.
Don’t repeat your words. Just phrase them instead.
Listen to what your listener wants…
Make the background noise less annoying…
You should be patient.
At What Stage Do Dementia Patients Forget Family Members?
Communication is a serious problem for the senior citizens in late-stage dementia as well as advanced dementia. A verbal exchange of thoughts and feelings may not take place. As a result of dementia, memory can also become deteriorate, leaving individuals unable to recall food that is served. Families may forget the names of their members.
Can People With Dementia Have Selective Memory?
Sometimes it’s difficult to find common cognitive patterns in people who are suffering from dementia or Alzheimer’s disease.
Can Alzheimer’S Patients Remember Certain Things?
Dementia sufferers often suffer from memory impairments in short-term memory, however, they are generally able to recall events many decades ago, but not in memory of what they were doing earlier.
At What Stage Of Dementia Do You Not Recognize Family Members?
In some cases, dementia can progress to the point that it may be a severe condition. Often, sufferers have very little memory of the events that occurred during this period. When someone with dementia recognizes their family, they may not realize they are there.
Can Someone With Dementia Remember Things?
Stories about past experiences, life experiences, and memories are described as being’reminiscences. Often, people with dementia are able to recall objects and words that were many years ago than those in their recent memories. Many of the conversations and interactions in our daily lives depend upon our short memories.
What Are The Signs Of Advanced Dementia?
An inability to move alone.
Being unable to speak or understand anything.
The elderly often need help with most of their daily activities, such as eating and taking care of themselves.
One of the most common symptoms of eating disorders is difficulty swallowing.
What Is The Last Thing Someone With Dementia Remembers?
A person suffering from dementia with poor memory or cognitive abilities will likely reach its late stages with significant memory loss and difficulty with memory. Several recent memories may be lost completely (for instance, who they ate breakfast or when they last saw their friend), and some may only be remembered a few decades from now.
How Do You Make Someone With Dementia Remember?
Make sure your interactions are positive…
Take special care of this individual…
Make your message clear….
Simple questions that are answerable should be asked…
Stay connected to your ears, eyes, and heart to hear what you’re saying…
A series of steps will help you to organize your activities.
Get the focus back on the path of the go when tough times arise.

instruction: How do different stages of dementia affect a patient's ability to remember family members and recent events?
response: Dementia impacts a patient's memory in a progressive manner, affecting their ability to remember family members and recent events differently at various stages. Initially, in the early stages, patients might retain the ability to recognize family members and recall recent events, although they may struggle with remembering recent conversations or the specifics of recent activities. As dementia advances to the middle stages, patients often experience more significant memory loss, making it harder for them to recognize family members and recall recent events. They may still have a sense of familiarity with family members but struggle to remember names or specific details about recent interactions. In the late stages of dementia, patients often lose the ability to recognize family members altogether. Their short-term memory is severely compromised, leading to difficulty in remembering recent events, such as what they ate for breakfast or when they last saw a loved one. This progressive decline in memory can be emotionally challenging for both the patient and their family members.

Objective: The authors assessed the prevalence of major depression (DSM-III-R) among Parkinson's disease patients and compared this rate with that of matched physically disabled subjects.
Method: The 30-item General Health Questionnaire and measures of physical disability were completed by all patients in Dunedin, New Zealand, identified as having Parkinson's disease. Patients scoring over 5 on the General Health Questionnaire were interviewed with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R--Non-Patient Version. Each patient living in the community was matched for age, sex, and level of physical disability with a comparison subject who did not have a neurological condition.
Results: Of the 73 subjects with Parkinson's disease who agreed to participate and were judged not to be demented, 34.2% scored higher than 5 on the 30-item General Health Questionnaire, but only 2.7% met the criteria for major depression. No difference from the comparison group was found.
Conclusions: The prevalence of major depression in patients with Parkinson's disease may be no greater than in age- and sex-matched physically disabled persons.
instruction: What methods are commonly used to assess the mental health of patients with chronic physical conditions, and how effective are these methods in identifying major depression?
response: The assessment of mental health in patients with chronic physical conditions often involves a combination of screening tools and diagnostic interviews. In the context of the study on Parkinson's disease patients in Dunebin, New Zealand, the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ) was utilized as an initial screening tool. The GHQ is a 30-item questionnaire designed to detect psychological distress and is commonly used in primary care settings. Patients who scored above a threshold of 5 on the GHQ were then evaluated using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID-NP), a more comprehensive diagnostic tool. The SCID-NP is a standardized interview that helps in diagnosing major depression according to the DSM-III-R criteria. The study found that while 34.2% of the Parkinson's disease patients scored above the threshold on the GHQ, indicating potential psychological distress, only 2.7% were diagnosed with major depression using the SCID-NP. This discrepancy suggests that while the GHQ is effective in identifying patients who may need further evaluation, it may not be as precise in diagnosing major depression. The use of a two-step approach—initial screening followed by a detailed diagnostic interview—ensures that patients with potential mental health issues are not overlooked, but it also highlights the need for more accurate initial screening tools to reduce the number of false positives. The effectiveness of these methods in identifying major depression is therefore moderate, with the GHQ serving as a useful but not definitive tool in the assessment process.

Shortly before his death, his family said he suffered from psychosis and schizophrenia. He also had lost his ability to walk.
Dr. Tara Chen, a resident at Rochester Regional Health, did not treat the man, who died in 2016, but did examine his case while she researched a report on Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease at the hospital over five years, according to Live Science.
Chen's report was presented earlier this month during a meeting of organizations discussing infectious diseases.
Other people whose medical records Chen examined who have the disease included a hotel housekeeper, a janitor, a chemist who somehow ate dog food, and a woman who had undergone surgery.
Those who contract CJD usually die within a year of being infected. There is no treatment or cure. About 1 in a million people come down with CJD in the world, with about 350 cases in the U.S. each year, according to the National Institutes of Health.
CJD occurs when proteins called prions leave holes in the brain, according to the NIH.
CJD was in the news when people in the U.K. ate contaminated beef after a mad cow disease outbreak.
instruction: What are the typical symptoms and progression of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), and how does it affect the brain?
response: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the rapid onset of cognitive and motor symptoms. The disease is caused by the abnormal folding of prion proteins, which form aggregates that damage brain tissue, creating a sponge-like appearance. Typical early symptoms include memory problems, behavioral changes, and difficulty with coordination. As the disease progresses, patients often experience severe cognitive decline, visual disturbances, and muscle stiffness or spasms. In advanced stages, individuals may become bedridden, lose the ability to speak or move, and may exhibit signs of psychosis. The progression of CJD is swift, with most patients dying within a year of diagnosis. There is no cure or effective treatment for CJD, and management primarily involves providing supportive care to alleviate symptoms and improve quality of life.

Natural Remedies for Insomnia (Adults & Children)
Have you ever tried any natural remedies for insomnia? Most of them work surprisingly well, and many are actually free. That’s right, you don’t even need to go to the store to buy a supplement to help you sleep better. However, you will need to take the time to do some work on yourself by changing some old habits and integrating newer, healthier habits. So what are some healthy habits that you should try to integrate if you want to overcome your insomnia condition?
Additional Related Article to Read : Medical Reasons for Insomnia: Why Insomnia Occurs
Natural Remedies for insomnia to try out
- Brainwave entrainment – With technology these days, you can actually change your brainwave patterns from high-beta (e.g. quicker brainwaves that cause you to feel stress and excitement) to slower, alpha brainwaves (e.g. those that are released when you relax). Most of these products work amazingly well, but there are some minor risks if you are susceptible to seizures and/or pregnant.
- Visualization – Simply closing your eyes for at least 20 minutes and imagining yourself relaxing will help you physically relax. It may help you to play some relaxing, ambient music, nature sounds, or white noise during this process, but those details are up to you. I visualize daily and I always feel relaxed afterwards. It definitely will help you fall asleep quicker if you have insomnia.
- Mindfulness meditation – People that practice this technique have reported deep feelings of relaxation following (as well as during) their meditation. It involves focusing on the present moment, and is somewhat tough to learn, but once you have it mastered, it will have been well worth it. Want an awesome natural remedy for insomnia? Try mindfulness meditation.
- Cardio exercises – If you do a hard cardiovascular workout for at least 1 hour daily, you are going to burn off the energy that would normally be bottled up inside of you when you go to bed. Cardio exercise is among the elite natural remedies for insomnia in children as well as adults. Nearly everyone can do some form of cardio – whether it’s playing soccer, running, rollerblading, or doing a tough beach body workout. If you burn calories and tire yourself out, you will be too tired to stay awake.
- Eliminating things from your diet – Many natural remedies for insomnia in adults and children can be gotten right from a healthy diet. If you are eating healthy foods, they will provide your brain with vital nutrients and give it what is needed to help you fall asleep at night. If you are loading up on caffeine and drinking alcohol (see: alcohol insomnia) consistently, you are likely going to struggle with insomnia. Cut out the unhealthy foods, drinks, and drugs, and you will improve – but the improvement is not going to be overnight; it may take a few months, but it will be well worth it.
instruction: How can brainwave entrainment and mindfulness meditation be used as natural remedies for insomnia, and what are the potential benefits and risks associated with these techniques?
response:
Brainwave entrainment and mindfulness meditation are two effective natural remedies for insomnia that can help individuals achieve better sleep. **Brainwave entrainment** involves using technology to alter brainwave patterns, shifting them from high-beta (which is associated with stress and excitement) to alpha waves (which are associated with relaxation). This technique can be particularly beneficial for individuals who struggle with racing thoughts or high levels of stress. By using audio or visual stimuli, such as binaural beats or flashing lights, brainwave entrainment can induce a relaxed state, making it easier to fall asleep. However, it is important to note that there are some minor risks associated with this method, especially for individuals who are susceptible to seizures or are pregnant.

**Mindfulness meditation**, on the other hand, focuses on being present in the moment and cultivating a non-judgmental awareness of one's thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations. This practice can help reduce the mental and physical tension that often accompanies insomnia. Regular mindfulness meditation can lead to deeper feelings of relaxation, both during and after the practice. It may take some time to master, but the benefits can be significant. Mindfulness meditation can also help individuals develop better sleep habits and reduce the anxiety that often comes with trying to fall asleep.

Both techniques can be used in conjunction with other healthy sleep practices, such as maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, creating a restful sleep environment, and avoiding stimulating activities before bedtime. The potential benefits of these techniques include improved sleep quality, reduced stress, and better overall well-being. However, it is always advisable to consult with a healthcare professional before starting any new treatment, especially if you have underlying health conditions.
