Student Dietitians Learn from Experience at Alzheimer Scotland
I really enjoy the initial moments of creating something new; envisioning potential, putting all the plans in place so that hopefully (fingers crossed), all will go well. But even better are the moments of satisfaction when plans have been realised and what was hoped for, has been achieved and more.
All 15 dietetics students currently in their 2nd year at Queen Margaret University recently took part in a learning experience that involved becoming a Dementia Friend (thank you Alzheimer Scotland’s Anne McWhinnie!) and a visit to one of Alzheimer Scotlands Dementia Cafes in the Lothian area (thank you to all of our Dementia Café facilitators too!).
With the help of a flipchart and pens, our feedback postcards and some evaluation forms too, programme leader Sara Smith and I met with students to hear feedback and to draw together all the learning. This was an important part of the educational process as well as giving us an opportunity to know more about how things had gone.
Because this was a new project, we were keen to find out as much as possible about how this experience had contributed to everyone’s learning. And I am pleased to say that the results are really very heartening. It was exciting to see how much could be achieved through such a simple, focussed programme. Through bringing together dietitians at an early stage in their training with people at an early stage in their dementia diagnosis, we can work together to develop a better understanding of dietetics and dementia – for better experiences now and in the future. Below is just a summary of our conversation with those who took part:
Students felt that they had increased knowledge of dementia. They commented that people with dementia are not all affected in the same way by the many types of dementia and that dementia does not define people.
The trainees highlighted the importance of dementia being understood by the general population, of dementia friendly societies. It had been useful to hear real-life examples of living with dementia in the community.
They had observed helpful approaches including using music, familiar activities and reminiscence projects to help people feel comfortable, engaged and connected and also had a good awareness of the ways in which people can maintain a good quality of life post-diagnosis; the importance of keeping active and the potential advantages of using memory aids to help with daily living.
It was suggested that this was an excellent opportunity to practice and reflect on communication skills, highlighting the importance of taking time and of patience in listening and responding. They also thought about the importance of conversing directly with the person in the presence of their carer.
The Dementia Cafes were described as: fun, varied, comfortable, social, familiar, consistent, supportive, empowering and as something for people to look forward to. Educational aspects were identified: sign-posting and information sharing, therapeutic elements: activities to stimulate and help with thinking and remembering. The importance of peer support for carers and people living with dementia was reflected upon, with students noticing that new and strong friendships had developed in the context of the dementia cafes.
Food and nutrition
In a café environment, trainees were able to consider how dementia may affect the person’s relationship with food and to see how staff applied their knowledge to adapt the environment to help (using contrasting coloured plates etc.)
It was agreed that the opportunity to come into contact with people living well in the community allowed the students to consider their role in working creatively, patiently and in a person centred way to contribute to people living better with dementia from the moment of diagnosis.
Knowledge & understanding
Students’ rating of their own knowledge pre and post visit (0= poor, 100= excellent) significantly increased across the board for the four questions they were asked, reflecting what came up in conversations – see table below
Unsurprisingly, after sharing all their great learning, everyone agreed that overall experience of Dementia Friends Training and Dementia café visits, had been a success and that it should be repeated in future. We hope that the project can become an annual integrated part of what student dieticians do. We are also working with Sara to build on our work to offer further and more in-depth learning opportunities that will allow students to progress from informed to skilled dementia practice levels.
It has been fantastic to hear about students’ experiences of dementia cafes. We would love to hear about your experiences too – what has been important for you?
And if you would like to know more about our Dementia Cafes or would like to become a Dementia Friend too, here are the links to get you started.
Alzheimer Scotland AHP Practice Education Facilitator
My role is to build on a programme of work of developing AHP student practice placements, an AHP internship programme and AHP volunteer opportunities in Alzheimer Scotland supporting the aspiration that all allied health professional students are skilled in dementia care on graduation. I have had some really positive experiences of joint AHP working in the past and am very much looking forward to this further opportunity to work together with AHP colleagues and Alzheimer Scotland to develop ways of working which are sustainable and best suited to meeting the needs of people living with dementia and their carers and families.
instruction: What are the key elements that make Dementia Cafes effective environments for both people living with dementia and their carers, and how can these elements be incorporated into other community settings to support a dementia-friendly society?
response: The effectiveness of Dementia Cafes in supporting both individuals living with dementia and their carers can be attributed to several key elements that foster a positive and engaging environment. Firstly, the cafes provide a comfortable and familiar setting that promotes social interaction and a sense of community. Activities such as music, reminiscence, and familiar tasks are designed to engage participants and help them feel connected and valued. The consistent and supportive atmosphere, characterized by patience and empathy, helps to reduce anxiety and enhance the quality of life for those with dementia. Peer support is another critical element, as it allows both carers and individuals with dementia to form strong bonds and share experiences, reducing feelings of isolation. To incorporate these elements into other community settings, it is essential to create inclusive spaces that prioritize comfort, social engagement, and meaningful activities. Training staff and volunteers in dementia-friendly practices, such as using memory aids and adapting the environment to be more accessible (e.g., using contrasting colors for plates), can significantly enhance the experience. Additionally, emphasizing the importance of communication skills, such as active listening and speaking directly to the person with dementia, can help build a more supportive and understanding community. By integrating these elements, other community settings can contribute to a more dementia-friendly society.

instruction: How does the buildup of cellular debris in the brain contribute to cognitive decline, and what mechanisms are involved in this process?
response: The buildup of cellular debris in the brain is a significant contributor to cognitive decline. In a healthy brain, the body naturally breaks down and eliminates this debris, which includes protein plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. However, when the brain's natural clearance mechanisms fail, this debris accumulates, leading to a slowdown in brain function and cognitive decline. The accumulation of these proteins can cause neurons to die, disrupting neural communication and leading to symptoms such as memory loss, difficulty concentrating, and confusion. This process is often associated with neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's, where the buildup of beta-amyloid plaques and tau protein tangles is a hallmark. Preventing this buildup through lifestyle changes, such as maintaining a healthy diet and managing stress, can help mitigate the risk of cognitive decline.

Scientists have identified what may cause that sudden “brain freeze” that comes from eating an ice cream cone or drinking a frosty beverage too quickly on a hot day: Changes in blood flow that mirror what happens in migraine sufferers.
The findings, presented at the Experimental Biology 2012 meeting in San Diego this week, may eventually lead to new treatments for other types of headache.
"The brain is one of the relatively important organs in the body, and it needs to be working all the time," said Jorge Serrador of Harvard Medical School, who helped lead the research. "It's fairly sensitive to temperature."
The research team noted migraine sufferers are more likely to experience “brain freeze” than people who don't have this often-debilitating condition, and sought to determine if a common mechanism is at work.
For the study – conducted by a team of researchers from Harvard, the Department of Veterans Affairs New Jersey Health Care System and the National University of Ireland – scientists induced “brain freeze” in the lab in 13 volunteers and studied blood flow in their brains. The researchers show that the sudden headache seems to be triggered by an abrupt increase in blood flow in one particular blood vessel -- the anterior cerebral artery -- and disappears when this artery constricts.
Serrador and his colleagues speculated that the increase in blood flow in response to cold may be to keep the brain warm – and safe from injury -- noting similar alterations in blood flow are at work in migraines, posttraumatic headaches, and other headache types.
The findings could lead to new ways to treat such conditions with drugs that control blood flow.
instruction: What are the potential benefits and risks of manipulating blood flow in the brain as a therapeutic approach for headache disorders, and how might this impact the overall health of the brain?
response: The potential benefits of manipulating blood flow in the brain to treat headache disorders are substantial. Given that changes in blood flow, specifically in the anterior cerebral artery, are linked to the onset of headaches like migraines, therapeutic interventions that target these changes could provide effective relief. For example, drugs that can constrict or dilate blood vessels could be developed to manage headache symptoms more precisely. This approach could significantly reduce the frequency and intensity of headaches, improving the quality of life for many individuals. However, there are also risks associated with this method. The brain's complex and delicate nature means that any manipulation of blood flow must be carefully controlled. Improper regulation could lead to issues such as hypoperfusion, which can cause brain tissue damage, or hyperperfusion, which can increase the risk of hemorrhage. Additionally, the brain's temperature and nutrient supply are tightly regulated by blood flow, and disruptions could have broader health implications. Therefore, while the therapeutic potential is promising, it is crucial to conduct extensive research and clinical trials to ensure that the benefits outweigh the risks and that the overall health of the brain is not compromised.

Numb fingertip tips can be an uncomfortable and painful condition.
If you have been suffering from this symptom, seek medical help right away. While it may be caused by a number of different factors, it is important to get a full diagnosis in order to find the best treatment.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is one of the main causes of numb fingers. This condition is caused by repetitive motions and can be mild or severe. 손끝저림
You should get treatment if you experience extreme numbness, tingling or swelling. Treatment options include pain relief medication, physical therapy, splints and surgery.
Another cause of numb fingertips is Raynaud’s disease.
It is a condition that can occur at any age. This disease affects the blood vessels in the body. However, it is usually found in middle-aged or older adults, but is also common among children.
There are two types of Raynaud’s: primary and secondary. Primary Raynaud’s is caused by a disease called scleroderma, while secondary Raynaud’s is caused by an autoimmune disorder.
Another reason for numb fingers is infection. A sexually transmitted disease, like syphilis, can cause this symptom.
The resulting sores can appear on the mouth, lips, genital area and vagina. In more serious cases, the sores can become large and infected. When these cysts become too large, they can press on the nerves and cause numbness.
Rheumatoid arthritis can also lead to numbness in the fingers.
Although there is no clear cure for the disease, regular exercise and other lifestyle changes can help. Some patients have found that taking a vitamin B6 supplement can reduce the symptoms.
Chronic overdose of this vitamin can damage sensory nerves, which can cause numbness in the fingers.
Guillain-Barre syndrome is a rare autoimmune disorder. This disease can occur at any age and is typically preceded by respiratory illnesses. 강서구정형외과
Patients have trouble controlling their breathing and may experience numbness, tingling or weakness in the arm. Surgery to relieve the pressure on the nerves in the neck is required in more severe cases.
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is another condition that can lead to fingertip numbness. MS most often strikes women between the ages of 20 and 50. Symptoms are also common at night. Other symptoms of this disease include double vision and muscle and limb weakness.
Fibromyalgia is another condition that can cause numb fingertips.
This condition is related to a number of autoimmune disorders. Fortunately, most of the time, the condition resolves on its own. Medications, acupuncture and other treatments can also ease the symptoms.
Excessive exercise can also lead to Fingertip Numbness. Exercises that require bending and lifting the wrist for long periods of time can put undue pressure on the median nerve.
Also, if you work with a desk setup that requires constant wrist contact, you may be more susceptible to carpal tunnel syndrome.
You can find out more about these conditions and other numbness-causing medical conditions by talking to your doctor.
Depending on the cause of your numbness, your doctor will likely perform a variety of tests to identify the issue and recommend a treatment plan.
instruction: What are the primary medical conditions that can cause numbness in the fingertips, and how do they differ in their symptoms and treatment options?
response:
Numbness in the fingertips can be a symptom of several medical conditions, each with its own unique set of symptoms and treatment options:

1. **Carpal Tunnel Syndrome**: Characterized by numbness, tingling, and sometimes pain in the fingers, caused by compression of the median nerve. Treatment includes pain relief medication, physical therapy, splints, and possibly surgery.

2. **Raynaud’s Disease**: Involves vasospasms in the blood vessels, leading to cold, white, or blue fingers. It can be primary (no underlying cause) or secondary (due to conditions like scleroderma). Treatment focuses on avoiding triggers and may include medication.

3. **Infections (e.g., Syphilis)**: Sores from syphilis can press on nerves, causing numbness. Treatment involves antibiotics to eliminate the infection.

4. **Rheumatoid Arthritis**: Chronic inflammation of the joints can affect nerves, leading to numbness. Treatment includes exercise, lifestyle changes, and supplements like vitamin B6, but caution is needed to avoid sensory nerve damage from overuse.

5. **Guillain-Barre Syndrome**: A rare autoimmune disorder causing rapid onset of numbness and weakness, often requiring hospitalization. Treatment may involve plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin.

6. **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**: Affects the central nervous system, causing a range of symptoms including numbness, double vision, and muscle weakness. Treatment includes disease-modifying drugs and symptom management.

7. **Fibromyalgia**: A chronic condition causing widespread pain and numbness, often related to autoimmune disorders. Treatment may include medications, acupuncture, and other therapies to manage symptoms.

Join top gaming leaders at the GamesBeat Summit 2023 in Los Angeles, May 22-23. Register here.
During a panel discussion at GamesBeat Summit this week, several experts in the field spoke about the rise of digital entertainment as a new form of treatment. More specifically, they talked about how video games can be used for a variety of healthcare applications, including neurological diseases and even patient care. The panelists were Eddie Martucci, the CEO and co-founder of Akili Interactive, Mirelle Phillips, the founder of Studio Elsewhere, and Laura Tabacof, Assistant Professor of Rehabilitation at Mount Sinai. Stanley Pierre-Louis, CEO of the Entertainment Software Association, moderated the panel.
Martucci’s studio Akili produces EndeavorRx, an FDA-cleared video game treatment for children with ADHD. As Martucci said, getting a game approved as a medical treatment wasn’t easy: “The route was to get it fully through clinical trials, so we did large-scale clinical trials, just like you’d expect a pharmaceutical product to do. ” . We put it through the FDA’s two-year review process for the first time, and EndeavorRx is still the only FDA-approved video game on the market. It’s been a long journey, it’s taken a long time and I think we can learn a lot now for the future.”

Akili Interactive's EndeavorRx, a video game designed for children with ADHD, has been FDA-approved, highlighting the potential of games as medical treatments. VR technology has also shown promise in treating chronic pain, with clinical trials at Mount Sinai demonstrating significant improvements. The benefits of these technologies include patient engagement, empowerment, and the provision of non-invasive and non-pharmacological alternatives to traditional treatments. Patients can gain control over their conditions through interactive and fun experiences, which can be particularly beneficial for those who do not respond well to conventional methods. Catherine Wolf, age 62.
When were you diagnosed with ALS? How did you react? Fall, 1997. First, I reacted with denial. I pursued treatments for Lyme disease and neuropathy. Then I told myself I'd be a slow progressor. Finally, I accepted the diagnosis and got proactive concerning my future needs. I also became active in the ALS community.
How did friends and family react? There was a range of reactions, from disbelief to supportive.
How do you manage your condition, emotionally and physically? I have an optimistic spirit and I don't give in. Friends and family help. Early on, I learned it was important to anticipate my future needs.
Has having ALS altered the way you look at the world? Life is mostly random, in that you can't control whether or not you get a disease like ALS. But you can control how you react to “bad luck.” I found strength I didn't know I had.
instruction: In what ways can a serious health condition like ALS influence an individual's perspective on life and personal strength, and how might this impact their relationships with friends and family?
response: A serious health condition like ALS can profoundly influence an individual's perspective on life and personal strength. For Catherine Wolf, the initial reaction to her diagnosis in 1997 was denial, as she sought treatments for other conditions. However, as she accepted her diagnosis, she discovered an inner resilience and strength she didn't know she possessed. This newfound strength allowed her to become proactive about her future needs and to engage actively in the ALS community. Emotionally, managing ALS required an optimistic spirit and a refusal to give in, which was bolstered by the support of friends and family. Her experience has taught her that while life's events may be random, one's reaction to them is within their control. This shift in perspective can lead to a deeper appreciation of life and a stronger sense of personal resilience. In terms of relationships, the range of reactions from disbelief to support from friends and family can either strain or strengthen these bonds. For Catherine, the support she received was crucial in her emotional and physical management of the condition, highlighting the importance of a strong support network.

Mom used to love to be with her family, but now she seems so distant and quiet. She often doesn’t remember names or faces and doesn’t participate in activities she used to enjoy. Frequently, she becomes lost just walking around the block. Her husband, a devoted and supportive partner, doesn’t know what to do to help his wife anymore. The woman who was once so independent and resourceful seems to be disappearing day by day and the whole family feels helpless.
The sad thing is that none of the conventional doctors seem to know what to do about it, either. Their only solution is expensive drugs that seem to cause more harm than good or forestall the inevitable. It’s only a matter of time before Mom will need constant care in an assisted living facility or nursing home. Everyone is dreading that day.
A diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease or any other cause of dementia that would shorten your cognitive lifespan is very frightening. While we hear so much about this disease, many of us may not understand what it is and what some of its early warning signs are. What is even more alarming, many of us do not know some of the simple things that can be done to prevent or reduce risk factors years before it occurs, mostly because there are very few actually talking about what can be done.
This book will tell you what dementia is, some of the things that contribute to it, and what you can do now to prevent or stall its progression.
About the Author
Lauren Russel, ND, is a board-certified licensed Naturopathic Physician in full-time practice at Tahoma Clinic in Washington State. In her medical practice, she focuses on bio-identical hormone therapy for men and women, thyroid imbalances, adrenal fatigue and stress management, gastrointestinal and digestive health, food allergies, sleep issues and nutritional optimization. She was the lead researcher on two studies investigating the effects of physiologic doses of the hormone, aldosterone, on hearing loss in study volunteers at Tahoma Clinic.
She received her doctorate degree in Naturopathic Medicine from Bastyr University in Kenmore, Washington, and undergraduate degree in the Biological Sciences from the State University of New York at Stony Brook. Dr. Russel also serves as an adjunct to the naturopathic medicine department at Bastyr University to facilitate key training and testing programs to improve the skills of medical students.
She has been a medical writer and editor for more than 25 years, working with several prominent, peer-reviewed medical and scientific publications and has developed continuing education materials for healthcare professionals throughout the United States.
She has been a contributing author to the publications, NDNR: Naturopathic Doctor News and Review, the Townsend Review for Doctors and Patients, and Life Extension Magazine. She has also co-authored articles with Dr. Jonathan Wright, MD, and researched topics for the newsletter, Nutrition and Healing.
instruction: What are some preventive measures and lifestyle changes that can be adopted to reduce the risk of developing dementia, and how effective are these strategies in delaying its onset?
response:
Preventive measures and lifestyle changes can play a significant role in reducing the risk of developing dementia and delaying its onset. According to the text and general medical knowledge, some effective strategies include:

1. **Regular Physical Exercise**: Engaging in moderate-intensity exercise, such as walking, swimming, or cycling, for at least 150 minutes per week can improve cognitive function and reduce the risk of dementia. Exercise helps increase blood flow to the brain and promotes the growth of new brain cells.

2. **Healthy Diet**: Adopting a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins, such as the Mediterranean or DASH diet, can lower the risk of dementia. These diets are high in antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds that protect brain health.

3. **Mental Stimulation**: Regularly engaging in mentally stimulating activities, such as reading, puzzles, and learning new skills, can help build cognitive reserve and delay the onset of dementia. Cognitive reserve refers to the brain's ability to cope with damage by using alternative neural pathways.

4. **Social Engagement**: Staying socially active and maintaining a strong support network can reduce the risk of dementia. Social interaction can provide mental stimulation and emotional support, which are both important for brain health.

5. **Stress Management**: Chronic stress can contribute to cognitive decline. Practicing stress-reduction techniques, such as mindfulness, meditation, and yoga, can help manage stress levels and protect the brain.

6. **Adequate Sleep**: Ensuring sufficient and high-quality sleep is crucial for brain health. Sleep helps consolidate memories and clear toxins from the brain. Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep per night.

7. **Avoiding Smoking and Limiting Alcohol**: Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption can increase the risk of dementia. Quitting smoking and drinking in moderation can help reduce this risk.

8. **Managing Chronic Conditions**: Controlling conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, and high cholesterol can lower the risk of dementia. Regular check-ups and following a doctor’s advice for managing these conditions are essential.

These strategies, when combined, can significantly reduce the risk of developing dementia and delay its onset. However, it is important to note that while these measures can be effective, they do not guarantee the prevention of dementia, as genetic and other factors also play a role.

How Healthy Living Affects MS
You’ve likely heard the expression, “An apple a day keeps the doctor away.” And for patients who are living with multiple sclerosis (MS), that expression may have some truth to it. New research has emerged that shows that a diet full of vegetables, fruits, and whole grains—and with few added sugars and processed and red meats—is associated with a reduced risk of disability in patients with MS.
But the benefits go beyond reduced disability risk, especially for those with a healthy lifestyle. For this research, a healthy lifestyle is defined as a healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining a normal weight, and avoiding smoking.
MS is characterized by the body’s immune system attacking myelin, the fatty substance that coats nerve cells, and the nerve cells themselves. The damage that is done can result in numbness, fatigue, tingling, dizziness, blurred vision, and walking problems.
MS and Diet
Researchers aren’t sure exactly how a healthy diet can help patients with MS, but it may be because healthy diets typically help to reduce inflammation. Since MS creates inflammation, it’s logical that a diet that reduces it will improve symptoms. Additionally, losing weight as a result of eating right can reduce pressure on joints.
MS and Exercise
In most cases, it is safe for MS patients to exercise—although the doctor should be consulted first. If tolerated, exercise can help to maintain muscle strength, allowing for a quicker recovery if a relapse occurs. Patients should aim for aerobic exercise three to four times a week and find a physical activity that they enjoy, if their doctor approves exercise.
While there is still research needed to determine how lifestyle factors improve MS, there are associations there that are worth exploring.
instruction: What are the potential benefits of regular physical activity for individuals with MS, and how can it contribute to their overall health and management of the condition?
response: Regular physical activity plays a significant role in the overall health and management of multiple sclerosis (MS). Engaging in consistent exercise can help individuals with MS maintain muscle strength and flexibility, which are often compromised due to the disease's impact on the nervous system. By keeping muscles strong, patients can improve their ability to recover more quickly from relapses and reduce the risk of secondary complications such as joint problems. Exercise also has psychological benefits, such as reducing stress and improving mood, which can be particularly important for managing the emotional aspects of living with a chronic condition. Furthermore, physical activity can contribute to better cardiovascular health, which is essential for overall well-being and can help mitigate some of the fatigue commonly experienced by individuals with MS. It is recommended that patients aim for aerobic exercise three to four times a week, with activities that they enjoy, and always consult with their healthcare provider to ensure the exercise plan is safe and suitable for their specific condition.

text:
New Information on Epilepsy
Author: Newcastle University
Published: 2009-11-30 : (Rev. 2011-08-28)
Synopsis and Key Points:
Research using human brain tissue removed from people suffering from epilepsy has opened the door to new treatments.
Main DigestPioneering research using human brain tissue removed from people suffering from epilepsy has opened the door to new treatments for the disease.
Scientists at Newcastle University have for the first time been able to record spontaneous epileptic activity in brain tissue that has been removed from patients undergoing neurosurgery.
Led by Newcastle University's Dr Mark Cunningham, the research has revealed that a particular type of brain wave pattern associated with epilepsy is caused by electrical connections between nerve cells in the brain - rather than chemical ones. This means the traditional drugs are useless to them.
Published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences ( PNAS ), Dr Cunningham said the findings marked a huge step forward in our understanding of a disease which affects an estimated 45 million people worldwide.
"Until now we have only been able to mimic epilepsy using experimental animal models but this can never give you a true picture of what is actually going on inside the human brain in epilepsy," explained Dr Cunningham who is based in Newcastle University's Institute of Neuroscience.
"Our findings help us to understand what is going wrong and are an important step towards finding new epilepsy treatments in the future."
The first line of treatment for patients with epilepsy uses anti-epileptic drugs to control seizures.
However, in almost 30 per cent of patients the drugs don't work. In this case, one course of action available to them is a neurosurgical procedure in which the brain tissue responsible for the epilepsy is removed from the patient.
Working in collaboration with the Epilepsy Surgery Group at Newcastle General Hospital and IBM Watson Research Center in New York, the team - with permission from the patients - have taken this epileptic tissue into the lab and 'fooled' it into thinking it is still part of the living brain.
They have then been able to record electrical signals from individual neurons and also networks of neurons.
Comparing this with normal brain tissue activity they managed to record an underlying 'noise' - a particular type of brain wave, or oscillation, which occurs in the intact epileptic human brain and which scientists believe is a precursor to an epileptic seizure.
Using a combination of experimental techniques, the team have shown that rather than being controlled by chemical signals which most conventional anti-epileptic drugs target, this oscillation relies on direct electrical connections.
"This may explain why the traditional drugs that target chemical connections don't work for patients with this kind of epilepsy," explains Dr Cunningham, who conducted the research with his colleague Professor Miles Whittington.
"These findings have massively increased our understanding of epilepsy and offer real hope in terms of finding new ways of tackling the disease.
"The next step is to understand what it is that triggers the transition between the underlying epileptic state of the brain cells and the fast oscillations that are responsible for causing a seizure."

instruction: How does the discovery of electrical connections between nerve cells in epileptic brain tissue impact the development of new treatments for epilepsy?
response: The discovery of electrical connections between nerve cells in epileptic brain tissue opens new avenues for the development of targeted treatments for epilepsy. Dr. Mark Cunningham's research at Newcastle University has revealed that the brain wave patterns associated with epilepsy in human brain tissue are primarily driven by direct electrical connections, rather than chemical ones. This finding is crucial because it explains why traditional anti-epileptic drugs, which target chemical neurotransmitters, are ineffective in a significant portion of patients. By focusing on the electrical connections, researchers can now explore alternative therapeutic approaches, such as developing drugs or devices that modulate these electrical signals. This could lead to more personalized and effective treatments, ultimately improving the management of epilepsy and reducing the burden of the disease on affected individuals.

SPONSORED POST – With more than 795,000 strokes occurring every year in the US across the age spectrum, it is critical that all Americans adopt preventive lifestyle habits, know the warning signs, and understand the treatment options available to themselves and their loved ones should a stroke occur.
May is Stroke Better Hearing & Speech Month – a time for Hutchinson and surrounding residents to become stroke savvy.
“During Better Hearing & Speech Month, we want stroke survivors and their loved ones to know that speech-language pathologists are here to help,” said Susan Kasal, MS, CCC-SLP-R, LSVT, at Hutchinson Health. “We offer a range of therapeutic services to meet the challenging needs of these individuals.”
Although it’s more common in older adults, stroke can affect anyone. In fact, stroke is trending upward in younger Americans.
A recent study showed that the rate of stroke increased by 147 percent in people ages 35 to 39, 101 percent in people ages 40 to 45, 68 percent in people ages 45 to 49, and 23 percent in people ages 50 to 54.
Although not all strokes are preventable, certain lifestyle habits can reduce a person’s risk of having a stroke.
Factors that work in a person’s favor include maintaining a healthy diet and low cholesterol, exercising regularly, limiting alcohol consumption, and refraining from smoking.
Early action is vital
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), only 38 percent of respondents to one survey were aware of all major symptoms and knew to call 9-1-1 when someone was having a stroke.
Patients who arrive at the emergency room within three hours of onset of their first symptoms often have less disability three months after a stroke than those who receive delayed care, thus recognizing the signs and taking quick action is key.
Of the 750,000+ Americans who suffer strokes annually in the US, more than 130,000 die.
For those who survive a stroke, quality of life is an important issue.
In addition to regaining physical abilities, such as the ability to walk, get dressed, and bathe independently, one’s capacity to communicate may also be severely damaged by a stroke.
“A person’s ability to communicate is the foundation of just about everything they do, and every interaction they have,” explained Susan Kasal, speech-language pathologist at Hutchinson Health. “Beyond just having their basic needs met, the degree to which communication skills are restored affects stroke survivors’ social interactions and relationships, employment status and success, and overall satisfaction and participation in life. Seeking treatment from a speech-language pathologist can make a transformative difference in helping people enjoy a fulfilling post-stroke life.”
One of the most common communication challenges that follow a stroke is aphasia, a disorder that affects a person’s ability to understand or produce language.
About 25 to 40 percent of stroke survivors acquire aphasia.
Other communication difficulties include slurred speech due to weak muscles, and difficulty in programming muscles for speech.
In addition to these challenges, speech-language pathologists help with cognitive challenges following a stroke – which may include memory and problem-solving skills – and swallowing problems that result from weakness and/or incoordination of muscles in the mouth and throat.
instruction: What are the key lifestyle changes that can reduce the risk of stroke, and why is it important for individuals of all ages to be aware of these changes?
response: Key lifestyle changes that can reduce the risk of stroke include maintaining a healthy diet, regular exercise, managing cholesterol levels, limiting alcohol consumption, and avoiding smoking. These changes are crucial for individuals of all ages because stroke can affect anyone, not just older adults. Recent studies show a significant increase in stroke rates among younger age groups, including a 147% increase in people ages 35 to 39 and a 101% increase in those ages 40 to 45. Adopting these preventive habits can help reduce the risk of stroke and its associated disabilities, which can severely impact quality of life. Early recognition of stroke symptoms and prompt medical attention are also vital, as patients who receive timely care often have better outcomes. For those who survive a stroke, the ability to communicate and perform daily activities can be significantly affected, making it essential to seek help from speech-language pathologists for rehabilitation.

instruction: How does chronic sleep deprivation affect the brain's ability to function, and what are some of the long-term health implications of this toxin buildup?
response: Chronic sleep deprivation adversely affects the brain's ability to function by disrupting the natural process of toxin removal. During sleep, the brain's glymphatic system becomes active, flushing out waste products that accumulate throughout the day. These waste products include harmful toxins like beta-amyloid proteins, which are associated with conditions such as Alzheimer's disease. When you consistently do not get enough sleep, this crucial detoxification process is compromised, leading to a buildup of toxins in the brain. This toxin accumulation can result in a range of cognitive impairments, including attention deficit disorder (ADD), memory loss, and decreased problem-solving abilities. Additionally, the brain's ability to recover from daily stress and maintain optimal neural function is compromised. Over time, chronic sleep deprivation can have long-term health implications, such as an increased risk of neurodegenerative diseases, weakened immune system, and other systemic health issues like cardiovascular and metabolic disorders.

instruction: How does the malfunction of the immune system contribute to the development of multiple sclerosis, and what are the current theories about why this malfunction occurs?
response:
In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system malfunctions and begins to attack the myelin sheath that insulates nerve fibers in the central nervous system. This autoimmune response causes inflammation, damage, and scarring of the myelin, leading to impaired nerve function. The underlying mechanisms of this immune system malfunction are not entirely clear, but research has identified several contributing factors.

One theory suggests that genetic factors play a significant role. Individuals with certain genetic variations, particularly in the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) complex, are more susceptible to developing MS. These genetic predispositions may influence the immune system's ability to distinguish between self and non-self, leading to the attack on myelin.

Another theory involves environmental triggers, such as viral infections. For instance, the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) has been linked to an increased risk of MS. The virus may trigger an immune response that cross-reacts with myelin proteins, leading to autoimmune attacks. Other environmental factors, such as low levels of vitamin D and exposure to certain toxins, are also being investigated for their potential roles in MS development.

Overall, the malfunction of the immune system in MS is a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors, and ongoing research aims to unravel these mechanisms to improve diagnosis and treatment strategies.

instruction: What are the potential benefits and drawbacks of using propranolol for migraine prevention, and how does its effectiveness compare to other common treatments?
response: Propranolol, a beta-blocker, is widely used for migraine prevention and offers several benefits and drawbacks. **Benefits:** 1. **Effectiveness:** Propranolol has been shown to reduce the frequency and intensity of migraines, as supported by clinical trials and patient experiences. Users often report a significant decrease in migraine episodes, making it a valuable option for chronic migraine sufferers. 2. **Multiple Indications:** Propranolol is not only effective for migraines but can also be used to manage conditions such as high blood pressure, anxiety, and performance anxiety, providing a multi-benefit treatment approach. 3. **Safety Profile:** It has a well-established safety profile, with many patients tolerating it well over long periods. **Drawbacks:** 1. **Side Effects:** Common side effects include fatigue, dizziness, and low blood pressure, which can impact daily activities. Some patients may experience more severe side effects, such as sleep disturbances or exacerbation of conditions like asthma or heart failure. 2. **Dosage Adjustments:** Determining the optimal dosage can be a trial-and-error process, and some patients may need to adjust their dose to find the right balance between efficacy and tolerability. 3. **Tolerance Issues:** Not all patients can tolerate propranolol, and some may need to discontinue use due to side effects. **Comparison to Other Treatments:** Other common treatments for migraine prevention include anticonvulsants like Depakote and Topamax, and calcium channel blockers like verapamil. **Depakote** is effective but can cause weight gain and sleep-related eating disorders. **Topamax** is also effective but is known for cognitive side effects such as difficulty concentrating and memory issues. Propranolol is often preferred for its fewer cognitive side effects and broader use in managing comorbid conditions.

text:
Myths About Neuropathy
Although many doctors commonly label Peripheral Neuropathy as “Idiopathic” (meaning the cause is unknown), there are a tremendous amount of research studies that discuss a vast multitude of well known causes of neuropathy. These studies have been published in acclaimed medical journals, such as, the Journal of The American Medical Association, The British Medical Journal, Journal of Pharmacokinetics, (et al.) The research further reveals the ability of these nerves to regenerate under the proper treatment conditions. However, many doctors have not stayed current with the scientific literature, and, as a result, continue to perpetuate myths and misinformation.
Here are some common myths along with the most up to date factual information about neuropathy.
Myth #1: Medication will cure my neuropathy.
False – The most common treatment for neuropathy is the…
Take- Some-Pills-And-Wait-And-See method. Some of the more common drugs given include gabapentin (Neurontin), pregabalin (Lyrica), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and Tramodol (Ultram)—all of which have serious side effects. While this may be necessary for the temporary relief of severe symptoms, the truth is that medications do absolutely nothing to reverse nerve damage. In fact, some medications, such as gabapentin, actually accelerate the nerve damage.
Myth #2: Neuropathy only affects people with diabetes.
False – Actually, diabetic patients account for less than 20 percent of all neuropathy cases. There are far more neuropathy sufferers that do not have diabetes, according to a 2009 study. A study published by the Neuropathy Association revealed the following findings: “Neuropathy is often misrepresented as only being diabetes-related. However, this survey demonstrates that for every diabetic neuropathy patient, there are at least six more patients suffering with other various forms of neuropathies.”
While neuropathy is common in diabetic patients, there are many other causes of neuropathy. Some common causes include: Chemotherapy, Statin medications, Blood pressure medications such as Norvasc (amlodipine), Fluoroquinolone antibiotics (Cipro, Levaquin, Floxin, Avelox, Noroxin), B-vitamin deficiencies, nerve damage or entrapment, and side effects associated with other commonly prescribed medications. If you feel pain, even if you’re not diabetic, your neuropathy may be due to one or more of the causes listed above.
Myth #3: My doctor told me, “Nerves don’t regenerate. once damaged…that’s it and I will just have to live with my neuropathy!!”
False – Your doctor is not up-to-date on the current research. There are extensive studies revealing the contrary. Research studies from Harvard Medical School, and Massachusetts General Hospital (Wellman Center for Photomedicine) with published articles appearing in the International Journal of Endocrinology, 2012 have revealed that an array of therapies including low-level-laser therapy, neurotrophic nutrition (nutrients that evoke nerve repair) and exercise and nutrition have been found to aid in nerve repair and regeneration.
Myth #4: I only have numbness and tingling, so it’s no big deal.
False – Many neuropathy patients who suffer from mild numbness or tingling think that their symptoms are no big deal. They don’t understand that what they are feeling is only the tip of the iceberg. They think because they can continue to function—business as usual—the numbness and tingling will fade away all by itself without any treatment.
A study published in the British Medical Journal proved this myth false, showing that 75 percent of sufferers who do nothing about the numbness and tingling, will have either signficant pain or disability, twelve months later. Let’s face it, if your neuropathy symptoms haven’t gone away by now, it’s not likely they will disappear on their own. Remember, studies have shown that if ignored, symptoms can intensify, causing loss of sensation, unremitting pain, and even disability.
Myth #5: Neuropathy is a natural result of aging.
False – You can grow old gracefully without ever experiencing these levels of nerve damage. Neuropathy, once seen only in the senior sector, is now affecting people as young as thirty years old. This disorder can be caused by injuries, chronic illnesses, and complications caused by medications, among other things. By taking the right steps early, you can avoid suffering from many neuropathic symptoms as you get older.
Myth #6: I have to accept my neuropathy and learn to live with it.
False – Neuropathy doesn’t have to be a life sentence. A combination of proper stimulation to your nerves at home and in the clinic, detox, glucose control, and appropriate nutrients plays a pivotal role in nerve repair and regeneration. Whatever you do, don’t go untreated! (see tab on: Treatments / Laser Treatments)
Myth #7: All neuropathy feels the same.
False – Neuropathy symptoms can vary dramatically, depending on the cause and the stage of neuropathy. We know that there are many causes of neuropathy (see Myth #2). Early-stage neuropathy symptoms are typically mild numbness and tingling, whereas late-stage neuropathy can show up as creepy-crawly sensations, burning feet or hands, sharp pains, a loss of balance, and even significant muscle weakness. An unhappy nerve (injured or damaged) can’t communicate as well to the brain, and the brain misinterprets the signals. This can manifest as a wide variety of different symptoms.
Myth #8: My neuropathy pain is well-controlled by medication, so I’m doing just fine.
False – Medications merely mask symptoms, while the underlying condition continues to get worse. Medicating the symptoms is like taking the battery out of your smoke alarm to stop the noise.
Your pain might be gone, but the meds might be hiding a gradual loss of nerve function, and you could be losing your ability to maintain good balance. Then one day, without warning, you might fall and break your arm—or worse, a hip. Remember, if your neuropathy is not getting better, it’s probably getting worse.
Myth #9: Neuropathy only affects the hands and feet.
False – Although neuropathy often begins in the hands and feet, it will eventually slowly creep up the calves and forearms, often presenting as severe cramps, heaviness, or weakness in the legs, a creepy-crawly sensation, and a dry discoloration of the skin. In some cases, neuropathy can even cause dangerous complications in organ function.
Myth #10: The best thing to do for my neuropathy is to wait and see what happens.
False – This is by far the worst thing you can do. The consensus of the professional healthcare community, including top neurologists, oncologists and surgeons, all agree that peripheral neuropathy rarely, if ever, improves on its own. More often than not, the condition continues to worsen and can become debilitating. By detecting and treating neuropathy early on, you are more likely to have a much better prognosis. That’s not to say that more advanced neuropathy cannot be resolved. However, people with more advanced neuropathy tend to need more care, and the results tend to be slower.
instruction: How can early detection and proper treatment of neuropathy help in preventing the progression of symptoms and improving the quality of life for patients?
response: Proper and timely management of neuropathy is essential for preventing the worsening of symptoms and enhancing the quality of life for patients. Early detection allows for the identification and treatment of the underlying causes, such as diabetes, chemotherapy, or vitamin deficiencies, which can significantly impact the progression of the condition. For instance, studies have shown that 75 percent of patients who ignore mild symptoms like numbness and tingling will experience significant pain or disability within a year. By contrast, early intervention with appropriate treatments, such as low-level laser therapy, neurotrophic nutrients, and lifestyle changes, can promote nerve regeneration and improve function. Furthermore, addressing neuropathy early can help patients avoid the need for medications that may have serious side effects and do not reverse nerve damage. Instead, a comprehensive approach that includes proper stimulation, detoxification, and glucose control can lead to better outcomes and a higher quality of life for neuropathy patients.

instruction: What are the primary causes and risk factors associated with peripheral neuropathy, and how do they impact the treatment options available?
response: Peripheral neuropathy can be caused by a variety of factors, including diabetes, exposure to toxins, HIV infection, and certain medications. Diabetes is a significant risk factor, as high blood sugar levels can damage the peripheral nerves over time, leading to diabetic neuropathy. Exposure to toxins, such as those found in Agent Orange, can cause early-onset peripheral neuropathy, which is recognized as a potential health issue in veterans. HIV infection can also lead to peripheral neuropathy, either directly from the virus or as a side effect of antiretroviral medications. These causes influence the treatment options available. For diabetic neuropathy, treatment often involves strict blood sugar control, pain management with medications, and preventive measures to avoid complications. In cases of toxin-induced neuropathy, the focus is on removing the source of exposure and providing supportive care to manage symptoms. For HIV-related neuropathy, antiretroviral therapy is crucial, and additional treatments may include pain relief and physical therapy to improve quality of life.

instruction: What are some common causes of recurrent strokes, and how do they differ in their mechanisms of action?
response: Recurrent strokes can have multiple underlying causes, each with its unique mechanism. Small vessel hypertensive disease is a frequent cause, characterized by chronic hypertension leading to damage in the small blood vessels of the brain. This damage results in microinfarcts and can lead to recurrent ischemic events. Cardioembolic disease, another significant cause, is often linked to atrial fibrillation (AFib) or endocarditis. In AFib, the irregular heart rhythm can cause blood to pool and form clots in the atria, which can then travel to the brain and cause a stroke. In endocarditis, particularly bacterial endocarditis, clots can form on infected heart valves and embolize to the brain. Hypercoaguable states, which can be genetic (e.g., factor V Leiden) or acquired (e.g., cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome), increase the risk of blood clot formation, leading to recurrent strokes. CNS vasculitis, which can be caused by infections like syphilis, tuberculosis, or certain bacteria, leads to inflammation and damage of blood vessels, reducing blood flow and causing strokes. Additionally, certain infections, such as those associated with zoster (especially in the head and neck region), can increase the risk of cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs) due to the inflammatory response and vascular damage.

instruction: What are the potential benefits of early detection of memory problems, and how can it impact treatment and management strategies?
response: Early detection of memory problems can have profound impacts on treatment and management strategies. By identifying memory issues early, individuals can benefit from a broader spectrum of treatment options, including medications and therapies that are more effective in the early stages of cognitive decline. This can lead to a slower progression of symptoms and a higher quality of life. Moreover, early detection enables individuals and their families to take proactive steps in planning for the future, such as setting up advance directives and making necessary lifestyle adjustments. Early intervention also allows for the implementation of coping strategies and support systems, which can significantly enhance the individual's ability to manage daily activities and maintain independence. Overall, early detection is crucial for optimizing both the medical and personal aspects of managing memory problems.

instruction: How does regular exercise influence cognitive function and neural plasticity in older adults, and what are the potential mechanisms behind these benefits?
response: The impact of regular exercise on cognitive function and neural plasticity in older adults is well-documented and supported by extensive research, including studies conducted by Professor Lindsay Nagamatsu and her colleagues. One key finding is that resistance training, as highlighted in the study by Nagamatsu et al. (2012) published in the Archives of Internal Medicine, can significantly enhance cognitive and functional brain plasticity in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. This improvement is attributed to the increased brain volume and enhanced neural connectivity, particularly in the hippocampus, a region critical for memory and learning. Another study by ten Brinke et al. (2015) in the British Journal of Sports Medicine further corroborates these findings, showing that aerobic exercise can lead to increases in hippocampal volume in older women with mild cognitive impairment. The mechanisms underlying these benefits include the promotion of neurogenesis, the formation of new neurons, and the enhancement of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which supports the survival and growth of neurons. Additionally, exercise has been shown to improve executive functions, which are essential for planning, problem-solving, and inhibitory control, as evidenced by the study by Liu-Ambrose et al. (2010) in the Archives of Internal Medicine. These cognitive enhancements are crucial for maintaining independence and quality of life in older adults.

instruction: In what ways does a stroke affect not only the individual but also their relationships and social life, and what strategies can be employed to mitigate these impacts?
response: A stroke can have far-reaching consequences that extend beyond the individual to their relationships and social life. Physically, post-stroke complications such as pain, headaches, and mobility issues can limit an individual's ability to participate in activities they once enjoyed, leading to a sense of loss and isolation. Emotionally, conditions like aphasia can affect communication, leading to frustration and misunderstandings with family and friends. This can put a strain on relationships, as loved ones may feel helpless or unsure of how to provide support. Socially, the individual may withdraw from social interactions, feeling embarrassed or self-conscious about their physical or cognitive changes. To address these challenges, a multi-faceted approach is recommended. Communication aids and therapy can help individuals with aphasia communicate more effectively. Support groups and community resources can provide a sense of belonging and reduce feelings of isolation. Rehabilitation therapies, such as occupational therapy, can help individuals regain independence in daily activities, enhancing their quality of life. Additionally, counseling and family therapy can facilitate open communication and emotional support, helping both the individual and their loved ones navigate the changes brought about by the stroke.

instruction: How can peer support and socialization impact the recovery process for stroke survivors, and what are some specific programs or initiatives that facilitate this type of support?
response: The role of peer support and socialization in the recovery process for stroke survivors is multifaceted and highly beneficial. Social interactions can improve mental health, reduce stress, and enhance overall well-being. By connecting with others who have experienced similar challenges, stroke survivors can gain practical advice, emotional support, and a sense of belonging. This can be particularly crucial during the initial stages of recovery when patients may feel overwhelmed and isolated. The American Stroke Association (ASA) has developed several programs to facilitate peer support. One key initiative is the Sharegivers Peer Visitor Program Kit, which pairs experienced stroke survivors with recent patients. These peer visitors provide support, share their recovery journey, and offer practical tips, which can boost the confidence and resilience of new survivors. Another valuable resource is Stroke Connection magazine, which features articles and personal stories from stroke survivors and caregivers. This magazine not only provides information on various aspects of recovery but also helps survivors see that they are part of a larger community of individuals who have overcome similar challenges. Both of these resources are designed to enhance the recovery process by fostering a supportive and empowering environment.

instruction: What are the primary research interests of Prof. Lemmens, and how do they contribute to the field of stroke treatment and recovery?
response: Prof. Lemmens, a leading figure in stroke research and treatment at the University Hospitals Leuven, has dedicated his career to advancing the understanding of stroke through two primary research interests: the role of neuroimaging in acute stroke and the neurobiology of stroke recovery. His expertise in neuroimaging, honed during his time at Stanford and through his leadership in the WAKE-UP project, has been pivotal in developing MRI-based protocols to guide thrombolysis treatment. This approach helps identify patients who can benefit most from this therapy, thereby improving treatment outcomes. Furthermore, his research on the neurobiology of stroke recovery explores the mechanisms that underlie the brain's ability to heal and adapt after a stroke, which is crucial for developing new rehabilitation techniques and therapies. His contributions to the field are further evidenced by his extensive publication record, supervision of PhD students, and his role in coordinating national and international clinical trials, all of which contribute to the advancement of stroke treatment and recovery strategies.

instruction: What factors do independent medical experts consider when evaluating the therapeutic effects of a drug like Naudicelle for treating multiple sclerosis?
response: When independent medical experts evaluate the therapeutic effects of a drug like Naudicelle for treating multiple sclerosis, they consider a range of factors to ensure the drug is both safe and effective. These factors include the presence of high-quality clinical trials, such as randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which provide the most reliable evidence. They also examine the biological plausibility of the drug's mechanism of action, in this case, the role of linoleic acid in affecting the disease. Experts review the consistency of results across multiple studies and the statistical significance of the outcomes to determine if the drug consistently shows a benefit. Furthermore, they assess the safety profile, including any potential side effects and drug interactions. For Naudicelle, independent medical experts have concluded that the evidence is insufficient to support its therapeutic effect on multiple sclerosis, primarily due to a lack of robust and consistent clinical data.

instruction: What are the potential reasons behind the increased risk of early death in men with restless leg syndrome, and how can these insights be used to improve patient outcomes?
response: The potential reasons behind the increased risk of early death in men with restless leg syndrome (RLS) are multifaceted. The study by Xiang Gao in the journal Neurology highlights that men with RLS face a 40% higher risk of dying earlier than their peers. One key factor is the significant sleep disturbance caused by RLS, which can lead to chronic fatigue and a host of health issues, including cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and diabetes. By addressing both the physical and psychological aspects of RLS, healthcare providers can help mitigate the associated risks and improve the quality of life for patients.

text:
Dementia Patients Who Wander
Dementia is the leading cause of dependency and disability amongst older adults, placing a heavy burden on economies and families’ budgets. Wandering is one of the most dangerous dementia-related behaviors, resulting in elopement (running off secretly), injury and even death. It is estimated that up to 31% of nursing home residents and between 25% and 70% of community- dwelling older adults with dementia wander at least once.
For caregivers — many times family members — wandering can be an extremely frightening and overwhelming. Wandering represents the “tipping point” for many family caregivers, as they are more likely to report significant depression and burden — which, in turn, can lead to the gut-wrenching decision to place a loved one in a nursing home or locked memory care unit.
Other than mechanical devices like alarms, GPS trackers, and locks or chemical restraints like sedatives (not considered acceptable practice), little else can be done to prevent or decrease wandering.
Woolsey Pharmaceuticals’ BRAVYL® (fasudil), a repurposed therapeutic, is a potent inhibitor of Rho-kinase (ROCK).
Fasudil is believed to reduce wandering behaviors of elopement and getting lost by improving blood flow in the hippocampus, a part of the brain that plays a major role in navigation, learning, and memory. Fasudil is non-sedating.
BRAVYL has been tested in a small study of dementia patients who had symptoms of wandering. The disappearance of wandering symptoms in patients was observed after the start of treatment. There was a return to the pretreatment state after discontinuation of the fasudil treatment. The effect was replicated more than once in the patients.
The FOUND Study
(Fasudil fOr redUcing elopemeNt and spatial Disorientation)
FOUND is a phase 2a study designed to assess the effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of BRAVYL (oral fasudil) in people with dementia who have wandering behaviors of elopement and/or getting lost. The study is actively recruiting patients now.
In addition, FOUND will assess whether BRAVYL improves wandering behaviors of excess movement and pacing, cognition, memory, neuropsychiatric symptomatology, and caregiver/nursing staff burden.
Participation will be for up to 26 weeks. While there is a placebo-controlled period in the study, FOUND is designed to ensures that participants will receive drug for at least 12 weeks (and up to 18 weeks) for those who complete the full study. Participants may reside at home, a group home, an assisted living unit, or in a long-term care facility.
FOUND is recruiting at approximately 15 sites in the United States and Australia.
instruction: How do wandering behaviors in dementia patients impact the decision-making process of family caregivers, and what are the psychological and financial burdens associated with these behaviors?
response: The wandering behaviors exhibited by dementia patients pose significant challenges for family caregivers, influencing their decision-making processes and imposing substantial psychological and financial burdens. Wandering is a particularly dangerous behavior, with up to 70% of community-dwelling older adults with dementia wandering at least once. This behavior can lead to elopement, injury, and even death, creating a constant state of anxiety and fear for caregivers. The psychological toll is heavy, with many caregivers experiencing significant depression and a sense of burden. Financially, the costs of additional safety measures, such as alarms, GPS trackers, and locks, can be substantial, adding to the economic strain of dementia care. These factors often push caregivers to the breaking point, leading to the difficult decision to place a loved one in a nursing home or locked memory care unit, which can be emotionally and morally distressing. The development of treatments like BRAVYL (fasudil) offers a glimmer of hope. By improving blood flow in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in navigation and memory, BRAVYL has shown promise in reducing wandering behaviors. The FOUND study, a phase 2a clinical trial, is currently evaluating the effectiveness and safety of BRAVYL in reducing wandering and its associated symptoms, which could provide a much-needed non-sedating alternative to current management strategies and help alleviate the burdens on caregivers.

Your morning cups of coffee and tea could be associated with lower risk of stroke and dementia.
The cup of coffee or tea you reach for in the morning — OK, maybe it’s a few — may be associated with a lower risk for stroke and dementia, according to a new study.
Among more than 360,000 participants studied over a period of 10 to 14 years, those who drank 2 to 3 cups of coffee, 3 to 5 cups of tea, or a combination of 4 to 6 cups of coffee or tea a day had the lowest risk of stroke and dementia, according to researchers from Tianjin Medical University in Tianjin, China.
“Our findings suggested that moderate consumption of coffee and tea separately or in combination were associated with lower risk of stroke and dementia,” the authors of the study said in a release.
Around the world, 10% of deaths are caused by stroke, according to a 2017 study published in The Lancet.Dementia refers to a general decline in brain function, but it can set in after a stroke.
Drinking coffee or tea alone also was associated with lower risk for both conditions, but people who had 2 to 3 cups of coffee and 2 to 3 cups of tea daily — 4 to 6 cups total — faired the best, with a 28% lower risk of dementia and 32% lower risk of stroke than those who didn’t drink either, according to the study.
The participants’ information came from the UK Biobank, a database of anonymous health information from around half a million volunteers in the United Kingdom gathered between 2006 and 2020. The study looked at health participants between ages 50 and 74 who self-reported their consumption of coffee and tea.
Over the course of the study period, 5,079 participants developed dementia and 10,053 experienced at least one stroke, according to the study, which was published in PLOS Medicine.
There have been many studies suggesting health benefits may be associated with drinking coffee and tea, but it is important to note that the researchers could only say the two were linked — not that the beverages necessarily offered protection.
There are limitations to the accuracy of the data because the participants reported their own tea and coffee drinking, and their estimates could be influenced by their own bias, Dr. Lee H. Schwamm, chair of the American Stroke Association Advisory Committee and chair in Vascular Neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital, said via email.
“We cannot impute causality, and say ‘drinking more coffee or tea is good for your brain.’ What we can only say is that in this study, people who reported moderate coffee/tea drinking were less likely to have a stroke or dementia occur in the 10 years of follow-up,” Schwamm said.
instruction: What are the broader health implications of regular coffee and tea consumption beyond stroke and dementia, and how do these beverages potentially contribute to overall brain health?
response: Regular consumption of coffee and tea has been linked to various health benefits beyond reducing the risk of stroke and dementia. Both beverages contain bioactive compounds that can positively impact brain health. For example, coffee and tea are rich in antioxidants and polyphenols, which can help reduce inflammation and oxidative stress, key factors in the development of neurodegenerative diseases. Caffeine, a primary component of coffee, has been shown to improve cognitive performance, memory, and mood, contributing to better overall brain function. Tea, especially green tea, contains L-theanine, an amino acid that can enhance relaxation and reduce stress, which can further benefit cognitive health. Furthermore, moderate coffee and tea consumption may improve cardiovascular health, which is closely linked to brain health. Improved blood flow and reduced risk of cardiovascular diseases can lower the likelihood of cognitive decline. However, it is crucial to consume these beverages in moderation, as excessive intake can lead to negative side effects such as increased heart rate and insomnia. The optimal intake, as suggested by the study, is around 2 to 3 cups of coffee and 2 to 3 cups of tea daily, which can provide the most significant benefits while minimizing potential risks.

instruction: What are the primary causes and symptoms of vascular dementia, and how do they differ from those of other forms of dementia?
response: The primary causes of vascular dementia are related to conditions that affect the blood supply to the brain, such as cerebrovascular disease, stroke, and hypertension. These conditions can lead to damage in the brain's blood vessels, resulting in reduced blood flow and oxygen to brain cells. The symptoms of vascular dementia can include difficulties with cognitive functions, particularly in areas such as attention, problem-solving, and planning. Memory issues are also common, but they may not be as prominent as in other forms of dementia like Alzheimer's disease. Unlike Alzheimer's, which typically presents with a gradual and continuous decline, vascular dementia often shows a stepwise progression, with periods of stability interrupted by sudden declines following further vascular events. This can make the course of the disease more unpredictable and variable compared to other types of dementia.

From the Department of Health
The Department of Health (DOH) today advised persons with epilepsy (PWEs) to take their medications regularly and have a regular check up to prevent seizures and lead a normal life as the country observes National Epilepsy Awareness Week on September 1-7, 2013.
This year’s theme, Epilepsy ABC: Awareness Begins in Communities (Kaya Natin ‘To!), underscores the need to promote epilepsy awareness and inclusion of PWEs in various levels of engagement like health, education, welfare, and development through community-centered activities.
Secretary of Health Enrique T. Ona revealed that epilepsy is present in around 1% of the global population and may be higher in developing countries.
In study conducted by the National Nutrition and Health Survey that was published in the journal of Neurology in 2003, disclosed that there are 230 persons with epilepsy per 100,000 populations in the Philippines. Epilepsy is the second most common consultation with a neurologist, second to stroke.
Ona added that epilepsy is more common among the very young and the very old, although it can strike individuals of any age. The mortality rate among people with epilepsy is two to three times higher than the general population and the risk of sudden death is 24 times greater.
“People with epilepsy can die of seizures and related-causes, including non-stop seizures, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy [SUDEP], drowning and other accidents,” Ona said, adding that the key to preventing seizures is regular medication and check-up.
Regular medication and check-ups are vital as 20%-30% of PWEs are severely affected and continue to have seizures despite treatment. Lack of knowledge about proper first aid procedures during seizure exposes affected individuals to injury, especially from objects that are needlessly forced into the mouth.
Epilepsy is a medical condition that sometimes results in seizures. These episodes of seizures are caused by a hyperactive and disorganized electrical activity of the brain.
However, more than their medical condition, PWEs are also faced with the non-medical problem of discrimination in education, employment, social acceptance, and extreme poverty.
“Epileptic persons deserve a place in our society. Let us be compassionate of their health conditions,” Ona concluded.
instruction: What are the key medical and social challenges faced by people with epilepsy, and how can regular medication and check-ups help mitigate these challenges?
response: People with epilepsy (PWEs) face significant medical and social challenges. Medically, the primary challenge is the unpredictable and often debilitating nature of seizures, which can lead to serious health complications such as non-stop seizures, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), drowning, and other accidents. The mortality rate among PWEs is two to three times higher than the general population, and the risk of sudden death is 24 times greater. Regular medication and check-ups are crucial in managing these risks. Medication helps control seizures, while regular check-ups allow healthcare providers to monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and make necessary adjustments. Socially, PWEs often face discrimination in education, employment, and social acceptance, which can lead to isolation and poverty. Community awareness and support are essential to address these social challenges. By promoting understanding and inclusion, communities can help PWEs lead more normal and fulfilling lives.

instruction: What are the primary factors that contribute to the development of movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and ataxias, and how do these factors interact to affect a person's functional independence?
response: Movement disorders like Parkinson’s disease and ataxias are multifaceted conditions influenced by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Genetic factors are crucial, as certain gene mutations can significantly increase the risk of developing these disorders. For Parkinson’s disease, mutations in genes such as LRRK2, SNCA, and PARK2 are well-documented. Similarly, ataxias can be linked to mutations in genes like ATXN1 and ATXN3. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins (e.g., pesticides, heavy metals), head injuries, and certain medications, can also contribute to the onset and progression of these disorders. The interplay between genetic and environmental factors is complex and can lead to the degeneration of specific neuronal populations. In Parkinson’s disease, this involves the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, while in ataxias, it affects the cerebellum, which is vital for coordination and balance. As these neurons degenerate, motor symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, and balance issues become more pronounced, significantly impacting a person's functional independence. Physical therapy plays a crucial role in managing these symptoms by focusing on improving strength, flexibility, balance, and gait. Through individualized programs tailored to each patient’s needs, physical therapists can help individuals maintain their functional abilities and perform daily tasks more safely and independently, thereby enhancing their quality of life.
