Natural healing: How to handle the affects of stress
We have been talking about things that interfere with the body’s ability to heal.
Last week we covered some of the affects stress has on the body. Since it is not always possible to avoid stress, how do we reduce the negative impact stress has on our bodies?
Well, let’s start with breathing. Under stress we begin to use what are call accessary muscles of respiration to increase oxygen intake. These muscles include neck muscles and the muscles in between the ribs. The long term consequence of driving these muscles is that we become shallow breathers, eventually leading to decreased oxygen absorption, increased muscle tension in our neck and shoulders and poor posture.
We can start breaking the stress response simply by doing breathing exercises. Start by breathing in as deeply as possible, hold the breath in for a few seconds and then breathe out for twice the time you used to breathe in. When doing deep breathing, try to breath into your stomach and expand the time it takes to complete a full breath cycle.
Also, use exercises that control breathing. Go for a walk, but only breathe through your nose. Reducing the speed of your walk so you can do it by only breathing through your nose will naturally force you to breathe more deeply. Over time you will become much more efficient at breathing slowly and deeply, which will provide a constant counter cycle to the stress response.
The next thing to do is to begin sipping water throughout the day. The process of swallowing activates the parasympathetic or anti-stress part of the nervous system. You may have heard the term “stress eating” or overeating in times of stress. While there are many aspects that play into this, one of the biggest is that you own body will try to balance itself by driving digestion processes. While constant eating tends to put weight on us that eventually causes more stress, constantly drinking water drives the same aspects of the nervous system.
By increasing your water intake you will also find yourself less hungry, which will help you eat appropriate amounts. When it comes to eating, remember stress deprives us of circulation to the digestive organ, so focus on eating easy to digest food. Soups, stews, and healthy, well cooked meals will be easier to absorb, and reduce the possibility of damage to the stomach and intestines.
Next, let’s not forget sleep. Remember, under stress your brain will already be in a hyper vigilant state. Counter that by doing as much as you can to get into a relaxed stated before bed. Don’t work on stressful projects right before bed, and don’t watch exciting movies or TV. Actually any complex visual stimulus like TV will only amp up your brain. Instead, read or listen to relaxing music, take a hot bath; give your body every opportunity to wind down.
Take sleep seriously, your brain will thank you!
Dr. Joseph Fraley D.C. is the owner of Alpha Omega Chiropractic at 106 Alpine Village Rd. Contact him at 575-258-5999.
instruction: What are the benefits of sipping water throughout the day for managing stress, and how does it activate the parasympathetic nervous system to counteract the stress response?
response: One of the significant benefits of sipping water throughout the day for managing stress is its ability to activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps to counteract the stress response. The act of swallowing water stimulates the vagus nerve, a crucial part of the parasympathetic nervous system, leading to a reduction in heart rate, lower blood pressure, and an overall state of relaxation. This is particularly important because stress typically activates the sympathetic nervous system, causing a 'fight or flight' response that can be detrimental to health if sustained over time. By regularly sipping water, you can help balance these systems, reducing the negative effects of stress. Furthermore, drinking water can also help manage stress-related overeating by reducing feelings of hunger, and it supports the digestive system, which is often affected by stress. This holistic approach to hydration can contribute to better overall well-being and stress management.

text:
An Unbelievable Stroke
When I think about what happened to me, it's hard for me to really believe everything that actually occurred. I am very grateful to my mother and my daughter who have done everything to help me and I thank God who saved me and continues to help me with my life.
In August of 2005 I had a bunionectomy performed on my foot. I was worried about staying out of work too long so I. returned a couple of weeks later. I was working two jobs: as the news director at KYW-AM and as an adjunct professor at Temple University's School of Communications.
Following the surgery, a blood clot formed in my leg, broke free, and caused me to have a pulmonary embolism. I started to feel lightheaded and then lost consciousness. A friend and pastor called 911 and took me to a local hospital.
The hospital treated the pulmonary embolism with blood thinners, but they had an unintended side effect. The side effect was that some of the blood that was thinned out of my heart and lungs traveled up into my brain. The blood in my brain caused me to have a series of strokes. At that point, the staff at a small community hospital where I was initially treated decided they couldn't do anything else for me and I was transported to another hospital.
The doctors moved quickly to perform a blood clot evacuation. They knew that the parts of my brain that control memory, speech and language comprehension had been affected by the bleeding. The doctors told my mother and my daughter that I might die. Nevertheless, the surgery was deemed necessary and they went ahead with it. This entire time I was put into an induced coma. I remember very little if anything about this time. After the clot evacuation doctors performed a craniotomy so that my brain could have room to heal and swell without bumping up against my skull. I was still in a coma throughout all of this. Finally, after a few weeks they decided to take me off the drugs that were keeping me in a medically induced coma.
When I came out of the coma, I hardly recognized myself. Half of my head was missing (though it was wrapped in a bandage) and I still had a tracheotomy in my throat. As far as talking and understanding, I was in pretty bad shape, for a while. But shortly after this God chose to make strides in my life and he continues to help me everyday! I moved into a rehab hospital and was there for a while doing exercise and speech therapy. By Christmas 2005 I left the rehab hospital and came home. It was a little difficult at first because my son lives with me. He was only 11 years old when I came back and I was very worried that he would not understand what happened to me. Today, he's 14 and happy that I'm doing fine again.
It wasn't until March of 2006, that the rest of my skull was reattached. From home, I continued doing speech therapy and now I continue going to rehab. I'm almost finished with a study I'm working on with them to understand what happens to people like me with Aphasia. I also attend a conversation group with others who have Aphasia and I go to a book group meeting where others with Aphasia are reading a book.
I'm now very glad to be volunteering at Abington Memorial Hospital. I love to help people who had a stroke and are trying to get better. I think I have a unique situation. Others may have had some of the same problems I've had and I'd love to be able to talk to them about how they can get better. While my life is very different now, it is far from over. I used to do some really wonderful things professionally and I love opportunities to do more wonderful things in my personal life that enrich others.
instruction: How can medical professionals and families better support patients who have experienced a series of strokes and are undergoing recovery, particularly in terms of speech and memory rehabilitation?
response: Medical professionals and families can better support patients who have experienced a series of strokes and are undergoing recovery, particularly in terms of speech and memory rehabilitation, by providing a comprehensive and multi-faceted approach. First, medical professionals should ensure that patients receive early and intensive speech and language therapy. This therapy should be tailored to the specific needs of the patient and may include exercises to improve articulation, word-finding, and comprehension. Additionally, cognitive rehabilitation can help patients with memory issues by using strategies such as memory aids, repetition, and cognitive exercises. Family members can play a crucial role by participating in therapy sessions, practicing exercises at home, and providing emotional support. It is also important for families to create a supportive environment that accommodates the patient's needs, such as simplifying communication and reducing distractions. Furthermore, involving the patient in social activities and groups, like the conversation group and book group mentioned in the text, can help maintain social connections and improve overall well-being. Regular follow-ups with healthcare providers and adjusting the rehabilitation plan as needed are essential for long-term recovery.

instruction: What are the potential impacts of gender on the prognosis and future treatment of multiple sclerosis, and how might these differences influence clinical approaches?
response: The impact of gender on the prognosis and future treatment of multiple sclerosis (MS) is a critical consideration in clinical practice. Women are diagnosed with MS at a higher rate than men, and they often experience more frequent relapses, particularly influenced by hormonal changes such as those during pregnancy and menopause. However, men tend to have a more rapid progression to disability. These gender-specific differences have several implications for clinical approaches. For women, treatment plans may need to be adjusted to account for hormonal fluctuations and the potential for increased disease activity during certain life stages. On the other hand, men may require more aggressive and early interventions to slow disease progression. Clinicians should also be aware of the potential for gender biases in clinical trials and ensure that treatments are tested and validated for both genders. By recognizing and addressing these gender differences, healthcare providers can develop more personalized and effective treatment strategies for MS patients.

|Motto||The Parkinson’s Association improves the quality of life for those affected by Parkinson’s through education, family services, and the support of promising research.|

The Parkinson's Association is a Southern California mental health care service organization, supports Parkinson's research and is a not-for-profit organization. The Parkinson's Association helps people with Parkinson's disease navigate the symptoms of Parkinson's through medical support programs, education, research, awareness and support. Parkinson's families are treated through managing the symptoms.
The organization was known as the Parkinson's Association of San Diego until it expanded into the greater Los Angeles Area. It re-branded in 2013 to become the Parkinson's Association, expanding services to all of Southern California.
The Parkinson's Association offered programs and services to assist Parkinson's patients, their family members, and care partners. Parkinson's support groups are positioned throughout San Diego, Orange and Los Angeles Counties. This is a Southern California-based information and referral center, while conducting community based symposiums, workshops and services. The Parkinson's Association serves local communities with innovative health care programs including Minds and Motion Health Services. These services include direct programs to help Parkinson's families with counseling, physical and voice therapies.
The national Parkinson's magazine, Parkinsonian.org, was established in 2013. Over 38,000 subscribers, including 17,000 medical professionals across the United States, read news articles, scientific findings and health and fitness tips for families living with Parkinson's disease.
The Parkinson's Association research scientists collaborate with other research organizations on Parkinson's-specific stem cell research and disease progression projects. The stem cell research uses patients' DNA through skin fibroblasts and converts them to stem cells, then to dopamine-producing neurons. Upon approval by the FDA, these cells are intended to be implanted in patients, replacing lost neurons. The disease progression studies are based on tracking cognitive behavior therapies and mental health counseling to track changes as the patients age. Jerry Henberger retired as the executive director in June 2015. Lisa Fine assumed leadership of the organization as the executive director. In November 2016, the organization downsized and is run mostly by activists, volunteers and the board of directors. The annual Walk for Parkinson's is one of the largest Parkinson's non profit events on the west coast of California.
The Parkinson's Association provides local support groups throughout Southern California, including San Diego, Los Angeles and Orange County.
Minds and Motion Health Services
The Parkinson's Association provides trained mental health specialists to help families deal with issues such as depression, anxiety, marital problems, loss and thoughts of suicide. Depression and anxiety are among the common mental health complaints of both people with Parkinson's and their families. Cognitive behavioral therapy can help patients learn to live better by teaching techniques that can help patients live better.
Minds and Motion counseling and mental health services include:
- Individual Counseling: These sessions provide a private and confidential environment for discussion of issues that may be difficult to discuss with doctors, loved ones, or even in support groups. Therapists will help clients to express, understand and explore non-motor symptoms, as well as learn effective, research based strategies for managing these symptoms in order to live a happier, healthier life, both mentally and physically.
- Family Counseling: Couples and families face unique problems and these sessions provide a safe and comfortable space for couples and/or families to discuss interpersonal issues. Sessions are aimed at understanding how family dynamics impact psychological health and developing tools to strengthen family relationships.
- Group Counseling. Group counseling sessions will encompass a variety of topics and will consist of processing difficult feelings that may arise. Examples of topics include avoiding caregiver burnout, managing conflict, dealing with grief and loss in everyday life, managing anxiety and overcoming depression.
instruction: What are the key services provided by the Parkinson's Association to support individuals and families affected by Parkinson's disease, and how do these services help manage the symptoms of the disease?
response: The Parkinson's Association offers comprehensive services to support individuals and families affected by Parkinson's disease, focusing on mental health, education, and physical well-being. Additionally, the Parkinson's Association supports research initiatives, including stem cell research and disease progression studies, which aim to develop new treatments and improve understanding of the disease. By providing these services, the association helps individuals and families manage the symptoms of Parkinson's disease more effectively, enhancing their overall quality of life.

instruction: How can the combination of Keppra and tramadol affect a person's mood and appetite, and what are some potential strategies to manage these side effects?

Friday, February 26th, 2016
The latest research shows that the brain is capable of rewiring and adapting after stroke. Therefore, arm and hand recovery is more possible than previously thought. However, in order to improve function in the upper limb, the client must be willing to incorporate the affected side purposefully, functionally, and repeatedly. In addition to functional training, other beneficial strategies include strength training, mental imagery, robotics, and gravity compensation.
Below are the key takeaway’s that highlight the current thinking from the scientific community.
Arm and Hand Research Findings
What Do These Interventions Mean?
An Arm is a stationary cycle designed to strengthen and condition the upper body, as well as the cardiovascular system, by using the arms.
Biofeedback or electromyography (EMG) is a non-invasive technique used for measuring muscle electrical activity that occurs during muscle contraction and relaxation.
Electrical stimulation or neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a technique used to elicit a muscle contraction using electrical impulses. Electrical current is then sent from the unit to the electrodes and delivered into the muscle causing a contraction.
EMG-Triggered Stimulation is based on the user’s voluntary movement, or intent to move. Electrodes, controlled by a unit, are placed on the skin over a specific area. Once the user attempts to contract his or her muscles and reaches the prescribed threshold, stimulation is triggered (delivered) to the same muscles. Various visual and auditory feedback options monitor the progress.
An Exercise Aid is a piece of equipment used during physical activity to improve strength and coordination of the body region targeted.
Hand Function Splint
A Hand Function Splint is a rigid or flexible brace that offers dynamic or static assistance to the weakened hand so functional activities and exercises can be possible.
In Mirror Therapy, a mirror is placed beside the unaffected limb, blocking the view of the affected limb. This creates the illusion that both limbs are functioning properly. Damaged areas of the brain’s motor cortex may improve by viewing movements of intact, functioning limbs.
Mobile Arm Support
A Mobile Arm Support (MAS) is a gravity supported mechanical device mounted on wheelchairs, tables, or base frames. A MAS is used to support the weak arm to improve motor function and strength. In addition, the device allows patients with shoulder weakness to perform self care tasks such as feeding, hygiene, grooming, and writing.
Shoulder Subluxation Sling
A Subluxation Sling is typically used on hemiparetic arms that are flaccid or exhibit minimal to no movement. They offer support, protection against injury and can prevent or reduce shoulder pain.
Upper Limb Contracture Splint
A Upper Limb Contracture Splint is a brace used to prevent or treat contractures. The goal of a contracture splint is to help keep the soft tissues (muscle and tendons) in the arm and hand stretched properly.
Upper Limb Robot-Assisted Therapy
Upper Limb Robot-Assisted Therapy consists of an electromechanical device, designed for the arm or hand, that is used to assist users (through powered mobility) with exercise training and activities of daily living (ADL).
Virtual Reality/Exercise Games
Virtual Reality/Exercise Games consists of computer-based, interactive exercise games and activities that allow players to engage in entertaining tasks while being physically challenged. These games rely on technology that tracks body movements or reactions. Some advanced games allow users to set goals, grade and customize, receive instantaneous feedback, reinforce behaviors, and record and analyze results.
instruction: What are the potential benefits and limitations of using robotic-assisted therapy and virtual reality exercises in the rehabilitation of upper limb function post-stroke, and how do these technologies integrate with traditional physical therapy methods?
response: The use of robotic-assisted therapy and virtual reality exercises in post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation presents a range of potential benefits and limitations, and these technologies can be effectively integrated with traditional physical therapy methods. **Benefits:** 1. **Neuroplasticity and Motor Recovery:** These technologies support the brain's ability to rewire and adapt, which is essential for recovering upper limb function. By providing structured and repetitive practice, they can enhance neuroplastic changes. 2. **Patient Engagement and Motivation:** Virtual reality games and robotic exercises can make therapy more enjoyable and engaging, potentially leading to increased patient compliance and better outcomes. 3. **Precision and Customization:** These technologies can offer precise and customizable training, allowing therapists to target specific impairments and adjust the level of difficulty as the patient progresses. 4. **Data-Driven Feedback:** Real-time feedback and performance tracking can help therapists make informed decisions and optimize treatment plans. **Limitations:** 1. **Financial and Logistical Barriers:** The high cost of robotic and virtual reality systems can limit their availability, particularly in resource-limited settings. 2. **Technical Challenges:** Both patients and therapists may need extensive training to use these technologies effectively, and technical issues can arise, disrupting therapy. 3. **Overreliance on Technology:** There is a risk that patients might become too dependent on these tools, potentially reducing the effectiveness of traditional physical therapy methods. **Integration with Traditional Physical Therapy:** Robotic-assisted therapy and virtual reality can be integrated with traditional methods to create a comprehensive rehabilitation program. For instance, robotic devices can assist with strength and range-of-motion exercises, while virtual reality can enhance functional and cognitive aspects of therapy. Traditional methods such as manual therapy, strength training, and functional training remain essential and can be used in conjunction with these technologies to ensure a holistic approach to recovery.

instruction: How might the combination of alcohol and smoking impact cognitive functions such as memory and problem-solving, and what are the implications for treatment programs focused on alcoholism?
response: The dual impact of alcohol and smoking on cognitive functions is a critical issue for individuals with alcohol dependence. Studies have found that alcoholics who smoke experience more pronounced difficulties with memory, problem-solving, and quick thinking compared to non-smokers. This is particularly concerning because the co-occurrence of smoking and alcoholism is common, and the cognitive effects are not merely additive but can be synergistic. For instance, while alcohol can cause neurotoxicity and damage to brain structures involved in memory, smoking can exacerbate these effects by promoting oxidative stress and inflammation. Treatment programs for alcoholism should, therefore, adopt a holistic approach that addresses both substance use disorders. Ignoring smoking in these programs can lead to suboptimal treatment outcomes, as cognitive impairments can hinder an individual's ability to fully engage in and benefit from therapy. Integrating smoking cessation strategies into alcohol treatment can lead to better cognitive recovery and improved long-term outcomes.

Google Glass Sets Its Sights On Easing Parkinson’s Symptoms [Video]
Technology gives people with chronic illnesses greater independence.
Researchers from Newcastle University’s Digital Interaction Group in the UK are currently working on a way that Google Glass could be used to slow the onset of Parkinson’s disease. Not only could the technology provide people with greater independence, but it would help mitigate the symptoms that they experience every day.
Working with a group of Parkinson’s volunteers aged between 46-70 years, the team are using the technology to provide discreet prompts linked to key behaviours typical of Parkinson’s. Reminding the individual to speak up, or swallow to prevent drooling, are prime examples. Glass can also be used as a personal reminder for things such as medication and appointments.
“People with Parkinson’s are already coping with so much and one of the main causes of social isolation is the stigma around behaviours such as drooling and tremor which they have no control over,” explains Roisin McNaney, a speech and language therapist studying for her PhD at the university.
A similar project to the Parkinson’s aid was created by Seattle-based tech product design and development company Artefact. It’s calledDialog, and helps people with epilepsy figure out what triggers their seizures, and therefore, how best to deal with the condition. Even though Google Glass still hasn’t been released yet, it’s clear there is huge potential for ideas that help monitor and treat all sorts of physical, and mental illnesses.
instruction: What are the broader implications of using technology to assist with the management of symptoms in chronic conditions, and how might this impact social stigma and patient independence?
response: The integration of technology, such as Google Glass, into the management of chronic conditions such as Parkinson’s disease has multifaceted implications for patients and society. On a personal level, technology can significantly enhance patient independence by providing real-time, discreet prompts for symptom management. For instance, reminders to speak up or swallow can help individuals maintain social interactions and reduce the risk of social isolation. Moreover, these technologies can serve as personal assistants, helping patients manage their daily routines, including medication adherence and appointment scheduling. This can lead to better overall health outcomes and a sense of empowerment. On a societal level, the use of such technology can help combat the stigma associated with chronic conditions. By discreetly addressing symptoms that are often stigmatized, such as drooling or tremors, patients may feel more comfortable in public, leading to increased social participation and a reduction in social stigma. This, in turn, can foster a more inclusive and supportive community environment. In summary, technology not only improves the day-to-day lives of individuals with chronic conditions but also plays a crucial role in promoting social integration and reducing the negative social impacts of these conditions.

Antiepileptic drugs for chronic neuropathic pain
ForfatterLagerlöf, Anders Joakim
Neuropathic pain is caused by damage or disease that affects the somatosensory nervous system, where the nerves react abnormal to small or no stimuli at all and produces pain. It is less understood than nociceptive pain arising from a healthy nervous system and hence is a notoriously hard condition to treat. Neuropathic pain tends to be chronic with an average duration of 7 years . The cost to society and the implications for the patient in regard to comorbidity tends to be severe . I decided to write a topical review to look closer at what evidence there is for the most commonly used antiepileptic drugs in the treatment of neuropathic pain (gabapentin, pregabalin, clonazepam, lacosamide, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, valproic acid and zonisamide), what efficacy and what adverse effects one can expect.

instruction: What are the potential adverse effects of commonly used antiepileptic drugs in the treatment of neuropathic pain, and how do these effects impact patient quality of life?
response: The use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) in the treatment of neuropathic pain can lead to a range of adverse effects that can significantly impact a patient's quality of life. Commonly prescribed AEDs for neuropathic pain include gabapentin, pregabalin, clonazepam, lacosamide, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, valproic acid, and zonisamide. These drugs can cause various side effects, including central nervous system (CNS) effects like dizziness, somnolence, and cognitive impairment, which can interfere with daily functioning and cognitive tasks. Gastrointestinal (GI) effects such as nausea, vomiting, and constipation can also occur, leading to discomfort and dietary restrictions. Other systemic effects include weight gain (common with valproic acid), ataxia (seen with phenytoin), and thrombocytopenia (a risk with oxcarbazepine). These adverse effects can lead to decreased adherence to the medication regimen, which can compromise the effectiveness of pain management. Moreover, the chronic nature of neuropathic pain, often lasting an average of 7 years, means that patients are at a higher risk of cumulative side effects over time. This underscores the importance of a personalized treatment approach, where healthcare providers regularly assess and manage side effects to ensure that the benefits of AEDs outweigh the risks and that patients maintain a good quality of life.

What Does An MCI Diagnosis Mean?
It’s difficult to come up with a short, easy explanation of what Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is. Please read through all of our FAQs to get a full and clear picture.
Here are the highlights:
- A person with MCI is at an increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s or another dementia. (It is estimated 10-15% of individuals with MCI go on to develop dementia each year)*
- MCI is a degree of cognitive impairment that is not normal for the individual’s age.
- MCI describes a set of symptoms rather than a specific medical condition or disease.
- Those with MCI have an increased risk of eventually developing Alzheimer’s or another type of dementia. (It is generally considered to be the symptomatic “pre-dementia phase” of Alzheimer’s disease.)
- Not all people with MCI get worse — the memory deficits associated with MCI can remain stable for years or improve over time.
- Memory problems and other cognitive complications may be minimal to mild and hardly noticeable to the individual, or they may be more pronounced and noticeable to family and friends.
- In contrast to Alzheimer’s disease, where many cognitive skills are affected, MCI’s deficits in memory and thinking ability may not significantly impact daily functioning.
*Alzheimer’s Association Facts & Figures, 2022
Here are several official definitions of Mild Cognitive Impairment:
- Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) causes a slight but noticeable and measurable decline in cognitive abilities, including memory and thinking skills. (Alzheimer’s Association)
- It is an intermediate stage between the expected cognitive decline of normal aging and the more serious decline of dementia. It can involve problems with memory, language, thinking and judgment that are greater than normal age-related changes. (Mayo Clinic)
- It is a condition in which a person has problems with memory, language or another essential cognitive ability that are severe enough to be noticeable to others and show up on cognitive tests, but not severe enough to interfere with daily life. (International / National Council of Certified Dementia Practitioners)

instruction: What are the key differences between Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer’s disease in terms of cognitive symptoms and daily functioning?
response: The key differences between Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer’s disease lie in the severity and impact of cognitive symptoms on daily life. MCI is an intermediate stage between normal age-related cognitive decline and the more severe cognitive decline seen in dementia. Individuals with MCI may experience mild memory problems and difficulties with thinking skills that are noticeable to themselves or others but do not significantly impair their ability to perform daily activities. For example, they might have trouble remembering names or recent events but can still manage their finances and household tasks. On the other hand, Alzheimer’s disease involves a broader and more severe range of cognitive impairments that significantly affect daily functioning. People with Alzheimer’s may struggle with complex tasks, lose the ability to manage their finances, and have difficulty with basic self-care activities. Moreover, while MCI can sometimes remain stable or even improve, Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive condition that leads to a continuous decline in cognitive and functional abilities, eventually requiring substantial assistance and care.

Introduction Ambulance transport of patients with stroke is common, with rapid sequence intubation (RSI) to secure the airway used regularly. Randomised controlled trial evidence exists to support the use of RSI in traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), but it is not clear whether the RSI evidence from TBI can be applied to the patient with stroke. To this end, we analysed a retrospective stroke dataset to compare survival of patients with RSI compared with patients that did not receive RSI.
Methods This study was a retrospective analysis of 10 years of in-hospital and out-of-hospital data for all patients with stroke attended by Ambulance Victoria, in Victoria Australia. Generalised boosted logistic regression was used to predict propensity scores, with initial vital signs, age and demographic variables as well as measures of illness severity and comorbidity included in the prediction model. This analysis employed a 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching which was applied to generate a dataset from which we calculated the OR of survival to hospital discharge of patients receiving RSI versus no-RSI. The sensitivity of these results to unmeasured confounding was assessed with deterministic sensitivity analysis.
Results The propensity score-matched cohort showed a decreased survival for RSI in strokes with an OR 0.61 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.82; p=0.001) when compared with no-RSI. A subgroup analysis showed no significant survival difference for ischaemic strokes: OR 0.66 (95% CI 40 to 1.07; p=0.09). The survival for haemorrhagic stroke was OR 0.60 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.90; p=0.01) lesser for RSI. Results were likely robust to unmeasured confounding and missing data.
Conclusions Our retrospective analysis shows a decrease in survival when RSI is utilised by paramedics for stroke. Since RSI is commonly used for strokes, controlled trial evidence to support this practice is urgently needed.

instruction: How might the findings of this study influence the current protocols for ambulance transport and treatment of stroke patients, and what additional research is needed to support any changes in practice?
response: The study's findings, which indicate a decreased survival rate for stroke patients who undergo rapid sequence intubation (RSI), could have significant implications for the current protocols in ambulance transport and treatment of stroke patients. The results suggest that the routine use of RSI, a common practice in stroke care, may be associated with poorer outcomes, particularly for patients with haemorrhagic strokes (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.90, p=0.01). For ischaemic strokes, while the difference was not statistically significant (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.07, p=0.09), the trend still raises concerns. These findings highlight the need for a critical review of existing protocols and the potential development of new guidelines that emphasize alternative airway management techniques. For instance, EMS providers might need to adopt less invasive methods or reserve RSI for specific, high-risk scenarios where it is absolutely necessary. Additionally, to support any changes in practice, further research is essential. This should include large-scale, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that specifically examine the effectiveness and safety of RSI in stroke patients. These studies should also consider a broader range of outcomes, including neurological function and long-term quality of life, to provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of different airway management strategies on patient outcomes.

Alzheimer's Disease is the most common form of dementia. It effects more than 6 million people over the age of 65. Increased awareness and prevention efforts have left a lot of people with questions. Perhaps two of the most common questions include How can I prevent getting Alzheimer's? And what treatments if any are there for people who already have it?
In terms of keeping your brain healthy, scientists recommend:
Getting Good Sleep - getting a good night's sleep helps boost our immunity and archive our memories.
Healthy Diet - people with diets low in saturated fat such as vegetarian or Mediterranean have less signs of brain changes associated with Alzheimer's.
Exercise - exercise is so important for the prevention of many diseases, including Alzheimer's.
Socialize - being social and avoiding isolation.
Disease Prevention: Reducing you risk of vascular risks, controlling blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, and weight have been shown to lower your risk of dementia.
Check Your Hearing - hearing loss can cause shrinkage of brain areas close to the memory centers. Wearing hearing aids if you have hearing loss and having your hearing checked regularly is important.
instruction: How does managing vascular health, such as controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, play a role in preventing dementia, and what are some practical steps individuals can take to achieve this?
response:
Maintaining good vascular health, particularly by controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, is essential in preventing dementia. High blood pressure and high cholesterol levels can lead to atherosclerosis, which narrows and hardens the arteries, reducing blood flow to the brain. This reduced blood flow can result in brain cell death, contributing to cognitive decline and dementia. Here are some practical steps individuals can take to manage their vascular health and reduce the risk of dementia:

1. **Adopt a Heart-Healthy Diet**: Choose a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins, and low in saturated and trans fats. The Mediterranean diet is a great example of a heart-healthy diet that can help manage cholesterol levels and blood pressure.
2. **Regular Physical Activity**: Engage in regular physical activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, for at least 150 minutes per week. Exercise helps improve cardiovascular health, lower blood pressure, and manage cholesterol levels.
3. **Monitor and Manage Blood Pressure**: Regularly check your blood pressure and work with your healthcare provider to keep it within a healthy range. Lifestyle changes, such as reducing salt intake and managing stress, can also help.
4. **Control Cholesterol Levels**: Maintain healthy cholesterol levels through a combination of diet, exercise, and medication if prescribed by your healthcare provider. Regular cholesterol screenings can help track your progress.
5. **Maintain a Healthy Weight**: Being overweight or obese increases the risk of high blood pressure and high cholesterol. Achieving and maintaining a healthy weight through a balanced diet and regular exercise can significantly reduce these risks.
6. **Avoid Smoking and Limit Alcohol**: Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption are major risk factors for vascular diseases. Quitting smoking and limiting alcohol intake can improve overall vascular health.
7. **Regular Medical Check-ups**: Regular visits to your healthcare provider can help identify and manage vascular risk factors early, preventing the onset of dementia.

By implementing these strategies, individuals can significantly reduce their risk of developing dementia and promote overall brain health.

instruction: What are the potential mechanisms by which caffeine might help reduce the risk of Alzheimer's disease, and how do these mechanisms relate to cognitive function?
response: The potential mechanisms by which caffeine might help reduce the risk of Alzheimer's disease are multifaceted. One significant mechanism is the elevation of cyclic AMP levels. By reducing amyloid formation, caffeine may help prevent the neurodegenerative changes that characterize Alzheimer's. Furthermore, caffeine is well-known for its ability to enhance attention, which is a fundamental aspect of cognitive function. Improved attention can lead to better memory performance, as attention is essential for the encoding and retrieval of information. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are supported by preliminary research, more definitive evidence from randomized clinical trials is needed to fully understand the relationship between caffeine and Alzheimer's risk.

Surgical options, such as angioplasty and stenting, can prevent strokes by addressing blockages in the arteries. Post-stroke rehabilitation programs, combining physical, occupational, and speech therapies, are vital for recovery and regaining functionality.

response: Catalepsy is a condition marked by a sudden suspension of sensation and voluntary motion, often described as a trance-like state. Catalepsy can be a symptom of various underlying conditions, including mental illnesses such as catatonic schizophrenia, physical disorders like epilepsy, or cerebellar disorders. instruction: What are the primary symptoms and progression patterns of Acute idiopathic neuritis (Guillain-Barré Syndrome), and how do they affect the patient's overall health and daily activities?
response: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), or acute idiopathic neuritis, is a rapidly progressive autoimmune disorder that affects the peripheral nervous system. The primary symptoms include symmetric muscle weakness, which typically begins in the legs and spreads to the arms, often within hours to days. This weakness is frequently accompanied by paresthesias, or abnormal sensations, in the extremities. As the condition progresses, it can lead to more severe complications such as paralysis of the respiratory muscles, cranial nerve involvement (affecting facial and bulbar muscles), and autonomic dysfunction, which can cause fluctuations in blood pressure, heart rate issues, and urinary problems. The disease reaches its peak within 2-4 weeks, and then a recovery phase begins, which can last from several weeks to 1-2 years. The impact on daily activities is profound, as patients may struggle with basic movements, speaking, and breathing. In severe cases, hospitalization is necessary to manage respiratory failure and other life-threatening complications, such as pneumonia and thromboembolism. Early and intensive treatment, including plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin, is crucial for improving outcomes and reducing the risk of long-term disability.

Epilepsy affects different people in different ways. For many of the 600,000 people in the country it can be debilitating - causing constant seizures and making life miserable.
We are all familiar with the convulsive seizures associated with the condition - they strike at any time and can be life threatening. But for others, epilepsy is an invisible affliction that they live with daily.
Dave Mee lives with the condition. The 23-year-old works with Eastwood Town Football Club, doing press and writing match reports.
He’s big on football, but he doesn’t play much anymore.
His seizures are well under control - he hasn’t had one for over a year now, and when he does have them it can be as easy as focusing.
“I was having partial seizures a few months ago. I can feel them in my mind, but if I put my mind on something else I can make it pass in a few seconds.
“I know when their coming, and just by concentrating on something else I can control them.”
A major issue, Dave says, as that people don’t realise how varied epilepsy can be. There are 40 different kinds of seizures ranging from short absence seizures to the Grand Mal seizures we have seen on TV.
“Everybody has a different experience. For me it’s usually my hands shake. I lose control of them and I can drop things. It can be pretty embarrassing.
“I’ve had a seizure while serving a customer once - they were dumfounded when I was behind the meat and fish counter and I had a seizure where I just couldn’t move for a minute and a half.
“My customer must have thought she’d said something horrible because I was totally motionless.
“I dread that kind of thing happening again.
“But I’ve been lucky,” he continues. “I know other people who have it much worse.”
Epilepsy can be debilitating - the threat of regular and serious seizures puts people at risk of serious harm from falling, losing control of the car and other accidents, as well as starving the brain of oxygen during a long seizure.
Staying away from danger, and the dread of another attack, can lead to a great deal of isolation and depression.
The national charity, Epilepsy Action, says one in three people with epilepsy will experience depression at some point in their lives.
Campaigns manager Stacey Rennard adds: “The links between epilepsy and depression are complicated.
“Many studies show that depression is more common in people with epilepsy than without, and having depression can be a risk for developing the condition.”
When you have epilepsy, any number of things can cause depression from continual seizures to the fear of a seizure, side effects from treatment, problems at work, problems with friends – and for some, depression can be linked directly to the seizure itself.
“Some people with epilepsy also experience a sudden worsening of their mood as the first part of their seizures, during their ‘aura’,” says Ms Rennard.
“This is more common in people with temporal lobe epilepsies and when depression happens after a seizure, it might not start for several hours or it could be delayed for up to seven days afterwards.”
Isolation could be the worst enemy of a person living with epilepsy – particularly as many of the medications available are linked to depression, anxiety, rage and even suicidal thoughts.
Dave knows what this feels like - his condition has meant he hasn’t been able to drive for the past four years.
“I need to get to the football club from where I live in Ripley, and not being able to drive has made me a lot less independent.”
But that could all be changing, he adds.
“I’m starting lessons in a few weeks.”
His condition is less serious so there is still so much he can do, but Dave hopes others will spare a thought for how isolating it can be to live with the life-long condition.
instruction: What are the psychological impacts of epilepsy, such as depression and isolation, and how do they contribute to the overall burden of the condition on individuals and society?
response: The psychological impacts of epilepsy, such as depression and isolation, significantly exacerbate the overall burden of the condition on both individuals and society. Epilepsy is a highly variable condition, with symptoms ranging from subtle, almost invisible seizures to more dramatic convulsive episodes. This variability can lead to a lack of understanding and support from others, which can contribute to feelings of isolation. For example, Dave Mee, a 23-year-old living with epilepsy, has experienced social discomfort and embarrassment due to his seizures, particularly in public settings. The fear of having a seizure can lead to avoidance behaviors, such as not driving or participating in social activities, which can further isolate individuals. Additionally, the constant threat of seizures can cause chronic anxiety and stress, contributing to the development of depression. According to Epilepsy Action, one in three people with epilepsy will experience depression, which can be influenced by various factors, including the direct neurological impact of seizures, the side effects of medications, and the social and emotional challenges of living with a chronic condition. The psychological burden of epilepsy not only affects the individual's well-being but also places a strain on family, friends, and healthcare resources, making it a significant societal issue.

instruction: What are the potential implications of overlooking subtle cognitive deficits in post-stroke patients for their long-term rehabilitation and quality of life?

However, KM's personal observations and subsequent testing using more sensitive cognitive measures revealed ongoing high-level cognitive deficits. Ignoring these subtle deficits can result in several negative outcomes: patients may face difficulties in performing complex daily tasks, maintaining social relationships, and returning to their pre-stroke level of employment. Ultimately, this can result in a diminished sense of well-being and a lower quality of life for the patient, emphasizing the need for comprehensive and patient-centered post-stroke assessments.

instruction: What are the different types of neuropathy, and how do they affect the body?
response:
Neuropathy, a disorder affecting the peripheral nerves, can manifest in several distinct forms, each with its own set of symptoms and impacts on the body:

1. **Mononeuropathy**: This type of neuropathy affects a single nerve. Common examples include carpal tunnel syndrome, which affects the median nerve in the wrist, causing pain, numbness, and weakness in the hand, and Bell's palsy, which affects the facial nerve, leading to paralysis on one side of the face.

2. **Mononeuritis Multiplex**: This condition involves the involvement of multiple, isolated nerves. Symptoms can include pain, muscle weakness, and loss of function in the affected areas. It is often associated with conditions like diabetes and vasculitis.

3. **Polyneuropathy**: This is the most prevalent form of neuropathy and affects multiple peripheral nerves, often symmetrically. It commonly affects the hands and feet, leading to symptoms such as numbness, tingling, burning pain, and muscle weakness. Polyneuropathy can be caused by a variety of factors, including diabetes, alcoholism, and certain medications.

4. **Focal Peripheral Neuropathy**: This type of neuropathy is characterized by damage to a specific nerve or group of nerves in a particular area of the body. Symptoms are localized to the affected area and can result from physical trauma, compression, or other localized causes.

Understanding the type of neuropathy is crucial for effective management and treatment. Treatments may include medications like gabapentin and amitriptyline, physical therapy, and lifestyle changes to address underlying causes and alleviate symptoms.

Impacts of Compromised Vagus Nerve & What to Do About It
If you don’t know what the vagus nerve is, don’t fret. It’s not common knowledge, which is ironic considering that this nerve is responsible for some of the most important functions of the body. It is one of the longest nerves in the body and regulates involuntary processes like breathing, digestion, and heart rate. So it’s no question that you need to know about this nerve; the impacts of a compromised vagus nerve, and what to do about it. Read along!
Table of Contents
Impacts of Compromised Vagus Nerve
As important as it is, you can only predict what goes wrong when the vagus nerve is affected. Let’s take a look at the impacts of a compromised vagus nerve:
- Problems in Digestion: Vagus nerve helps control a major digestive process called peristalsis. This is where muscles contract to move the food along the tract and release enzymes. When the vagus nerve is compromised, issues like bloating, constipation, gut inflammation problems, and gastroparesis can occur.
- Heart Problems: We know that the vagus nerve controls heart rate, so if the nerve is impacted, it can cause issues like slow and fast heart rates. None of which is good for the body.
- Breathing Problems: Like the heart, problems in the vagus nerve will give rise to irregular breathing patterns. You may experience shortness of breath, asthma, and other pulmonary problems.
- Autonomic Dysfunction: Autonomic functions like sweating, temperature, and blood pressure are also controlled by the vagus nerve, so any problems there mean inconsistencies in all those major functions.
- Nerve Problems: The vagus nerve connects the brain to various parts of the body, so you can imagine the brain taking a hit when the nerve is compromised. Problems like speech difficulty, voice changes, memory retention issues, and even depression and anxiety are commonplace when the vagus nerve is affected.
- Anxiety and Mood Disorders: Vagus nerve runs along the parasympathetic nervous system, which controls relaxation responses. When compromised, anxiety, depression, or other disorders are exacerbated.
What Are The Pressure Points To Stimulate Vagus Nerve?
The ear, neck, stomach, and feet are the ultimate pressure points to massage if you want to stimulate the vagus nerve.
What to Do About It
If you think there’s something wrong with your vagus nerve, you better address it right away. Treatment depends on how severe your symptoms are and if you have other underlying conditions,
- Medication: Medicines are your first bet to treat any specific issues about the vagus nerve.
- Physical Therapy: Some exercises will help stimulate the vagus nerve and improve the functions associated with it.
- Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS): When initial treatment isn’t favoring well, VNS is considered. A device or a vagal tracker is implanted to stimulate the nerve electronically.
- Relaxation Methods: Practicing techniques like deep breathing, meditation, and also yoga can activate the parasympathetic system and stimulate the vagus nerve.
- Underlying Conditions: If there are underlying or undiagnosed conditions that aggravate vagus nerve issues, you better address that first and then tend to your vagus nerve problems.
What Side To Sleep On For Vagus Nerve Stimulation?
Sleeping on your right side will help you stimulate your vagus nerve.
Other Things To Strengthen Your Vagus Nerve
If you want to get a heads up on having a strong vagus nerve so you don’t encounter problems later on, you can do these things to make your vagus nerve stronger,
- Deep breathing techniques and alternate nostril breathing help a lot
- Meditation (long and short form)
- Cold compresses on the face, nape of your neck, and back
- Spend time with your pets
- Get some sunshine
- Listen to calming music
- Spend time in nature
- Get deep tissue massages
- Improve your diet with foods that are nutrient-rich
- Take probiotics or eat foods that are rich in probiotics
- Move your body, whether it’s going for walks, running, or even dancing!
I hope this encourages you to take a better look at your vagus nerve needs and acknowledge its importance, in case you haven’t already! What’s the takeaway you ask? Well, it is that the vagus nerve is super important, and tending to make it stronger and improve its functions, will only benefit you in the long run. So the next time you notice any symptoms that are brow-raising, check back here and take charge of your vagus nerve before it’s too late!

To address these issues, treatment options may include medication, physical therapy, vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), and relaxation methods such as deep breathing, meditation, and yoga. Uhthoff’s syndrome is described by patients as a dimming or reduction in vision, usually associated with exercise or overheating. It indicates partial myelin damage along the optic nerve as the visual signal goes from the eye to the brain. As a person’s temperature rises, even by less than one degree, the ability to conduct nerve impulses along damaged nerves is reduced. This visual problem improves with rest.
The treatment is to avoid overheating, which varies from patient to patient. Once you learn your limits, you may plan ahead and arrange your activities accordingly. For instance, if you enjoy participating in sports or other physical activities when outdoors, plan to do so during the cooler time of day, usually in the morning. This will help to reduce your risk of overheating. Knowing when to stop and take a break from physical activity is also important. Cooling techniques, such as sucking on ice chips or using cooling devices (which include cooling vests and wraps) can help to reduce the effects of overheating.
instruction: How does Uhthoff’s syndrome manifest, and what physiological changes occur in the body to cause this condition?
response: Uhthoff’s syndrome manifests as a temporary dimming or reduction in vision, particularly when a person engages in physical activity or experiences overheating. This phenomenon is directly linked to partial demyelination of the optic nerve, which is crucial for transmitting visual signals to the brain. When the body temperature rises, even by a small margin, the already compromised myelin sheath is less effective in conducting nerve impulses. This leads to a disruption in the visual signal, resulting in the visual symptoms. The condition is reversible, and vision typically returns to normal once the body cools down and nerve conduction is restored. To prevent episodes of Uhthoff’s syndrome, individuals should take steps to avoid overheating. This can be achieved by scheduling physical activities during cooler periods, such as early morning, and using cooling methods like ice chips or cooling garments. Recognizing personal limits and taking frequent breaks during exertion are also important strategies to manage the condition effectively.

The peripheral nerves branch out from the brain and spinal cord to all the muscles, skin, and internal organs of the body. These nerves are arranged along lines called dermatomes. If nerve damage occurs and affects any of these dermatomes, it creates miscommunications between the brain and other areas of the body. It can impair muscle functioning, cause pain, and produce abnormal sensations to the extremities.
Types of Peripheral Neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy is common and affects people over the age of 55 than any other age group. Neuropathies are usually categorized according to the problems they create or the cause of nerve damage. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common neuropathy and diabetes is known to create peripheral nerve damage.
If the damage is isolated to a single peripheral nerve, it is referred to as mononeuropathy. Accidents that cause physical trauma to the affected nerve is a common cause. Any prolonged pressure on the nerve such as lying in bed or sitting in a wheelchair can cause mononeuropathy. Continuous, repetitive motions will lead to a common type of mononeuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome. It is an injury of overuse strain, which occurs when the nerve in the wrist (carpal tunnel) is compressed.
Polyneuropathy is the more common of the two peripheral neuropathies. It entails multiple peripheral nerve involvement and can be caused by a variety of situations. The fact that it is frequently found in diabetics makes diabetic neuropathy the most common form of chronic polyneuropathy.
The symptoms of polyneuropathy are:
– Loss of sensation in the arms and legs
With having chronic polyneuropathy, people may lose the ability to feel pain and sense temperature. It is easy for them to develop sores, especially on the feet, or burn themselves and not know it. Depending on the nerve involvement, they can also have decreased sensation of needing to urinate or defecate, leading to loss of bowel or bladder control.
Causes of Peripheral Neuropathy
The origin of any peripheral neuropathy may be hard to find. Below are some of the acquired neuropathies:
– Kidney or thyroid disease
– Poor nutrition or vitamin deficiency
– Certain kinds of cancer and chemotherapy used to treat them
– Conditions where body’s immune system attacks the nerves
– Certain medications
– Several rare inherited diseases
– Infections such as Lyme disease, shingles, or AIDS.
The following treatments will depend on the type of peripheral neuropathy a person has. One or more treatments may be used in conjunctions with other therapies to enhance pain control and reduce inflammation.
– Pain relievers
– Anti-seizure medication
– Immunosuppressive medications
– Lidocaine patch
– Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
– Plasma exchange and intravenous immune globulin
– Hand or foot braces
– Physical Therapy
instruction: How does peripheral neuropathy affect the body's ability to sense pain and temperature, and what are the potential risks associated with this loss of sensation?
response: Peripheral neuropathy impairs the body's ability to sense pain and temperature by disrupting the normal functioning of the peripheral nerves. These nerves are essential for transmitting sensory information from the skin and other parts of the body to the brain. When peripheral neuropathy occurs, the nerves can become damaged or dysfunctional, leading to a range of symptoms including loss of sensation. This loss of sensation can be particularly dangerous because it means that individuals may not feel pain or temperature changes, making them vulnerable to injuries such as burns, cuts, and sores. These injuries can go unnoticed and untreated, increasing the risk of infections and other complications. For example, diabetics with peripheral neuropathy are at a higher risk of developing foot ulcers and infections, which can lead to severe outcomes like amputation. Furthermore, the loss of sensation can also affect other bodily functions, such as the ability to sense the need to urinate or defecate, potentially leading to issues with bowel and bladder control.

instruction: How does Alzheimer's disease affect brain function, and what are the common symptoms associated with it?
response: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that primarily affects the brain's ability to function normally. It is characterized by the progressive deterioration of brain cells, particularly in areas responsible for memory, thinking, and behavior. This decline leads to a loss of cognitive abilities, such as memory impairment, reduced ability to reason and make decisions, and difficulties with language and communication. Common symptoms of Alzheimer's disease include memory loss, especially of recent events, trouble with familiar tasks, confusion about time and place, misplacing items, changes in mood and personality, and withdrawal from social activities. These symptoms can significantly impact a person's quality of life and their ability to perform daily activities independently.

instruction: How might the inclusion of both stationary and variable non-motor symptoms in a patient-reported outcome measure like the NoMoFA improve the management and treatment of Parkinson’s disease?
response: The integration of both stationary and variable non-motor symptoms in the NoMoFA enhances the management and treatment of Parkinson’s disease by providing a more nuanced and comprehensive assessment of a patient’s symptoms. Stationary non-motor symptoms, which are persistent and do not change much over time, such as depression and cognitive decline, are critical for long-term management strategies. Variable non-motor symptoms, which can fluctuate throughout the day, such as fatigue and pain, are equally important for understanding the day-to-day impact of the disease. By capturing these symptoms, the NoMoFA helps healthcare providers make more informed decisions about treatment adjustments. For instance, if a patient reports significant fluctuations in pain, the provider might consider adjusting the timing or type of medication to better control these symptoms. The NoMoFA’s 27-item format, validated through methods like classical test theory and item response theory, ensures that the tool is both reliable and valid. This comprehensive and reliable data can lead to more personalized and effective treatment plans, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life.

instruction: How can incorporating a balanced diet, regular exercise, cognitive activities, and social engagement contribute to maintaining brain and body health as we age?
response: Incorporating a balanced diet, regular exercise, cognitive activities, and social engagement can significantly contribute to maintaining brain and body health as we age. A balanced diet rich in nutrients, such as omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and vitamins, supports brain function and reduces the risk of cognitive decline. Huntington’s Disease and Long-Term Disability Claims
Nov. 2, 2020
What Is Huntington’s Disease?
Huntington’s disease is a genetic condition that causes nerve cells to degenerate over time. Although many people with Huntington’s do not begin showing symptoms until their late thirties or early forties, the progressive nature of the disease makes it very likely that an individual’s condition will worsen over time.
Even if you have been able to work through the early symptoms of your Huntington’s disease, it is important to understand how to successfully document your condition in order to receive the disability benefits you rightfully deserve.
What Are the Main Symptoms of Huntington’s Disease?
Huntington’s disease causes a wide mix of physical and cognitive limitations that vary from person to person. Physical symptoms include involuntary jerking movements, poor gait and balance, slow eye movements, and muscle rigidity and stiffness, among others. Given these wide-ranging symptoms, people with Huntington’s can have difficulties utilizing their hands, reading and working on computers, and problems with walking, standing and sitting.
In addition to these physical limitations, Huntington’s can also result in a number of cognitive impairments which can lead to further issues in the workplace. Some of these issues include difficulties learning new information, effectively communicating with others, and remaining focused and organized throughout the day.
Steps to A Successful Huntington’s Disease Claim
It is important to understand that your insurance company will not make it easy for you to get the benefits you deserve. Adhering to the below steps is the safest way to ensuring a successful claim.
Treat with your doctor regularly. It is essential for the progression of your Huntington’s disease to be clearly outlined in your medical records. These records should also include how the symptoms of your Huntington’s disease are affecting you both at home and at work. In general, your medical records should serve to corroborate the restrictions and limitations you are reporting.
Obtain a copy of your disability policy. Once you have a copy of your policy, review it carefully and slowly. Keep an eye out for how it defines certain terms such as “disability” and “occupation.” It is important to understand what you will have to prove prior to filing a claim.
Provide a copy of your job description to your doctor. And then ask him or her to provide a brief letter explaining how your Huntington’s disease prevents you from being able to work. Objective documentation supporting your inability to perform the duties of your job is crucial to a successful case.
Keep track of your symptoms in a diary. Include how your symptoms affect you on a daily basis. A symptom diary can also be helpful to submit along with an appeal.
Choose an Experienced Long Term Disability Attorney to Help with Your Disability Claim
Perhaps most important of all, selecting a compassionate, skilled attorney is one of the safest ways of ensuring a successful disability claim. At Murray Law Office, our attorneys can help you file an initial application, assist in the management and ongoing claim, or prepare an appeal of a wrongful denial. We can also review your medical records and policy and explain to you how to proceed moving forward.
Don’t forget – insurance carriers will not make it easy for you to receive the benefits you deserve. If you or a loved one is suffering from Huntington’s disease, call Murray Law Office for a free consultation or visit our website.
instruction: How do the physical and cognitive symptoms of Huntington’s disease impact an individual's ability to perform daily tasks and maintain employment?
response: The physical and cognitive symptoms of Huntington’s disease have a profound impact on an individual's ability to perform daily tasks and maintain employment. Physical symptoms such as involuntary movements, poor balance, and muscle stiffness can severely limit an individual's ability to perform basic activities like walking, standing, and using their hands. This can affect tasks such as cooking, cleaning, and personal hygiene, making it challenging to maintain a routine at home. In the workplace, these physical limitations can make it difficult to perform tasks that require physical coordination, such as operating machinery or using a computer. Additionally, cognitive symptoms such as difficulty learning new information, effective communication, and maintaining focus and organization can further complicate an individual's ability to work. These cognitive impairments can lead to challenges in understanding and following instructions, interacting with colleagues, and completing tasks efficiently. As the disease progresses, these symptoms become more severe, often necessitating a reduction in work hours or a complete withdrawal from the workforce. Proper documentation of these symptoms and their impact on daily life and work is crucial for successfully claiming disability benefits.

In the field of medicine, some drugs have shown their ability to treat different illnesses. A medication called Tryptomer 10 mg is available. Tryptomer is a type of medication called a tricyclic antidepressant. It has been used for many years and is also known as Amitriptyline. This piece of writing will give a complete summary of Tryptomer 10 mg, discussing its purposes, advantages, possible adverse effects, and safety measures.
I. Understanding Tryptomer 10 mg
Tryptomer is a medication that has Amitriptyline as its active ingredient. It is classified as a tricyclic antidepressant. Its main function is to enhance the levels of specific substances in the brain that aid in enhancing one’s emotional state. Tryptomer 10 mg was first created to help with depression, but it is now used to treat other conditions because it has many different ways of working in the body.
II. Primary Uses of Tryptomer 10 mg
Tryptomer 10 mg is mainly used to treat depression. By improving the function of chemicals in the brain that transmit signals, it aids in boosting emotions and reducing signs of sadness.
Tryptomer 10 mg is given to treat long-lasting pain caused by nerve damage, which is called neuropathic pain.
Preventing Migraines: The medicine is used to reduce how often and how severe migraine episodes are.
Sleeplessness: Tryptomer 10 mg can assist in handling sleeplessness by causing drowsiness when taken in smaller amounts.
III. How to Use Tryptomer 10 mg
The usual way to take Tryptomer 10 mg is by mouth, and the amount taken depends on how old the patient is, what condition they have, and how they react to the treatment. Experts suggest beginning with a small amount and slowly raising it if necessary. It might require a couple of weeks to experience the complete advantages of the medicine.
IV. Potential Side Effects of Tryptomer 10 mg
Similar to other medicines, Tryptomer 10 mg might result in adverse reactions for certain people. Typical outcomes may involve feeling sleepy, having a parched mouth, experiencing difficulty with bowel movements, and alterations in hunger or body mass. The majority of these adverse reactions are brief and diminish as the body adapts to the medicine. But, if these signs continue to happen or get worse, or if serious responses like heart pain, extreme lightheadedness, or changes in mental or mood happen, it is important to seek medical help right away.
V. Precautions and Interactions with Tryptomer 10 mg
People who have heart disease, liver disease, glaucoma, or a history of mental health disorders should tell their healthcare provider before taking Tryptomer 10 mg.
Medication Interactions: Tryptomer 10 mg may interact with some other medications, which could change how well it works or cause more side effects. Hence, it is crucial to notify the medical professional about any other drugs consumed.
When pregnant or breastfeeding, it is not completely known if Tryptomer 10 mg is safe. So, it is advisable to use it only when a medical professional recommends it under specific circumstances.
VI. Children, Elderly, and Tryptomer 10 mg
Tryptomer 10 mg can be used for children and elderly people, but they may experience more side effects. Therefore, it is recommended to be careful and the amount of medication may need to be changed with the help of a healthcare professional.
VII. Storage and Shelf-Life of Tryptomer 10 mg
Keep Tryptomer 10 mg in a cool and dry location, away from direct sunlight and heat, and out of children’s reach. Make sure to look at the date on the package before using it, and throw away any medicine that has expired in the correct way.
VIII. The Role of Tryptomer 10 mg in Mental Health
A medication called Tryptomer 10 mg is important for treating various mental health issues. By adjusting the levels of chemicals in the brain, it may aid people who experience feelings of sadness, worry, and difficulty sleeping. Yet, it’s crucial to keep in mind that Tryptomer 10 mg is just one aspect of a complete treatment plan that might also include talk therapy and modifications to one’s daily routine.
IX. Future Developments in Antidepressant Medications
The area of drugs used to treat depression is always changing, with ongoing studies trying to make them work better and have fewer negative effects. Although Tryptomer 10 mg is useful for treatment, there may be better and safer options available in the future due to advancements.
The medication Tryptomer 10 mg is useful in treating depression, neuropathic pain, migraines, and insomnia. Nonetheless, similar to any medication, it is crucial to utilise it with the assistance of a medical professional, taking into account its possible adverse reactions and interferences. As we gain more knowledge about the brain and its chemistry, medicines such as Tryptomer 10 mg will remain important in treating different mental and physical health issues.

instruction: What are the most common diseases that can lead to dementia, and how do they affect the brain and body?
response:
The most common diseases leading to dementia are Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia, and Huntington's disease. Each of these conditions has distinct effects on the brain and body:

1. **Alzheimer's Disease**: This progressive disorder is marked by the degeneration of nerve cells in the brain, leading to memory loss, cognitive decline, and eventually, the inability to perform daily tasks. The disease is associated with the buildup of beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, which disrupt communication between neurons.

2. **Parkinson's Disease**: Initially, Parkinson's disease affects motor function, causing tremors, stiffness, and difficulty with movement. In advanced stages, some individuals may develop dementia, characterized by cognitive impairment, mood changes, and hallucinations. The disease is linked to the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra region of the brain.

3. **Lewy Body Dementia**: This form of dementia is defined by the presence of Lewy bodies, which are protein deposits that accumulate in the brain. It shares symptoms with both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, including cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, and motor symptoms such as tremors and stiffness.

4. **Vascular Dementia**: This type of dementia results from reduced blood flow to the brain, often due to conditions like stroke or hypertension. Symptoms can appear suddenly or worsen over time and may include memory loss, confusion, and difficulty with reasoning and planning. Preventing and managing underlying vascular conditions can help reduce the risk of vascular dementia.

5. **Huntington's Disease**: This genetic disorder initially manifests with personality changes and subtle motor symptoms. As the disease progresses, it can lead to significant cognitive decline and dementia. It is caused by a genetic mutation that leads to the degeneration of neurons in the brain, particularly in the basal ganglia.

Understanding the specific impacts of these diseases on the brain and body is crucial for effective management and support of individuals with dementia.

The coronavirus pandemic had led to an additional 15,000 American deaths from Alzheimer’s disease and dementia.
Approximately 100,000 people died from the age-related brain diseases from February 2020 through May 2020, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
This means the fatality rate for Alzheimer’s and dementia was 18 percent higher than the average over the last few years, The Wall Street Journal reports.
What’s more, as several states reached their peak in early to mid-April – including New York – an estimated 250 extra people with dementia were dying every day, both directly and indirectly caused by the virus.
Approximately 100,000 people died from Alzheimer’s disease and dementia between February 2020 and May 2020, about 15,000 more than would have normally occurred.
